#3525. Sega’s Most Influential Platformer Deserves Its Big Remake Moment Next

With The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and even Star Fox recently proving there is still an appetite for remakes done right, other game publishers are likely looking at their backlogs for inspiration. Sega, no stranger to fantastic franchises, suddenly finds itself once more in an enviable position. It has a bunch of great old games ripe for revival, and several of them seem capable of making a mark again.

One franchise that deserves to make its triumphant return celebrates its 25th anniversary this month. After its arcade launch earlier that year, Super Monkey Ball arrived as a GameCube launch game in November 2001. With proper care, that simple but effective game could thrive in 2026, even though recent entries in the series haven’t made quite the same splash.

Super Monkey Ball’s main event lets players choose one out of four monkeys. The simian is then enclosed in a ball that resembles the capsules we used to collect from toy machines at the supermarket as children. From there, they roll toward goal posts on floating platforms, collecting bananas along the way to improve their score. If they fall off the platform or run out of time before reaching their destination, they lose a life.

In the traditional sense of the term, Super Monkey Ball isn’t a platformer. There’s no sign of Mario, for instance, and jumping isn’t a central mechanic. But there are platforms and pits, so the label fits in a more general sense.

When Super Monkey Ball debuted, it reminded me immediately of an old NES favorite of mine, Marble Madness. But that pioneering older game could be completed in five minutes. There were only a few stages, all of them far too short for my liking. I wanted more of that sort of experience, which Super Monkey Ball delivered. There are dozens of stages. Most of them are smaller than the typical Marble Madness level, but they’re similarly compelling, and their quantity makes up for their brevity.

At the start of Super Monkey Ball, rolling through the goal tape is easy enough. Even by the end of that first set of courses, however, the process grows tense. Then there are 30 more courses of more difficult vintage to tackle, and an even larger and more demanding batch after that.

As they advance, players control not the monkeys themselves but the platforms they occupy. Mastery requires the player to tilt each board, which in turn allows the balls to build up enough speed to launch from small bumps in order to clear gaps, or to negotiate rougher terrain, all without moving so quickly that it becomes impossible to proceed along razor-thin beams that span wide gaps.

A full-fledged remake of that original game could add visual polish. It might also double down on the personality of the starring characters, who make irresistible mascots. AiAi even drove a cart in 2012’s Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed, besides starring in various Super Monkey Ball sequels. The included party games and competitive play, which feature attractions such as launching balls toward distant targets, could provide satisfying online play with friends or strangers, especially if they were expanded with additional content.

Sega certainly hasn’t forgotten about Super Monkey Ball. In fact, Super Monkey Ball Triple Pack, a physical-only bundle for Nintendo Switch, will be released on Nov. 10. That compilation is welcome, gathering several recent installments in the series, like Banana Rumble. It also includes Banana Mania, which remastered the stages from the original GameCube releases. But none of those modern installments have managed to have quite the impact that the original one once did, and might again if it were to receive an ambitious remake like Nintendo produced with Ocarina of Time. The main question now is whether Sega has the desire to make it happen.

#3524. Gene Roddenberry Wrote An Unmade Pilot For A Non-Sci-Fi Show About A Classic Hero

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

In David Alexander's book "Star Trek Creator: The Authorized Biography of Gene Roddenberry," it was revealed that back in 1967, Roddenberry wrote a pilot episode for a Robin Hood TV series called — what else? — "Robin Hood."

1967 was when the second season of "Star Trek" was airing, and it's worth remembering that the show wasn't a crackerjack hit at the time. "Star Trek" didn't find mass audiences until after it had been canceled in 1969 and began appearing regularly in syndication. As such, Roddenberry was likely working on other projects constantly, not necessarily putting all his eggs in the USS Enterprise, so to speak. We've actually ranked all of Gene Roddenberry's non-"Star Trek" projects, from the military drama "A.P.O. 923" to posthumous projects like "Earth: Final Conflict" and "Andromeda." Roddenberry is known today as the "Star Trek" guy, but back in the '60s, he was eager to explore many different kinds of shows and genres.

Little is known about his "Robin Hood" pilot, although Alexander's biography does contain a letter that Roddenberry wrote to "a friend" about the script he was working on. Roddenberry wanted to make a revisionist version of Robin Hood, adding a modern edge to the character. He wanted to rid Robin Hood of his traditional corniness and fresh-faced heroism, as one might see in Michael Curtiz's legendary 1938 feature film "The Adventures of Robin Hood." Several decades after Curtiz's movie, Roddenberry wanted to make an updated Robin Hood wherein he was meant to be something of an antihero.

The writer was seemingly taking the "dark and gritty" path, decades before that became trendy in Hollywood. As for things like casting, direction, and individual stories, we can only speculate.

In the letter mentioned above, Gene Roddenberry was clearly still hammering out his "Robin Hood" script, and was asking for some input. He wrote:

"By a strange coincidence, your letter came at a time in which I was preparing a pilot in the 'Robin Hood' area, and was at the moment wrestling with the problem of hero and antihero. I realized that Robin Hood could not succeed in today's market if he were the wimpy 'St. George and England!'-type hero and yet how far could I go in the other direction without completely destroying the value of the legendary figure? I think I have the problem solved, but it would be fun if you were here so I could sit down over coffee and discuss the questions involved."

These seem like the kinds of questions that many makers of modern reboots might ask themselves, as we live in an entertainment marketplace that is lousy with pop figures that are many decades old. Superman and Batman, both created in the 1930s, are still being refreshed and rebooted to this day, for instance. Heck, even "Star Trek" itself, now 60 years old, is also constantly undergoing changes and reboots, with the most recent season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" coming out in 2026.

Sadly, the above passage seems to be all the information the world has about Gene Roddenberry's "Robin Hood." The script is not readily available online (as far as I was able to find), and there are seemingly no outlines or treatments around, either.

"Star Trek" and Robin Hood did eventually cross over, albeit in an oblique way, and it happened early enough in "Star Trek" history that Gene Roddenberry was able to see it before his death in October of 1991.

In the "Star Trek: The Next Generation" episode "QPid," the impish trickster deity Q (John de Lancie) witnesses that Captain Picard (Patrick Stewart) is experiencing a pinched relationship with Vash (Jennifer Hetrick), a woman he hooked up with on his last vacation. To give Picard an opportunity to express some old-fashioned chivalry, Q magically teleports Picard and his senior staff into a living, breathing version of Sherwood Forest, with Picard playing the role of Robin Hood. Q becomes the Sheriff of Nottingham, and Vash becomes the imprisoned Maid Marian whom Robin Hood must rescue.

It's one of the most whimsical episodes of "Next Generation," and is often pointed to by Trekkies as an example of how silly the franchise can sometimes become. (That's a gentler way of saying that some fans have written missives with titles like "QPid is the stupidest episode in human history.") Personally, I think the humor works, as it's a good contrast with the ordinarily stern and serious "Next Generation" characters who typically endeavor to remain professional at all times. The comedy episodes of "Star Trek" are great, but the franchise can occasionally go overboard.

The script for "QPid" is credited to Ira Steven Behr and Randee Russell, so it's unlikely that Roddenberry contributed to it in any significant way. But one can hope that it was the final realization of Roddenberry's Robin Hood fantasies that begun 24 years earlier.

#3523. Sarah Michelle Gellar Passed On A Martin Scorsese Movie Because Of Buffy The Vampire Slayer

Martin Scorsese's filmography is filled with films that took decades to get off the ground. By the 21st Century, Scorsese had settled into a statesman of cinema stature, and (to the joy of cinephiles everywhere) he's cashed in decades of chits and clout to deliver passion projects like 2016's "Silence," 2019's "The Irishman," and 2002's "Gangs of New York."

The latter draws on a 1928 nonfiction book, "The Gangs of New York" by Herbert Ashbury, that tracked the history of New York's organized crime from the 19th to 20th Century. As the book and movie show, that tale is intertwined with how Irish and Italian immigrants settled in New York went from spat-upon outsiders to true Americans.

Scorsese read "The Gangs of New York" in 1970 and acquired the rights to make a movie out of it in 1979, but development took over 20 years. It's no surprise that in that time, Scorsese's plans for "Gangs of New York" evolved. The final film — set mostly in the 1860s — is an epic revenge narrative starring Leonardo DiCaprio as the fictional Amsterdam Vallon and Daniel Day-Lewis as a fictionalized version of real New York gang leader Bill the Butcher (named William Cutting in the film, but William Poole in real life).

One change close to the finish line was the casting of female lead Jenny, Amsterdam's love interest and a thief in Bill's organization. Sarah Michelle Gellar, a star thanks to her role on the then contemporary TV series "Buffy the Vampire Slayer," was considered for the part. However, her commitments to "Buffy" (which was in its fifth season when "Gangs of New York" shot from December 2000 to March 2001) meant she couldn't sign on. Jenny went on to be played by Cameron Diaz instead.

Now, Cameron Diaz wasn't Martin Scorsese's first choice understudy for Jenny. He was also interested in casting Sarah Polley, but now-disgraced producer Harvey Weinstein insisted on a bigger name. (Weinstein was the reason Scorsese made sure the film debuted as his director's cut, too.) So, Diaz, a comedy starlet after 1998's "There's Something About Mary," won the part. Her turn as Jenny has since been called one of the worst performances in any Scorsese movie.

Now, Jenny is a pretty thankless role (she's a fairly typical love interest character), but Diaz is still out of her depth. She can't keep her Irish accent down, and like Leonardo DiCaprio as Amsterdam, her wooden performance stands out all the more next to Daniel Day-Lewis' show-stopping turn as Bill the Butcher. Granted, most actors will have trouble outshining Day-Lewis (his latest film "Anemone" at least gives him a worthy scene partner in Sean Bean), but in "Gangs of New York," it's not even a competition.

That's what makes it sting to know that Sarah Michelle Gellar turned down the role. She's a great actor who carried seven seasons of "Buffy the Vampire Slayer" on her back. She might've still not stolen the show from Day-Lewis, but I feel confident saying she'd probably out-charisma DiCaprio's stilted Amsterdam and make Jenny a livelier character. Moreover, you can't help but wonder if Gellar's career could've soared even higher if she had a Scorsese movie on her resume.

But Gellar doesn't regret it. In 2023, she told The Guardian that she doesn't worry about the projects she missed out on due to her commitments to "Buffy," not even "Gangs of New York." This "Buffy" and Scorsese fan, though, is always going to feel a little differently.

#3522. How the Newly Elected Congress Can Save the Smithsonian

This is the November 6, 2026 edition of True Colors, a look inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

It’s True Colors. The Democrats have flipped the House and the Senate, which could usher in a new era of funding at the Smithsonian—or, at the very least, a vibe shift in DC. There are a ton of gallery shows opening around New York, and on the West Coast, LACMA Art+Film Gala goes down tomorrow night. We got the rare chance to sit down with one of the night’s honorees, Vija Celmins.

Mentioned in this issue: Donald Trump, Lonnie Bunch, Alma Allen, Tilman Fertitta, Yoshitomo Nara, Loïc Gouzer, Vija Celmins, Matthew Marks, Leonardo DiCaprio, Eva Chow, Denis Villeneuve, Gary Hume, Jacqueline Tran, Michael Govan, Katherine Ross, James Turrell, Riko Mizuno, Matthew Barney, Roni Horn, Meshell Ndegeocello, Steve McQueen, Matthieu Blazy, Rosemarie Trockel, Carrie Mae Weems, Marina Abramović, Wade Guyton, Christopher Wool, Rashid Johnson, Felix Rödder, Calvin Marcus, James Ensor.

Trump has spent the last two years attacking Washington’s cultural hub with executive orders and legally dubious firings issued via fiat. But the Smithsonian gets its funding through Congress—what if Congress actually acted on that authority?

Sure, Congress has more pressing issues to address once the deeply blue House and Senate get sworn in early next year. But here at True Colors I think it’s fair to ask the question: Will lawmakers wind back the years of impact the Trump administration has had on the Smithsonian Institution?

Although Congress has authority over the cultural behemoth, the White House has in just the last two years issued executive orders, been extremely hands-on in its public signage, and mounted pressure campaigns to fire directors and censor artworks. Congress could have stopped all of this, but didn't. Republicans naturally didn’t want to cross Trump and support the beleaguered arts mecca. But Democrats have every reason to—after the new Congress is sworn in they’ll have the power to appropriate massive amounts of funding to each Smithsonian museum—or even create new museums. Plus, that can impact how the whole institution is run on a day-to-day basis, as Congress has the power to shake up the Smithsonian’s board of regents. That governing body will choose the next Smithsonian secretary, after Lonnie Bunch resigned earlier this year.

I’m particularly interested in who takes over as the director of the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden. Melissa Chiu, who held the position for 12 years, stepped down earlier this year to be the director of the Guggenheim Museum in New York, and rumors are swirling about who will succeed her in the post. The prospect of a culture-living Congress—and, who knows...a Democratic president come 2029?—could make the Smithsonian seem like a swell place to be long term.

Add in the prospect of a new crop of congressional staffers and the attendant cottage industries of consultants and lobbyists all flocking to Washington, and I could see the Hirshhorn getting caught up in the vibe shift, pronto. There’s expected to be a sea change of DC residents in town, and there’s every reason to believe they’ll make the (free! always free!) contemporary art museum a constant stop on the rotation. Plus, the long-gestating renovation of the Sculpture Garden literally just opened this past weekend. I don’t have any inside intel on who’s in the running for the job —but it’s looking like a pretty great gig these days.

Read True Colors: Inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

Meanwhile, the artworks that filled the American Pavilion at the Venice Biennale, made by State Department–tapped artist Alma Allen, might be stuck in Italy for the foreseeable future. Funding has run out, and there’s nothing in the budget for moving the works. I wonder how that can be resolved. Seems like a job for an art-loving, restaurant-owning Italian ambassador, Tilman Fertitta!

The massive two-location Yoshitomo Nara show opened at David Zwirner last night, truly one of the great gallery moments here in New York this season. Don’t miss the pop-up one-painting exhibition of Nara’s In the Milky Lake / Thinking One, which will be sold by Loïc Gouzer’s one-lot auction business, Fair Warning. It’s on view at 534 W. 22nd Street. The lot opens for live bidding November 19 and is expected to sell for the eye-popping sum of $10 million to $15 million.

You can also see Nara’s work in Washington, DC, where the aforementioned Hirshhorn just opened a grand survey of the artist timed to the inauguration of its sculpture garden. And if you want to check out some of Nara’s artworks in a very unexpected place, head to the Avenue A dive bar Niagara, where Nara drunkenly created a masterwork on the walls late one night after an opening at Pace. The bar wisely conserved the artwork behind glass, and it remains there nearly two decades later.

It’s not usually worth reporting on the toasts given at gala dinners here in the prized real estate that is this newspaper’s Table Hopping section, but the Dia Fall Night had some good honorary toast content! On Monday, Matthew Barney proved himself to be a very deep Roni Horn fan with his toast. Then Meshell Ndegeocello went super outside the box, honoring Steve McQueen by stepping in front of the podium and leading a band around the gala. The whole evening was like that. Chanel wasn’t just a sponsor—the brand’s creative director Matthieu Blazy, a true contemporary art head, chaired the whole thing alongside artists Rosemarie Trockel and Carrie Mae Weems. Marina Abramović was at my table; she told me she reads Vanity Fair every time she’s on a plane and appreciates how thick the issues have been lately. Marina, it’s an honor. Thank you for reading.

Matthew Marks hosted a party on Wednesday night for Wade Guyton’s excellent new show at Bridges, the best restaurant on Chatham Square. Fun fact: Christopher Wool’s old studio was right next to the restaurant some decades back.

On Election Day, as the results started coming in, Rashid Johnson opened a show of new work at Hauser & Wirth’s Wooster Street gallery, which has recently become my favorite of the mega-gallery’s dozen or so global outposts. It’s a throwback of sorts, a small space in the neighborhood that was once the city’s gallery nexus, with an excellent track record of great shows. The dinner was at the gallery’s restaurant, Manuela, right around the corner on Prince Street. There was caviar, and while it was served to celebrate Johnson, it happened to come out right as the news networks indicated the Democrats were going to flip a Senate seat in South Carolina. Spirits were high.

If you’re making your way to The Met to see “Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous,” do stop by Rodder, the gallery founded by Felix Rödder, to see one of the most inspired artist pairings in the city right now. Calvin Marcus, the fanatically talented and free-wheeling Los Angeles painter, has new and recent paintings, drawings, and ceramics installed alongside work by the great Belgian weirdo James Ensor. The chemistry between these two artists from different centuries and continents is uncanny. The dinner for the show was held somewhere unusual: House of the Redeemer, the Episcopalian Church in a former Italian Renaissance Revival townhouse once owned by a Vanderbilt heiress.

#3521. These Sony ANC Headphones Are on Sale for $128 Right Now

It's hard to convince yourself to spend nearly half a grand on premium headphones, like the Sony WH-1000XM6, even if you consider yourself an audiophile. Not everyone can afford those prices, which is why the budget, mid-tier, and premium tiers exist. While the premium 1000XM6 headphones are over three times the price of the mid-tier Sony WH-CH730N, they're not three times as good. The Sony WH-CH730N are $128 (originally $179) right now, the lowest price they've ever been according to price-tracking tools, and they offer an amazing value for your money.

It's pretty impressive what $128 in headphones gets you in 2026. The CH730N uses the same Sony Connect app as the premium headphones; as a result, you get a 10-band slider on the EQ menu, a battery care feature that extends the longevity of your battery life, 50 hours of juice, ANC, Ambient Sound (transparency mode), Multipoint to connect to two devices at once, and Bluetooth 6.0. The Adaptive Sound Control feature can detect your activity (walking, sitting down, loud environment, etc.) and automatically switch the level of ANC and transparency to make your experience as comfortable and seamless as possible.

The microphones are decent and use a feature to isolate your voice in noisy environments. I love that there's an AUX connection to give you the option, which seems to be coming back with newer headphones. The design is light and will feel like plastic, but they are comfortable to wear for long sessions. If you're looking to maximize the quality of headphones you can get for your money, the Sony WH-CH730N offer a pretty compelling option at $128.

#3520. All 4 Cillian Murphy Performances In Christopher Nolan Movies, Ranked

Like many filmmakers, Christopher Nolan often works with the same actors across different projects. Sir Michael Caine has appeared in eight Nolan films total. In second place, with room to eventually become no. 1 given Caine's retirement, is Cillian Murphy.

Murphy has acted in six films directed by Nolan, in chronological order: "Batman Begins," "The Dark Knight," "Inception," "The Dark Knight Rises," "Dunkirk," and their shared magnum opus "Oppenheimer." This prosperous creative relationship all started when Murphy auditioned to play Bruce Wayne in "Batman Begins." The two recall that they both knew Murphy wasn't the right pick for the Dark Knight, but Murphy's acting impressed Nolan enough that he fought, and won, to cast Murphy instead as one of the movie's villains: Doctor Jonathan Crane, the Scarecrow.

Since then, Nolan has always known just the right way to use Murphy, to the point you could call the actor his secret weapon. Until "Oppenheimer," Murphy had never played the lead in a Nolan movie, but the director always cast him in important supporting roles (ones that needed the right actor or the whole film around them would suffer). With "Oppenheimer," Murphy carried the entire movie on his back, and his previous Nolan film performances show why he had earned the trust needed for that casting.

Even Cillian Murphy's smallest role in a Christopher Nolan movie still has meat on the bones. Nolan's World War II film "Dunkirk" depicts the 1940 evacuation of British troops from the eponymous French shoreline. Murphy plays one of those thousands of troops, specifically one whose boat gets destroyed by a German U-Boat. He's rescued by a civilian ship volunteering as a rescue boat, but taking that ride means sailing back into the carnage he just escaped.

Murphy's character doesn't even have a name, being known only as "the Shivering Soldier." Pulled from the cold water by Mr. Dawson (Mark Rylance) and boys Peter (Tom Glynn-Carney) and George (Barry Keoghan), he indeed shivers, wrapping himself in a blanket onboard. The soldier already counts himself one of the lucky ones for surviving, and he refuses to let the ship continue heading towards Dunkirk, which he believes is certain death.

With the terrifying scene the movie paints of the battle, it's hard to dismiss the soldier's fears. Peter asks if the soldier is a coward, but Mr. Dawson counters he's only shell-shocked. Murphy can pull off a thousand-yard stare like few other actors can (something he'd again do to great effect in "Oppenheimer"). That silent and haunted quality he can project makes him perfect for this part: A man who stared death in the face while watching it work all around him ... and is now being asked to do so again after getting no time to recover.

Cillian Murphy's Scarecrow is the only villain to appear in all three of the "Dark Knight Trilogy" films. During "Batman Begins," Jonathan Crane, reimagined as the head of Arkham Asylum, is in bed with both the mob and the League of Shadows, who plot to destroy Gotham City with Crane's fear toxin. Crane then returns for cameos in "The Dark Knight," being captured by Batman (Christian Bale), and "The Dark Knight Rises," serving as a judge in Bane's (Tom Hardy) kangaroo court.

Murphy is relishing playing a super-villain without ever going into pure camp territory. Though Dr. Crane admittedly isn't physically imposing, his frosty blue-eyed gaze still makes him look like a guy who can and would kill you. He's even the first villain to get one over on Batman, dosing the Dark Knight with his fear toxin and setting him on fire. Crane does the last part with a cruel quip befitting his psychologist background: "You look like a man who takes himself too seriously. Do you want my opinion? You need to lighten up."

Crane is both a sadist and a psychologist obsessed with studying the effects of fear. He relishes putting people on edge, particularly pesky crusading lawyer Rachel Dawes (Katie Holmes). But Murphy's best Scarecrow scene is definitely when he pulls rank on imprisoned mob boss Carmine Falcone (Tom Wilkinson). Murphy completely changes the tenor of the scene with Crane's line: "Would you like to see my mask?" It instantly shows Crane is not some mere corrupt bureaucrat.

Scarecrow always shows a catty sense of humor, too. So, it's fitting that his last scene in the trilogy is sentencing Jim Gordon (Gary Oldman), and others who refuse to choose between "death or exile," to "death — by exile."

In between "Dark Knight" movies, Christopher Nolan and Cillian Murphy made a little film you might've heard of called "Inception." It's a heist/con movie, but it's set inside a dreamscape. Murphy plays the dreamer and the crew's mark: Robert Fischer, the heir to an oil empire reeling from the death of his disapproving father (Pete Postlethwaite). Dominic Cobb (Leonardo DiCaprio) and his crew are hired by Fischer's rival, Mr. Saito (Ken Watanabe), to plant an idea inside his head that'll make him resolve to break up his father's empire instead of inheriting it.

Speaking to Irish Central in 2010, Murphy mentioned he researched the sons of Rupert Murdoch to understand how being raised in a titan of industry's shadow would shape someone (and this was well before "Succession" gave us a Murdoch roman à clef). Murphy added that he played Fischer as "a petulant child who's in need of a lot of attention from his father." But while "Inception" is all about tricking Fischer, the movie isn't unsympathetic to him.

"Inception" is widely read as an allegory for filmmaking itself. Fischer is the audience, the one who needs to be deceived by the craft and illusion, to believe that something is real in their gut even when their brain knows it isn't. The entire movie hinges on the titular inception, where Fischer sees an illusion of his father on his deathbed and gets what life denied him: reassurance that his dad did care about him. And just as the inception has to convince Fischer, Murphy has to convince us of the emotional sincerity. An overwhelmed Fischer tears up, and as his face crumbles, it's hard not to get a lump in your own throat. It's extra painful since it's all a falsehood.

"Oppenheimer" cleaned house at the 96th Oscars, including Cillian Murphy winning Best Actor for playing the father of the atomic bomb — or, as Oppenheimer infamously called himself later in life, "death, destroyer of worlds."

On the surface, it's a transformative performance. Murphy lost weight to better capture the gaunt Oppenheimer's physique, and he completely re-modulated his voice. (Murphy based his soft but deep and rhythmic baritone as Oppenheimer on a combination of Orson Welles and Fred Rogers). But despite those hallmarks of actor transformation, the kind that often feel cynically used to win an Oscar, Murphy as Oppenheimer isn't gaudy acting. No, it's more like a chameleon shifting into a new color: Murphy becomes Oppenheimer, utterly.

"Oppie" may have been eccentric, but "Oppenheimer" is much more interested in exploring how his foibles led to his downfall — and perhaps humanity's — than venerating them as the cost of his scientific know-how. Oppenheimer is willfully naive about how the bomb he's building will be used and pathologically incapable of taking too strong a stand on anything. His equivocation often only digs him deeper. Indeed, Murphy excels in scenes that show the weighty consequences of Oppenheimer's awkwardness, like when he meets with violently anticommunist Colonel Pash (Casey Affleck) or stumbles while urging U.S. President Harry Truman (Gary Oldman) to push for nuclear de-escalation.

Oppenheimer seeking absolution from Truman by talking about the "blood on [his] hands" makes it hard to disagree with Lewis Strauss' (Robert Downey Jr.) argument that Oppenheimer wanted to be both the maker of the bomb and a martyr for its destructiveness. But in Murphy's moments of silent stillness (particularly the ending when his character imagines the world's fiery end), he shows how Oppenheimer's guilt, though self-inflicted, was all too real and impossibly heavy to carry.

It’s no secret that Heated Rivalry is one of the biggest book-to-screen adaptations of recent years. The smutty, queer hockey romance stole the hearts of fans everywhere when it was released in late 2025, and its popularity hasn’t wavered at all. Fans are only going to get more intense now that news has dropped that Hudson Williams and Connor Storrie will be suiting up for a third season as well. However, I'm concerned about one detail.

Fans of Heated Rivalry have already known about Season 2 kicking off production, as photos from the set have been leaked despite the show’s creator, Jacob Tierney, kindly asking fans to give them space while filming. The news about a third season has been highly speculated, and now, that has been confirmed as well. Both seasons are reportedly being filmed back-to-back. This theoretically means that there shouldn’t be a huge wait between seasons, and maybe fans could get all twelve episodes sometime next year.

In addition to two more seasons with Shane and Ilya, Deadline reports that Tierney is working on a standalone theatrical release that the trade believes will be a “Christmas special” or “holiday-themed episode” centered around Season 1, Episode 3 couple Scott (François Arnaud) and Kip (Robbie G.K.). It’s not the Heated Rivalry-centric bonus episode fans have been hoping for, but the holiday special could be inspired by the short holiday story author Rachel Reid penned for the couple and earlier this year took down from her official website.

As a fan of the sports drama series, I’m overjoyed at the news, but I do have one concern heading into these news seasons when it comes to what it might mean for Shane and Ilya’s relationship.

Unlike the other couples in Reid’s Game Changers book universe, Shane and Ilya’s relationship unfolds over several books. When the series was released (and subsequently renewed for a second and a secret third season), the couple’s second book, The Long Game, was the final installment in their relationship. But then Reid announced she was writing a third book, Unrivaled, centered on the fan-favorite couple.

Had Reid not made the announcement that she was writing Unrivaled, I would have confidently said that Tierney and the creative team behind Heated Rivalry planned to split The Long Game into two seasons. This would allow the show to really dig deep into Shane and Ilya’s relationship challenges and give fans a faithful adaptation like the first season did. It would also provide space for the show to explore some of the other couples in the Game Changes universe, which seems to be happening based on casting announcements for Season 2.

Splitting The Long Game into two seasons might still be the case, which is great news for fans of the novel; however, it does raise concerns about the potential for an adaptation of Unrivaled. After all, if Seasons 2 and 3 are centered on the second novel, then the show would need to be renewed for a fourth season in order to see the third book and the presumed conclusion of Shane and Ilya’s love story on screen.

Given the show’s popularity, a hypothetical fourth season seems like a no-brainer, but one also has to consider the schedules of the cast and crew. With Storrie and Williams both cast in new shows and movies, it might be hard to get them on board for another season beyond these next two. Still, I’d like to believe that the talented actors would be eager to see Ilya and Shane's storyline through to the end.

All of this is purely speculation, as we don't know much about Season 2 of Heated Rivalry other than it's expected to drop in Spring 2027. When that happens, we'll know what to expect from Season 3. Until then, I’ll be streaming, or as fans have dubbed it “reheating,” Season 1 of Heated Rivalry with my HBO Max subscription. Fans can also catch the episodes playing for a limited time in theaters in the US and Canada.

#3518. Michael Fassbender's Underrated 2015 Western Is Worth Revisiting

Lots of modern Westerns take the adventurous romance out of the genre, like director John Maclean's 2015 "Slow West." A major hit at the 2015 Sundance Film Festival, it won the World Cinema Grand Jury Prize in the Dramatic category, and then made its way into theaters (with a simultaneous video-on-demand release). More than a decade on, "Slow West" remains one of the best Westerns of this century. And you can watch it on Netflix right now — although it's leaving soon, so act fast. It's also free, with ads, on YouTube.

"Slow West" lives up to its title with a leisurely pace, but it's also a tight 84-minute movie. In 19th century Colorado, a young Scottish man named Jay Cavendish (Kodi Smit-McPhee) sets off in search of his supposed one true love, Rose (Caren Pistorius) — who left Scotland with a price on her head. Jay meets bounty hunter Silas Selleck (Michael Fassbender) by chance and Silas becomes his guide and guardian. They also run afoul of Payne (Ben Mendelsohn), leader of a gang Silas once belonged to; Payne is interested in collecting the bounty on Rose.

Smit-McPhee later appeared in the acclaimed 2021 Western "The Power of the Dog," which similarly paired him up with Benedict Cumberbatch just as "Slow West" does with him and Fassbender. In "The Power of the Dog," Smit-McPhee is a wolf in sheep's clothing, one who weaponizes his unassuming innocence. In "Slow West," that innocence is exactly what you get with Jay Cavendish. He has naive ideas about adventure and love — Rose never actually reciprocated his feelings, but he's convinced the grand gesture of tracking her down will sway her. While the frontier forces him to defend himself with a gun, it's clear throughout the film Jay isn't built for the gunslinging life.

Jay's origins as a Scotsman traveling through America in "Slow West" are almost autobiographical for John Maclean, who is from Scotland himself. (Notably, while the parts of the film set in America were filmed in New Zealand, flashbacks to Scotland were filmed in the real country.) Speaking to the International Business Times in 2015, Maclean said how, when he first decided to write a Western, one of the first "seeds" of the story for him was to depict a frontier filled with European immigrants moving west. Jay and Rose are Scottish, Michael Fassbender uses his Irish accent to play Silas, and (without spoilers) Jay and Silas meet a Swedish family during their travels.

Unlike Jay, a newcomer to America, Maclean had seen plenty of America before making "Slow West" — which was what drew him to the Western: "After college [a few friends and I] took cars through America delivering them. So, I did a lot of traveling in America. That probably led to me wanting to do a Western."

"Slow West" was McLean's first feature film; before that, he'd been a musician and part of a group called The Beta Band, where he played keyboards and directed music videos. According to Maclean, Fassbender agreed to act in his short films because he'd been a fan of those Beta Band videos.

"He was shooting ['Inglourious Basterds'] at the time, so the fact that he even offered his services was a great thing," said Maclean to the BBC. Considering that creative partnership led to "Slow West," one of Michael Fassbender's best movies, the actor's judgment was sound.

#3517. How Elizabeth Taylor’s Childhood and Career Were Defined by Her Overbearing Mother

Elizabeth Taylor, like many other actors of her time, experienced the demands of Hollywood from a very young age. Her parents could never have imagined on February 27, 1932, just how much their newborn baby would achieve artistically. Sooner rather than later, however, they recognized her potential. Although she spent most of her life in Southern California in the heart of the movie industry, Taylor was born in Hampstead, England, to an American family consisting of her father, Francis Lenn Taylor, her mother, Sara Sothern, and their son, Howard, the movie star’s brother with whom she was close. They didn’t remain in Great Britain long, returning to the United States in 1939, shortly before World War II.

Sara Sothern with her children, Elizabeth and Howard Taylor.

The family sailed from London to New York and then settled in Los Angeles. By then, Taylor already had some experience in the performing arts, as she had been taking ballet lessons since she was just three years old. She made her debut in a recital that same year. Once in California, the father of the violet-eyed legend opened an art gallery featuring works imported from the UK. This would turn out to be an important step that brought the Taylors into the world of Hollywood. As biographer Alexander Walker would recount in Elizabeth: The Life of Elizabeth Taylor (Grove Press), the space “opened many doors for the Taylors, leading them directly into the society of money and prestige.”

Despite their differences, mother and daughter grew closer as they matured.

Sothern, the mother of this acting prodigy, saw her daughter as the perfect excuse to live the dream she didn’t fulfill because she was focused on caring for her family. If she couldn’t pursue an acting career, her daughter would. Seeing the effect that Taylor’s beauty had on others, Sothern set out to introduce her to people in the film industry. “Elizabeth Taylor probably wouldn’t have been an actress if it hadn’t been for her mother,” notes actor George Hamilton in the BBC documentary Elizabeth Taylor: Rebel Superstar. In this same documentary, Liz herself can be heard saying in an old recording: “My mother was an actress, but then she married my father, and he didn’t want her to be one, so she gave it up. I think she lived her life through me.”

Kate Andersen Brower, author of Elizabeth Taylor: The Grit and Glamour of an Icon (Harper Collins), explains that Sothern was behind the scenes trying to control every aspect of her daughter’s life in order to make her famous. This included sending Taylor to the same schools as the children of movie studio executives. Soon, thanks to a meeting with the fiancée of a high-ranking Universal Pictures exec who visited the gallery run by Taylor’s father, Elizabeth made her big-screen debut. Her early Hollywood years were propelled by connections her mother painstakingly built.

In 1949, Elizabeth Taylor and Sara Sothern pose at their home in Beverly Hills.

Taylor’s first movie was There’s One Born Every Minute, filmed when she was only 10 years old. Also starring Carl Switzer, who played Alfalfa in Our Gang, it was not a success, and Universal chose not to extend her option. Andersen Brower quotes the studio’s casting director: “The kid has nothing. Her eyes are too old; she doesn’t have the face of a kid.” Sara persisted, however, and through her husband, she met Sam Marx, a producer working on an MGM film, Lassie Come Home. Taylor would be cast in a small role.

Elizabeth Taylor and her mother in a 1948 photo taken in London.

Its success paved the way for another milestone in Taylor’s early career. At age 12, she landed the role of Velvet Brown in National Velvet, alongside Mickey Rooney and Angela Lansbury. Released in December 1944, it grossed almost $6 million worldwide, making it one of MGM’s top films of that period. Taylor signed a new contract with the studio, though she later complained about how she was treated by its head, Louis B. Mayer.

Elizabeth Taylor helps her mother prepare hot dogs and hamburgers at their home in Los Angeles in 1947.

At the same time, her father was both astonished by and jealous of his teenage daughter’s success. An alcoholic and physically abusive, on one occasion he punched her in the jaw, and for the rest of her life, she suffered from TMJ, or lockjaw. Andersen Brower writes, “She explained it away—as she always had—saying that her father was embarrassed that Taylor was the breadwinner of the family and that he felt emasculated.”

Sothern was a practicing Christian (though she was also interested in Judaism, which may have contributed to Taylor’s decision to convert to that religion so that she could marry Eddie Fisher, her fourth husband), and she taught her daughter from an early age that she could not sleep with any man until she was married to him. It’s a view that Taylor appears to have adopted: “Nothing comes off until the ring goes on,” she told gossip columnist Louella Parsons. Sothern, however, had her doubts. Before Taylor married Conrad “Nicky” Hilton in 1950, when she was just 18 years old, Sothern paid a doctor to confirm that her daughter was still a virgin and also to open her hymen to spare her pain during the first time she had sex.

Years later, Taylor would admit that her early years in the film industry were not easy. Her parents spent practically all the money she earned as a child actor. In a 1997 interview with Barbara Walters on 20/20, she described her childhood as “lonely.” She once confided to her close friend George Hamilton that she just wanted “to be a little girl again,” to relive those years that she never got to enjoy.

Originally published by Vanity Fair Spain.

#3515. Zelda: Ocarina of Time and WoW: Forever Are the Good Kind of Remakes

Zelda: Ocarina of Time and World of Warcraft: Forever were made for different reasons than most remakes, and you can tell

Why are there so many video game remakes these days? We think we know the answer. New ideas are hard to come by, and big games are harder, more expensive, and take longer to make than ever before. Even a new sequel in an already-popular franchise is a huge, risky undertaking. But game companies need reliable products to put on the shelves quicker than they can make new ones. Remakes answer that need, as well as keeping back catalogs relevant for an industry whose relentless technological advances swiftly render classics obsolete.

That's all accurate. But what if the game developers working on remakes had reasons of their own for revisiting the classics — reasons that weren't just learning their way around Unreal Engine 5, plugging a gap between new releases, or answering market forces? We got an emphatic answer this week, in the form of not one but two remarkable new versions of two of the greatest and most influential games ever made. Those two games, released on consecutive days, are The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and World of Warcraft: Forever.

A few months ago, I said that we need to decide what we want from remakes. This is what we want.

Nintendo’s excellent Switch 2 remake recaptures the soul of a masterpiece

Blizzard's retro MMO is about to sail into uncharted waters, but right now, it's clearly something special

These games have some similarities in their approach to remaking a classic, and some differences. Both games make smart modernizations while working hard to retain the spirit of the original. Ocarina of Time is a faithful recreation of a masterpiece that takes few liberties with its content and design, but makes a forceful departure in its lavish and technically dazzling art style.

WoW: Forever preserves the original WoW's art beneath a subtly impressive new rendering layer, and is built out from the same content. But it makes substantial additions, gets its hands dirty under the hood of the design, and, with its promise of a fixed progression cap and "horizontal" expansion, even seeks to boldly recontextualize WoW — and MMOs in general, and maybe even live-service games — in a new form.

In both cases, the developers have talked in interviews about their desire to preserve and carry forward something intrinsic about the games' design that they think has been lost in modern games.

Nintendo's top Legend of Zelda producers talk the remake, the future, and more

In a Nintendo "Ask the Developer" interview, Zelda producer Eiji Aonuma spoke about his desire to educate a new generation of Zelda developers who worked on Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom and weren't intimately familiar with the intricate mechanical mesh of classic Zelda design.

"By learning the game structure and development style behind the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and by actually rebuilding it as a full remake, it may trigger new insights that they can carry forward into future development," Aonuma said. "If we could achieve that, I thought it would be incredibly valuable. That’s what led us to the conclusion that now is the right time to revisit The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time once again."

It's incredible to think that Nintendo's primary motivation in mounting this expensive production might have been bolstering institutional knowledge. But that's what makes Nintendo Nintendo.

The grassroots reimagining of classic World of Warcraft seems huge, but the team wants to stay small

Meanwhile, at Bizzard, a desire to see and play a "Classic Plus" version of WoW bubbled up naturally among the developers at the same time as it did in the WoW Classic community. This makes sense, since the WoW Classic team was mostly staffed by enthusiasts of the original game. It was the small, enterprising Classic team that experimented with the idea during the Season of Discovery event and then pitched it to leadership.

Lead Forever designer Kris Zierhut, who admits to having "drifted away" from modern WoW, explained it to me as a kind of thought experiment, a chance to imagine a different path the game might have taken. "Imagine if that team from 2004 — you know, Jeff Kaplan, and Eric Dodds, and Tom Chilton, and Scott Mercer, Pat Nagle, all those people — they've given them two more years to develop the game and add more stuff to it and perfect it," he said. "What would they have done with the time?"

What Zierhut and Aonuma are articulating is not a desire to preserve these epochal game designs for posterity. It's a desire to get inside them and explore them, find out what they can teach us, and maybe point out some things we've lost to progress — like an epic adventure game that puts craft before sheer scale, or a live-service game that's about the journey and not the destination.

Both these remakes were made with sincerity, passion, and above all, purpose. You don't have to take my word for it, or the developers'; you can tell when you play them. That's why they're so exciting, and how they honor two classics while bringing them alive for a new generation of players. Don't be too quick to dismiss remakes as cynical cash-grabs and schedule fillers. They can be beautiful acts of creation in their own right.

#3514. One Of Willy Wonka's Most Memorable Scenes Was An Absolute Nightmare To Shoot

Most Gen-Xers know Mel Stuart's 1971 musical movie "Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory" by heart and will — perhaps recoiling in disgust — remember the scene where Augustus Gloop (Michael Böllner) falls into a river of chocolate. It seems that moment was equally revolting to film.

The scene in question occurs about halfway through the movie, by which point Willy Wonka (Gene Wilder) has opened the doors to his ultra-secretive chocolate factory to five sweepstakes-winning children. Wonka is a zany eccentric who seems to grow rare and exotic chocolate plants that produce fully manufactured candy. One of the first stops on the factory tour is a stroll through his candy garden, and the contest winners are allowed to feast on all the unusual edible flora their stomachs can handle. This sequence alone makes "Willy Wonka" one of the best food movies of all time.

Running through the middle of the garden is Wonka's chocolate river. He explains that a river is the best way to keep chocolate mixed, and it is the one thing that is verboten to touch. It should be noted that the chocolate river, from a production standpoint, looks more like mud or sewage than chocolate. It's watery and unappealing. Augustus, however, cannot help spooning some of the chocolate river into his mouth. He then slips and falls into the water, splashing around for a bit before being sucked into a drainage pipe.

According to Polygon's 2021 oral history of this scene, that river was as gross in person as it looked on camera. Böllner recalled having to film this moment for a long stretch, forcing him to repeatedly fall into, in his words, "stinky water." Also, it was cold. So, much less fun that actually swimming in liquid chocolate.

Michael Böllner added that he had to fall into a deep aperture under the water every time he dove into the river. The aperture, however, wasn't very large, and he repeatedly risked slamming his head into the solid river floor. As he put it:

"It was actually not chocolate. It was terribly cold. It was stinky water! And it was all day long, jumping in and jumping out, and being around with wet clothes. [...] The river was just 10 centimeters deep. And there was a hole about a square meter that I had to hit. So, I was very scared that I would not hit the square meter and would punch my head in the ground of the chocolate river."

Böllner didn't say what, exactly, the river smelled like, but its brackish, near-translucent brown might make one suspect that it was colored with paint. Julie Dawn Cole, who played the spoiled Veruca Salt in "Willy Wonka," also recalled poor Böllner's experience falling into that river all day. According to her, the water was not the least bit fresh, remaining stagnant for weeks. What's more, it seems that the film's cast and/or crew kept using it as a means of disposing of their drinks (which may very well explain the odor):

"Michael had to fall into this disgusting stuff that had been sitting there for three weeks. It had the lights on it, and people were emptying their coffee cup dregs into it."

So, Böllner had to splash into an unseen trough covered by three-week-old brown coffee water. Movie magic!

At the end of the chocolate river scene, Augustus, as mentioned, is sucked up a transparent pipe. His body blocks the pipe, though, and one can see his screaming face through the glass while chocolate pressure builds up beneath him. To film this moment, Michael Böllner had to be lowered into a tube, about six feet long in actuality, that was then filled with chocolate water. Naturally, Böllner did not enjoy this, either, explaining:

"It was a really tough thing because they took about two meters tube around me and filled it up with water up to my mouth. So, I couldn't move anything. I couldn't do anything. I just had to rely on the guys that were around me that don't drop me."

Peter Ostrum, who played Charlie Bucket, the protagonist of "Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory," also commented on the whole river scene, recalling that it looked utterly miserable. He knew the water was cold and gross, so he was merely relieved he didn't have to do the stunt himself. To quote him directly:

"When I saw Michael do take after take after take of falling in the cold river, that cold, dirty river, I just thought, 'I'm glad that's him and not me!'"

Indeed, this scene is but one of many reasons why folks of a certain age remember "Willy Wonka and the Chocolate Factory" as being delightful nightmare fuel. That and Willy Wonka is quite the twisted trickster in the film (something you can partly thank Gene Wilder himself for). As for its young stars, they all largely went on to enjoy various careers outside of acting. Luckily, none of them ever had to deal with brackish fake rivers again.

#3512. 39 Years Later, Inigo Montoya's Princess Bride Line Is Still The Greatest Movie Quote Ever

Do you love big, sweeping, epic romances where the lovers are kept apart for years, only to reunite in a scene that takes your breath away? Do you love clever, quippy, dialogue? Do you love swashbuckling adventures with a touch of vengeance? Great news. "The Princess Bride" has literally all of those things.

In 1987, writer-director Rob Reiner released "The Princess Bride," an adaptation of William Goldman's novel of the same name — and with Goldman adapting his own work into the screenplay, every second isn't just true to the book, but elevates the material. Robin Wright made her feature film debut as Princess Buttercup, a lovelorn woman who mourns the apparent loss of her one true love, a stable boy named Westley (Cary Elwes), and, believing him dead, agrees to marry the horrible Prince Humperdinck (Chris Sarandon). Elsewhere, swordsman Inigo Montoya (Mandy Patinkin), who always travels with the friendly giant Fezzik (André the Giant), wants revenge on the man who killed his father, and when Westley reappears as the Dread Pirate Roberts, he ends up teaming up with Inigo and Fezzik to also rescue Buttercup. Wallace Shawn, Carol Kane, and Billy Crystal play pivotal supporting roles in this film. It's basically perfect.

If you've seen "The Princess Bride" — and the odds are that you have — you know it's chock-a-block full of quotable lines. Today, though, we're celebrating one of its most beloved and well-known quotes, 39 years after its release.

Throughout "The Princess Bride," Mandy Patinkin's dashing and skilled swordsman Inigo Montoya has one goal: to find the six-fingered man who killed his father when Inigo was just a boy. For years, Inigo has been searching for this specific killer to avenge his dear old dad — and he finds him in the film in the form of Count Tyrone Rugen (Christopher Guest). So why is this line so important to the film, and why is it so beloved after nearly four decades?

For one thing, Inigo says it, like, 80 times in the movie, so it's easy to remember. It's a testament to Rob Reiner's sharp, exacting sense of comedic timing that the line never loses any luster, but remains funny every single time Patinkin delivers it (which is also a credit to Patinkin, a truly formidable performer who's been excellent for generations at this point). It's also connected to the movie's enduring message of love, even though it definitely seems a little more murdery than the flowery declarations of passion exchanged between Westley and Buttercup. Inigo truly loved his father, and once he kills the genuinely evil Rugen, the character delivers a line that defined Patinkin's actual life.

Reiner, who was tragically killed alongside his wife Michele Singer Reiner in late 2025 at his home in Los Angeles, made movies with big jokes and even bigger hearts. This line perfectly exemplifies that, and across the board, "The Princess Bride" is one of his very best films. So what other "Princess Bride" quotes stand the test of time?

#3511. 10 of the Most Iconic Patrick Stewart Roles Beyond Captain Picard

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

Sir Patrick Stewart, an actor equally at home onstage at the Royal Shakespeare Company and on the bridge of the Starship Enterprise, has died at the age of 86. Unexpectedly for most of us, in part because he kept his final illness private, but more so because it once seemed as though nothing could fell the man who looms so large in our cultural consciousness.

The thoughtful, erudite performer who had a troubled childhood in working-class Yorkshire; the committed socialist who was eventually knighted by Queen Elizabeth; the advocate who put his money and his considerable voice toward the fights for LGBTQ+ acceptance and animal welfare and against domestic violence, his presence and performances meant the world (the galaxy, even) to myself and so many others. But those who knew him personally can offer better tributes; perhaps it's best left to Shakespeare's Player King, performed by Stewart himself opposite David Warner's Hamlet back in 1965:

Where joy most revels, grief doth most lament;Grief joys, joy grieves, on slender accident.

Much of Stewart's finest work was on the stage; other performances remain rather shockingly hard to come by (whither I, Claudius?). Nonetheless, he left a true legacy behind him, well beyond Captain Picard and Professor X. Here are 10 of his most iconic other roles.

A goofy, feel-good gay rom-com with the HIV/AIDS crisis still very much in the foreground, Jeffrey was a near-impossibility in the mid-1990s: a movie that neither villainized its queers nor treated them as pitiable martyrs. Steven Weber and Michael T. Weiss are the leads, joined by a cast that includes Christine Baranski, Victor Garber, Nathan Lane, Olympia Dukakis, and Sigourney Weaver but, for all those names, Stewart is the undeniable standout as Sterling, the irrepressible gay best friend: a swishing, mincing, sassy, high-camp character who steals every scene without ever becoming a caricature. He's the leader of the "Pink Panthers," a squad of queers who defend locals from gay bashers, and that is the key to the character's power: He's as gay as they come, but not ashamed and not even a little weak. This movie, and the presence of Captain Picard himself in it, might have saved my life back in 1995. Stream Jeffrey on Prime Video, Tubi, and The Roku Channel.

A sprawling, epic, and appropriately lusty take on the King Arthur stories from John Boorman, Excalibur is a mixed bag full of stunning visuals and iconic moments that never quite coalesce into something entirely coherent. Standing out among the film's many characters, Stewart is entirely memorable as Leodegrance, the boisterous, boorish, but ultimately faithful father of Guenevere who is among the first to pledge his loyalty to Arthur. Rent Excalibur from Prime Video.

Darcy Banker is erudite and intellectual, in his way, and even capable of charm, but otherwise has no redeeming qualities whatsoever. It's bad enough for the punk band Ain’t Rights that they've booked a last-minute gig at an Oregon bar without realizing that it's a haven for white supremacists. It's even worse when they witness a murder and become trapped in the title's green room, with Stewart as the lead skinhead. He's quite simply one of the all-time great (meaning absolutely terrifying) villains in this thriller that's pretty much a horror movie. Stream Green Room on Netflix.

Patrick Stewart's role as Professor Xavier in the X-Men is almost as pop-culture iconic as that of Captain Picard, spanning 26 years and nine movies, including the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday. In most of those, he looks like he's having an awful lot of fun, but he gives his finest performance in the role in this elegaic installment, playing a dying Professor in profound cognitive decline, his dream in tatters and his bravado worn down to prickly dependence. We rarely get to see our superheroes at the ends of their days, and there's a lovely bravery to this depiction of the Charles' journey. Logan will likely be the toughest of his films to rewatch in the coming days. Stream Logan on Disney+.

This stagey television movie isn't the most sumptuous of the many filmed versions of the Dickens story, but you won't be surprised to learn that there are few better portrayals of Ebenezer Scrooge. It's rather a shame that Patrick Stewart didn't do more Dickens adaptations, since his booming voice and ability to play thoroughly heightened characters without ever resorting to caricature is as valuable as in Shakespeare. Rent A Christmas Carol from Prime Video.

Famously referred to as that "unknown British Shakespearean actor" when starting out on Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stewart was an associate of the Royal Shakespeare Company for twenty years before his most famous role came along. As is the way of live theater, much of his career lives on as an essential link in the chain of Shakespeare performances in the twentieth century...but not in a way that we can conveniently stream. We do, however, have this impressively mounted modern-dress stage production, in which Stewart plays King Claudius with characteristic brilliance against David Tennant's melancholy prince. Buy Hamlet from Prime Video and Apple TV.

As a cinematic actor, Stewart's greatest strength was bringing humanity to larger-than-life, even operatic roles, whether they be Arthurian knights, Dickensian villains, or superheroes. That ability is an absolute necessity if one is going to have any success doing Shakespeare, as Stewart did for decades. Match is something rather different, though, and it's rather lovely to see him play something just a bit more mundane—even if the film's Tobi Powell is a choreographer with a nearly legendary reputation. Teaching at Juilliard School, with his career winding down, he's confronted with the living embodiment of the past he left behind to pursue his career. The ensuing relationships grow more complex, with the film building to a climax that's surprising and deeply devastating, made all the more so by Stewart's muted, subtle performance. Stream Match on AMC+.

This is not the greatest Mel Brooks movie, not by a long shot, but it is a great comedic performance from Patrick Stewart. He loved to recount, with self-effacing embarrassment, the story of having shouted "We are not here to have fun" at his co-workers during a rowdy day on set at Star Trek: The Next Generation. By 1993, he was clearly past any such pomposity, and clearly having fun in his cameo as King Richard, a memorably silly take on a character he might well have played with seriousness elsewhere. Rent Robin Hood: Men in Tights from Prime Video.

Stewart's first real foray into science fiction was in this big, bold, divisive, and thoroughly bonkers Frank Herbert adaptation from director David Lynch. Stewart plays troubadour and warrior Gurney Halleck, and does what he does best: bringing gravitas and believability (and it must be said, bald sexiness) to even the wildest material. Stream Dune on Tubi.

Stewart plays an aged Merlin in this rather shockingly good modern reimagining of the King Arthur legendarium. His Merlin is all wild hair and rock band T-shirts, possessed of an essential kindness that makes him a valued mentor, and one deserving of his character's poignant farewell at the film's conclusion.Stream The Kid Who Would Be King on Disney+ and Prime Video.

#3510. Will Josh O’Connor Be The Next James Bond?

Let’s clear up any potential misunderstandings: there are no official announcements on who will play James Bond at this time. But a British tabloid says that a conversation at a pub has revealed the top-secret casting—if an anonymously sourced rumor is to be believed.

A long list of stars are reportedly auditioning for the 007 role, but even former James Bond Pierce Brosnan says the casting process is a mystery. “I’m just the man in the street who is eager to see who is going to play this epic role of cinematic history,” Brosnan tells Vanity Fair. “All the men who are on the list now are actors I admire.”

According to UK publication The Sun, the decision is rumored to have been made: a recent colleague of Josh O’Connor, a 36-year-old actor from Cheltenham, Gloucestershire, says Disclosure Day star has been cast in the role. If true, Turner beat out likely contenders including Callum Turner and Aaron Taylor-Johnson.

Josh O'Connor at UK premiere for Disclosure Day on June 04, 2026.

The news comes as a bit of a game of telephone. Until last week, O'Connor was in the case of Golden Boy, Clifford Odets' 1937 drama about a violin player turned boxer in Depression-era New York City. Citing the claims of one of O'Connor's cast mates, an unnamed source tells The Sun “I bumped into one of Josh’s Golden Boy cast mates at The French House."

“Out of nowhere, and oiled by a few glasses of lager, they blurted out that Josh was the next James Bond."

When the source pushed back, the thespian grew more insistent. “They said that he had confided in them about getting the role when the cast of Golden Boy had celebratory drinks after the play finished its run on Halloween," a claim that implies the decision has been made for over a week.

Josh O'Connor, winner of the Outstanding Lead Actor In A Drama Series award for The Crown, at the 73rd Primetime Emmy Awards on September 19, 2021.

If this rumor comes to fruition, it would not be the first time O'Connor took on an iconic UK role. In 2021, he took home the outstanding lead actor Emmy for his role as then-Prince, now-King Charles III, in Netflix series The Crown. While in his role as the future king, he was encouraged to tap into a side that one might not expect.

“It’s Prince Charles as Walter White," he told The Guardian in 2020, making a reference to crime series Breaking Bad. "Our job was to make people feel sorry for [Charles], so that in season four, when he turns into this at times monstrous character, we understand how he got there.” A heel turn that isn't unBond, especially the darker Bond we grew used to with Daniel Craig. (Craig, in fact, has a direct connection to O’Connor, as the pair co-starred in Knives Out: Wake Up Dead Man.)

Speaking with the BBC, O'Connor did not confirm the casting rumor—but he didn't deny it either. (Vanity Fair has reached out to O'Connor's representatives for comment, but has not yet received a response.)

"To be considered in that same sort of bracket is extraordinary," O'Connor said this week.

"It's an incredibly bizarre pinch me moment...even being uttered in that same sentence and being considered for something like that. But I am afraid, there is nothing to say beyond that."

#3509. Set Phasers To Stun: Star Trek's Different Phaser Settings Explained

Welcome to Trekspertise, a series where we break down the technology, history, details, and decisions that make the Star Trek universe so complex — and so fun.

When Gene Roddenberry was first assembling "Star Trek" in the mid-1960s, the term "laser guns" was common enough sci-fi parlance that he astutely wanted to avoid using it. To make "Star Trek" seem a little more futuristic, Roddenberry invented "phasers" instead of "lasers," and the weapon became a staple of the franchise. Starfleet vessels are equipped with powerful phaser weapons used for ship-to-ship combat, and Starfleet officers carry hand-held phasers into potentially dangerous situations.

In the pilot episode for "Star Trek: Enterprise," a series set a century prior to the events of the original "Star Trek," Captain Archer (Scott Bakula) was shown a hand-held phaser — then called a phase pistol — for the first time, so Starfleet has been using them since the very start. Phasers tend to fire single, confined beams, but would also eventually come to fire brief, bullet-like pulses.

"Star Trek," however, is also meant to take place in a peaceful utopia, so the phasers were said to have a "stun" setting that could render an attacker unconscious from a distance. Only in extreme scenarios would a phaser be adjusted to the "kill" setting, which could blast the life out of someone. Indeed, throughout "Star Trek," the powerful kill setting was seen to vaporize a person's body entirely.

On "Enterprise," phasers only had "stun" and "kill" settings, but later on, there were other, gentler settings. Throughout the franchise, characters have been explicit about the various settings a hand phaser was capable of using, sometimes referring to "light stun," "heavy stun," or a numerical system.

What do those numbers and settings mean? Let's take a look.

Eagle-eyed "Star Trek" viewers might notice that Starfleet officers typically use two different types of phasers. The Type-1 phasers are the smaller, thumb-activated, remote-control-looking widgets, while the larger, pistol-shaped phasers are Type-2. On "Next Generation," the Type-2 also became a thumb-operated device. Only very occasionally would one see a larger phaser rifle, like the one Captain Kirk (William Shatner) used in the episode "Where No Man Has Gone Before."

In the "Star Trek: Discovery" episode "Saints of Imperfection," Tilly (Mary Wiseman) also noted that the rifle is designated a Type-3 weapon by saying, "It is more powerful and generally larger than the Type-1 or Type-2, which I guess is why they call it a 3."

The original phaser sound effect, a high-pitched whine, was repurposed from the 1953 film "The War of the Worlds." The common "Star Trek" phaser sound has remained a variant of that whine ever since.

It was in the episode "The Enemy Within" that "setting one," a phaser's lowest setting, was first mentioned. This was enough to, well, stun the average humanoid. In the episode "The Return of the Archons," the Enterprise crew set their phasers to a wide-beam setting that could essentially spray across a crowd, stunning multiple people at once. (It's a good thing I don't have a phaser with a wide-beam setting; I would never wait in line for a ride at Disneyland ever again.)

On "Star Trek: Deep Space Nine," specifically in the episode "Homefront," there was some mention that setting 3.5 or 3.6 constituted a "heavy stun." It wouldn't be until a phaser was set to setting 10 that it would be capable of vaporizing someone. Starfleet seems more interested in gradations of stunning someone before it considers a kill setting ... but those puppies can do a lot of damage.

In the "Next Generation" episode "Frame of Mind," Riker (Jonathan Frakes) has a scene where he sets a Type-2 phaser to its maximum setting of 16. He states out loud that if a phaser were to fire at such a setting, it would destroy half the building. Phasers, if wielded irresponsibly, could apparently do a great deal of damage. Of course, these are hand-held devices and don't have an infinite power supply. I think it's safe to assume that a phaser, firing a level-16 blast, could only do it once. I'd hate to live in a world where someone could stroll through a city, blasting open multiple buildings willy-nilly with a single handgun-sized object.

A stun setting could knock someone out without leaving a mark, but, judging by various makeup jobs seen throughout "Star Trek," heavier settings left bruises or even burn marks on people. Before you think you could withstand a heavy stun, watch one of those foolish online videos where macho idiots — or perhaps just the cast members of the "Jackass" crew — test to see if they can withstand a taser or pepper spray. I imagine a phaser blast would be the sci-fi version of that.

Of course, throughout "Star Trek," officers also used phasers for things other than tactical confrontations. They could be used as cutting torches, or to heat up rocks in order to keep warm in frozen climates. In the "Next Generation" episode "Disaster," a phaser's power cell was used as a power source for a computer terminal. Phasers may have the ability to explode entire buildings, but they are more often used as tools in a Starfleet officer's toolbox.

#3508. Ramayana Producer On How Being A ‘Fanboy’ Of Chris Nolan Films Inspired One Thing About The Epic

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

India’s most expensive movie ever is Ramayana, which is one of the latest 2026 movie releases to hit theaters. The movie was a massive undertaking, and that's evident just by watching the trailer. All in all, the film is firmly steeped in the culture its representing. But, even though the flick was made thousands of miles from Hollywood, a producer was very much inspired by one of our greatest filmmakers, Christopher Nolan, as CinemaBlend recently learned.

Did you know that Ramayana is co-composed by Hans Zimmer? The German musician has become one of the most beloved and prolific composers of modern cinema, and that’s exactly why the movie's producer, Namit Malhotra, asked for him to come aboard the filmmaking team. Here’s how he told us the story during CB’s exclusive Ramayana interview:

I grew up in India completely fanboying on A.R. Rahman, who I absolutely love and his music has sort of formed a big part of my growing up and childhood and youth. And then, I moved to L.A. in 2010, the year Inception came out. I started to fall in love with Chris Nolan and Han Zimmer's music that was done for The Dark Knight and all the films that came subsequent to that. And, it was one of those moments when we decided to make Ramayana. I said literally as a fanboy, ‘What if I could take Han Zimmer and A.R. Rahman together and they would create a new sound, a new feeling, a new energy that the world has not heard before?’ And everybody is like, ‘Yeah, why not?’

Malhotra called himself a self-described “fanboy” of Nolan movies who's been in awe of his movies for a while. So, when he went on to make his own epic, he thought he'd take the long-shot move to try to get Zimmer on board for Ramayana alongside his favorite composer from India, A.R. Rahman. (Did you know Zimmer actually helped convince Nolan to make Interstellar, by the way? A greatly overlooked detail is just how important musicians like him are pivotal to the filmmaking process.) As Malhotra added:

One thing I learned in America, there's no harm in asking because the worst you'll be told is ‘No’. That's not how we grew up in India. Like you normally don't ask the question if you think the answer is no.

Even though Namit Malhotra had never met Zimmer and didn't know would react to the request, the producer took “a cue from [his] American friends” and reached out to the Interstellar composer. This is what happened next:

I made a pitch and a presentation to him. I couldn't have been more surprised by his intellect, his intuitive judgment because he was like, ‘Namit, you don't have to sell me on Ramayana. If something has existed in the world for over 5,000 years and generation after generation, more people are excited to consume it, learn from it, and it's still not lost its relevance, there must be more than what you and I can understand. So we should just figure out how we do this and not worry about whether we should do it.’

Ramayana Is Making A Huge Global Push. I Still Can't Tell From Reviews What I'm Getting Into

The idea really does sell itself, doesn’t it? Ramayana is a Hindu epic poem that’s very central to India’s culture. It has inspired the celebrations of Diwali and Dussehra, and the story also serves as a moral cornerstone as well. It focuses on two characters: Rama and Ravana. Prince Rama is the seventh incarnation / avatar of Lord Vishnu, who becomes responsible for taking down King Ravana from having uncontrollable power over people. It's India's own classic good vs. evil story, and it has really stood the test of time.

I'm no sure how aware Zimmer was of the legend of Ramayana before it was pitched to him, yet he was apparently sold quite quickly. He got the importance of it being told for the big screen. Malhotra told us that Zimmer’s reaction to his pitch even “revalidated” his own reasons to make it and “reinvigorated [his] own confidence” since he respects the composer so much.

Hans Zimmer is a busy musical savant, who’s recently worked on the Dune movies and the upcoming Harry Potter TV series, so he could have easily passed, but he clearly didn’t want to. And, as a result of his participation, one of Hollywood's best got to put his mark on a historical Indian film. You can hear Zimmer’s original music for Ramayana, which is playing in theaters around the world right now.

#3507. Kate Middleton, Prince William, King Charles, and Queen Camilla Gather For Remembrance Day

This Sunday, November 8, King Charles III, Queen Camilla, Kate Middleton, Prince William, Princess Anne and other members of the royal family came together to observe Remembrance Sunday, one of the most solemn events on the United Kingdom's calendar. The day marks the anniversary of the armistice that ended World War I, signed on “the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month” in 1918.

The focal point of every Remembrance Day is the Cenotaph in Whitehall, the Portland stone monument where tribute is paid to those who fell in the wars and conflicts in which the country has participated. Every year, representatives of the royal family, political leaders, the Armed Forces, and veterans gather there: This year, more than 10,000 marched alongside the king and the prime minister.

True to tradition, Charles III laid a wreath at the memorial on behalf of the nation and led the royal family. At his side was Prince William, Princess Anne, and the Duke of Edinburgh, who also paid their respects with a floral tribute. Queen Camilla and the Princess of Wales, Kate Middleton, watched the ceremony from the balcony of the Foreign Office, as is customary. On the political front, Prime Minister Andy Burnham laid a wreath on his first Remembrance Sunday as head of the government, accompanied by Opposition Leader Kemi Badenoch and other political leaders.

The day before had already been a day of remembrance: the King, the Queen, and the Princes of Wales attended the Festival of Remembrance at the Royal Albert Hall, the major tribute to the armed forces that precedes Remembrance Sunday.
