#3493. This Canceled 2010s Fantasy Series Deserved More Time To Flesh Out Its Ambitious Premise

The supernatural TV series "The Secret Circle" debuted on The CW in 2011, falling squarely into the network's penchant for teen dramas and YA-inflected soaps. Sadly, it only lasted for one 22-episode season, ending its run in 2012. And like other TV shows that possess as much lore, backstory, and interpersonal relationships as this one, "The Secret Circle" needed to live a lot longer to fulfill its potential.

Based on the series of novels created by L.J. Smith (best known for writing "The Vampire Diaries"), "The Secret Circle" stars Britt Robertson (who also fronted the guilty pleasure that is Netflix's "Girlboss") as Cassie, a teenager who recently lost her mother in a fire and has since moved to Chance Harbor, Washington, to live with her grandmother, Jane (Ashley Crow). Cassie doesn't initially know this, but she's secretly a witch and has eerie magical powers. However, it doesn't take long for the other teen witches at her new high school to recognize that Cassie is a witch and invite her to be part of their Secret Circle.

Cassie isn't just a witch, she learns, her matronly lineage goes all the way back to the beginning of witchcraft. Cassie's father, it's revealed, is John Blackwell (Joe Lando), a mysterious dark warlock who lurks in the show's margins. Other members of the Secret Circle include Adam (Thomas Dekker), Faye (Phoebe Tonkin), Diana (Shelley Hennig), Melissa (Jessica Parker Kennedy), and Nick (Louis Hunter).

True to the soap opera spirit of The CW, there are romantic dealings between the Circle's members. For example, Nick and Melissa are dating, and Nick eventually has to learn to respect Melissa more. That is, in addition to being killed and resurrected (!). Cassie, meanwhile, instantly falls for Adam, which upsets Diana, who has always had a thing for Adam.

In addition to the kids in the Circle, Gale Harold plays Charles, Diana's father and a former Circle member. Elsewhere, Natasha Henstridge from "Species" plays Faye's mother, another former Circle member, and the principal of the high school where the show's action takes place.

"The Secret Circle" belongs to a vast and well-populated matrix of teen supernatural dramas that were very much in vogue on television in the 2000s and early 2010s (although L.J. Smith started publishing her "Secret Circle" novels in 1992). Indeed, it's worth recalling that The CW had already scored a hit when its TV adaptation of "The Vampire Diaries" began its run in 2009, to the point that the network would go on to develop multiple spin-offs (like the since-canceled "Legacies"). Clearly, "The Secret Circle" was an attempt to bottle the same lightning. Vampires, witches, teen drama, magic: It was all boiling together on The CW.

And "The Secret Circle" certainly doesn't lack conflict. It carefully balances the magic of a witch coven with the drama of being a regular high school student. As such, it features just as many stories about school dances and friend-group inter-flirting as ones about spell books and dark witchy forces that aim to attack the Circle for nefarious purposes. Case in point: The show includes three episodes that center on school dances, and its penultimate episode takes place at Prom. On the witch side of things, several plot lines focus on magic crystals that are coveted by various magical players for a variety of reasons.

Back in 2015, writer Gavin Hetherington penned a post-mortem on "The Secret Circle" for Spoiler TV, revisiting it three years after its cancelation. Hetherington noted that "The Secret Circle" actually began quite strong in the ratings, but it fell off quickly, falling far behind "The Vampire Diaries." For Hetherington, this was a tragedy, as he declared the show's finale to be its best episode up to that point, arguing that it only showed more potential going forward. In fact, four new characters arrive in that episode, with all of them being part of Cassie's witch ancestor's lineage. Sadly, though, the show ended before audiences could learn their whole story.

When "The Secret Circle" was canceled, its many fans tried to convince The CW to keep it going via a letter-writing campaign, but it was not successful. "The Vampire Diaries" simply left a deeper impact and is generally regarded as one of the best vampire shows of all time. Due to its truncated run, "The Secret Circle" just can't compete with that series.

It probably didn't help that critics were less impressed with "The Secret Circle" than its loyal fans. Reviewing the series for Variety in 2011, Brian Lowry even described it as "'One Tree Hill,' only with witchcraft," writing that "nothing in the pilot conjures any genuine magic, TV-wise." Still, it's a vestige of what the old CW used to be in all its glory.

#3492. 27 Years Later, Science-Fiction's Groundbreaking 4-Part Saga Is Free to Watch on Streaming

The machines are winning, but at least the movies are free

Some science fiction franchises are so ambitious they become their own cinematic languages. Star Wars built an entire galaxy with a mythology that’s still growing almost 50 years later, while Blade Runner helped define the vision of a far-future Los Angeles through rampant tech advancement and unchecked capitalism. They’re the kinds of franchises that can change the way we imagine the future, influencing everything from fashion and technology to the stories other filmmakers want to tell. Plenty of franchises have tried to capture that same vibe, but few have managed to pull it off quite like The Matrix.

Released in 1999, Lana and Lilly Wachowski’s cyberpunk action thriller introduced one of the most original sci-fi concepts in modern cinema (by shamelessly ripping off cyberpunk literature and golden age anime). The story follows Thomas Anderson (Keanu Reeves), a computer programmer and net surfer living under the hacker alias "Neo," who discovers that the everyday world of the late 1990s is just a complex simulation called the Matrix. Built by sentient machines, this fake reality keeps humanity docile and unconscious while harvesting their bioelectric energy in a real-world wasteland. Neo violently wakes up to the truth, joining forces with a mysterious rebel leader in Morpheus (Laurence Fishburne) and a skilled operative named Trinity (Carrie-Anne Moss). With the entire four-movie saga currently streaming free on Pluto TV, what better way to spend a weekend than by delving back into the digital rabbit hole that changed cinema forever?

Landing on the doorstep of the new millennium, The Matrix hit upon the exact cultural fears and anxieties surrounding the internet at the time. On the cusp of the impending Y2K bug, a widely feared computer glitch that threatened to disrupt everything from banking systems to power grids when the calendar rolled into 2000, the Wachowskis captured a palpable dread about future technologies, transforming fears of rogue code and automated systems into a leather-clad action movie that completely rewired 2000s sci-fi and action cinema. It’s no surprise that The Matrix became the blueprint for a whole decade of internet-obsessed action-thrillers, from Kurt Wimmer’s Equilibrium to Michael Bay’s The Island.

Despite striking gold, the Wachowskis weren't working from a blank slate. Mamoru Oshii's 1995 masterpiece Ghost in the Shell shaped the film's aesthetic and ideas, with the Wachowskis even reportedly showing the film to producer Joel Silver while pitching their vision. The Matrix inevitably combined those influences with Western cyberpunk, religious imagery, and martial arts cinema to create a singular blend of philosophical science fiction and blockbuster spectacle unlike any other. Its famous bullet-time sequences became a sensation, with the iconic rooftop showdown between Agent Smith and Neo still one of its slickest. It was visual storytelling at its finest, physically demonstrating that Neo was finally beginning to understand the rules of the simulation as he surpassed the boundaries of his human limitations.

The original film's breakout success led to The Matrix Reloaded and The Matrix Revolutions, which expanded the mythology into a multi-layered epic exploring the political machinery of Zion. The sequels might not have captured the same cultural lightning as their predecessor, but they deserve credit for refusing to simply repeat the first film's formula. Reloaded introduced more complicated questions about the cyclical nature of the Matrix, while Revolutions brought Neo's conflict with the machines to an appropriately operatic conclusion. The franchise also expanded into the digital realm with The Animatrix, a nine-part anime anthology featuring legendary Japanese directors, as well as assorted video games, and other multimedia projects, creating a sprawling sci-fi universe that showed little signs of dying.

Eighteen years after Revolutions brought Neo’s journey to a definitive close, The Matrix seemingly still had stories left to tell with 2021’s The Matrix Resurrections. Directed solely by Lana Wachowski, the fourth installment reunited Reeves and Carrie-Anne Moss, but its greatest ambition also proved to be its biggest stumbling block. Rather than delivering another nostalgic action spectacle, Resurrections tried to tackle Hollywood’s relentless obsession with reboots and legacy sequels through a self-referential lens. It was a hard sell for fans hoping for another revolutionary sci-fi leap, with the film struggling to strike a satisfying balance between its cerebral commentary and the blockbuster storytelling that made the 1999 film a masterpiece.

Still, an uneven fourth installment can't erase what The Matrix accomplished. Its vision of artificial intelligence and simulated reality feels particularly relevant today, even if we're still waiting for someone to invent a pair of sunglasses that look quite as cool. For anyone who missed the phenomenon the first time around, or simply wants to revisit one of Hollywood's most influential sci-fi universes, there's never been a better excuse to follow the white rabbit again.

#3491. The Bose Premium Smart Ultra Soundbar Is Now Cheaper Than It Was During Prime Day

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon has dropped the Bose Smart Ultra Soundbar to $649 from its usual $999, taking $350 off and bringing it to the lowest price we've seen so far, according to price trackers. PCMag rated the Smart Ultra "outstanding," highlighting its ability to deliver surprisingly immersive Dolby Atmos audio without requiring a room full of additional speakers. If you don't need Bose's top-tier model, there's a less expensive option as well: the Bose Smart Dolby Atmos Soundbar ($399, down from $429), which sits below the Smart Ultra in the lineup.

The Smart Ultra uses a 5.1.2-channel design with nine drivers, including two upward-firing drivers that bounce sound off the ceiling to create height effects. In practice, that means movies, TV shows, and games feel larger and more spacious than they do through most single-bar setups. Bose also includes its AdaptiQ room-calibration system, which measures your room's acoustics and adjusts the sound accordingly. The process takes a few minutes, but it helps the soundbar perform better across different spaces rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all tuning profile. The soundbar also works as a smart speaker, with Amazon Alexa built in and support for Apple AirPlay 2, Google Cast, Spotify Connect, Bluetooth, and multi-room audio through the Bose app.

Its biggest compromise is bass—for a single soundbar, its low end is respectable, but it can't fully replace what a dedicated subwoofer brings to action movies, concerts, or bass-heavy music. The good news is that Bose allows you to expand the system later with compatible wireless subwoofers and surround speakers if you decide you want more impact. For anyone looking for a premium one-piece soundbar that delivers convincing Dolby Atmos effects, clear dialogue, built-in smart features, and a much larger soundstage than TV speakers can provide, the Smart Ultra remains one of the strongest standalone options available, especially at this price.

#3490. How Every Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtle Officially Dies In TMNT: The Last Ronin

Warning: Spoilers Ahead For Major Character Deaths In TMNT: The Last Ronin!

The Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles have proven to be enough of an enduring franchise to cross the generational gap rather seamlessly, engaging old fans continuously while remaining approachable to newcomers. Its origins at Mirage Studios through the present at IDW have been confirmed as such, in addition to numerous successful theatrical releases and video games, have proven audiences continue to respond. But while TMNT is timeless, its characters are not immortal, with The Last Ronin standing as its The Dark Knight Returns in terms of a grim future where not everyone survives as they would have in their prime.

Michelangelo was the sole survivor in this dark alternate future, and while it's not broadly accepted as canon, it arguably doesn't matter. The story following this continuity by Kevin Eastman and Tom Waltz has been the most acclaimed over the past decade, even if every new chapter and sequel piles on the heartache with new loss amid pyrrhic victories. In a vengeance arc spurred on my merciless killing, with only more death seen to be the way to balance the scales, every member of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles eventually meets their demise in this series, along with key foes and tragically even more friends.

The Foot have always been treacherous nemeses to the Ninja Turtles, but the first to truly experience their deadliness in the strictest way imaginable was Raphael. After Master Splinter was gravely injured by an ambush attack, this triggered a rage in Raphael, prompting him to pursue and confront Oroku Karai, the leader at the time and daughter of Oroku Sakai (Shredder), getting fatally wounded and being left to sink into the East River. Karai survives, but also sustains a grave wound, going into a coma later and dying at the hands of her resentful son, Oroku Hiroto.

With Hiroto assuming leadership of the Foot and 10 years having passed, the next to come would be Leonardo, then Donatello. While Donatello and Master Splinter would come to Japan to meet with the Foot Clan on the presumption that they were entering peace talks, Leonardo remained in New York, in which the next tragedy would occur.

A compelling one-shot significantly expanding The Last Ronin, Training Day is an ambitious, character-driven story of an unexpected mentor.

Under attack by Baxter Stockman's forces, Leonardo, Casey Jones, and April O'Neil faced down the invasive attack by Stockman's Synjas, having tracked down and in pursuit of Zayton Honeycutt. Honeycutt attempted to self-destruct his physical robot body, only for Stockman to have the Spider Mousers explode to finish the job for him, the ensuing blast claiming the lives of both Leonardo and Casey, maiming April in the process while she was still pregnant.

The peace talks, meanwhile, devolved as predicted. Upon arriving at the agreed-upon meeting location at the Hamato Village, they are soon met with Hara and then Hiroto, who unleash an attack using the Foot ninjas at their disposal. Splinter and Donatello, the ones who arrived for the peace talks, fight back valiantly, only to eventually be killed by the Foot's archers.

While the other Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles died tragic deaths, Michelangelo was left behind, their youngest member, haunted by their memory and wracked with survivor's guilt, striking back at Hiroto's forces while hanging by a thread. With the help of the surviving April and Honeycutt's consciousness, surviving his previous shell being destroyed, and Casey and April's daughter, Casey Marie Jones, carrying the flame as well. Michelangelo is thankfully not alone. And with Casey Marie carrying similarly mutated genes like her father due to proximity with the Turtles, she even shows promise as his eventual disciple.

Michelangelo carried all but one of the mementos of each of his brothers and Splinter into battle, them genuinely serving as vital to his fights as he inched closer to his goal. His personal quest is to kill Hiroto, the main loose end, ahead of clearing his conscience before he could die. So upon their final confrontation in The Last Ronin #5, the two draw their fight out into the sewers, Hiroto actually being the one to deal both of them the last grievous wound by detonating an electrified burst and then an explosion in his armor.

Having left behind Master Splinter's journal, Casey Marie brings it to him, pleading with him not to die and urging him to stay and continue to teach her. Instead, Michelangelo turns the back cover over the page tastefully revealing the poignant lesson, "Know Peace" as he bleeds out in front of Casey Marie with April soon seeing his lifeless body, as his dying mind relives memories of his youth alongside the other Turtles.

Michelangelo, or "Mikey", fought to his last while making sure he did right by his lost brothers, with others like April soon to follow in subsequent stories. Fortunately, Casey Marie had begun raising a successor generation of her own with Uno, Odyn, Yi, and Moja, functioning as their parent while imparting Michelangelo's ninja training upon them as he did for her. Mikey can return to his brothers, having avenged their legacy, while a new generation of Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles begin featuring more heavily in The Last Ronin II: Re-Evolution, Training Day, and The Last Ronin III yet to release. May Mikey's successors know peace as well, once this is all over.

#3489. Was This Short-Lived '60s Sitcom Really The Worst Show To Ever Air On TV?

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

The 1960s was truly a golden era for weird little shows that melded the quotidian and the fantastical. This was the decade that gave us the great fantasy sitcoms, in which some larger than life character with supernatural abilities would be slotted into a suburban setting for laughs. "Mister Ed" was one of the first, featuring a talking horse who could only be understood by his architect owner Wilbur Post (Alan Young). The much lesser-known "The Hathaways" was sort of in that vein as well. Rather than featuring an animal with fantastical powers, however, it featured three chimpanzees whose owners treated them as if they were actual children.

You might already be able to see why this series didn't last longer than a single season. But not only was "The Hathaways" short-lived, it seemed to stoke significant ire among certain critics. In "Watching TV: Four Decades of American Television," authors Harry Castleman and Walter J. Podrazik outright described the show as "possibly the worst series ever to air on network TV."

Of course, such a claim is subjective. But there was an undeniably uncanny and slightly unsettling air to "The Hathaways," which saw Peggy Cass' Elinore Hathaway and Jack Weston's Walter Hathaway acting as "parents" to their three chimpanzees, referring to them as "the kids" and dressing them in human clothing. The suburban Los Angeles couple seemed to have completely lost the plot, yet it was all played for laughs. At least, it was for about 10 months. After that, ABC quite sensibly pulled the plug.

The sheer volume of failed shows in TV history is kind of breathtaking when you consider the amount of effort that goes into these things. Scripts are written, casts and production teams assembled, sets designed, and significant amounts of money are spent. (In the case of the swiftly-cancelled 1970s TV flop "Supertrain," we're talking major sums.) How many actors have been convinced that they were on the verge of their big break, only to become yet another footnote in TV history? It's weirdly tragic to think about. In the case of "The Hathaways," its chimpanzee stars were likely unfazed by the show's hasty cancellation, due to the fact they were in high demand elsewhere. That and they were literally animals.

Non-chimp leading man Jack Weston stars as Walter Hathaway, a real estate agent whose wife Elinore Hathaway acts as a mother to Candy, Charlie, and Enoch. These ape "kids" were part of the Marquis Chimps, a group of trained chimpanzees owned by Gene Detroy that were popular at the time. As the New York Times noted in a contemporaneous report ahead of the premiere of "The Hathaways," "The chimps got their new job through a TV guest appearance on 'The Jack Benny Show' [...] Robert Sparks, executive producer of the new series, saw them on the 'Benny' program and decided to develop a series."

That series saw Walter and Elinore taking care of their chimpanzee children while also booking them as a performing act, in which they would ride bicycles and build things. Otherwise, they would hang out at home, earning the Hathaways some strange looks from their neighbors. Other non-chimp cast members included Harvey Lembeck as talent agent Jerry Roper and Belle Montrose as neighbor Mrs. Harrison.

Was "The Hathaways" really one of the worst sitcoms of all time? Well, it was certainly strange. Perhaps, viewed in retrospect, the show feels a little too close to the unforgettable "Gordy" scene in Jordan Peele's "Nope," in which a chimpanzee mauls the entire cast and crew on the set of his sitcom. (Thankfully, nothing of the sort happened during filming on "The Hathaways.") But there's just something unsettling about the series, which seemed like a particularly cynical attempt at leveraging the chimps' popularity, even at a time when fantasy sitcoms featuring similarly unusual setups were coming to the fore. As Harry Castleman and Walter J. Podrazik write in their book, "The premise itself was utterly degrading to both the audience and the actors," adding that "The Hathaways" "stood as an embarrassing example of the depths programmers had reached in their desperate search for a chance hit in any format or premise."

Unsurprisingly, the sitcom didn't last long. "The Hathaways" debuted on ABC in October 1961 and was canceled by August 1962. A decade later, CBS tried its luck at a chimpanzee-led sitcom with "Me and the Chimp," which starred Ted Bessell as a dentist who lives with his family and a chimpanzee named Buttons. It, too, lasted one season. For some reason, NBC thought it could do better and unleashed "Mr. Smith" in 1983, a sitcom about a talking orangutan (played by the same ape who accompanied Clint Eastwood in his controversial project "Any Which Way But Loose") who becomes a political advisor after ingesting an experimental drug. Yep, one season. But "The Hathaways" remains the first and arguably the worst of these ape-led sitcoms.

#3488. Why Michael Stuhlbarg Left HBO's Boardwalk Empire

In "The Godfather Part II," Michael Corleone (Al Pacino) meets with the aged gangster Hyman Roth (Lee Strasberg) in his modest Florida home. Roth muses, "I've loved baseball ever since Arnold Rothstein fixed the World Series of 1919."

That reference isn't a movie embellishment. New York racketeer Arnold Rothstein really was alleged to have fixed the 1919 World Series in what's called "The Black Box Scandal," the blowback of which is explored in Season 1 of HBO's Prohibition period piece "Boardwalk Empire," featuring Michael Stuhlbarg as Rothstein. "AR," as his men often call him, remains a fixture of "Boardwalk Empire" during its first four seasons, and Stuhlbarg gives one of the show's standout performances.

Historians describe Rothstein as the one who put the "organized" in organized crime, thanks to a sharp knack for math and business. Stuhlbarg's Rothstein lives up to the history books. He's often shown playing pool or gambling and notes a great gambler never makes a bet without fixing the odds in his favor. He's extremely eloquent but only polite except in the most surface-level ways. Ice water runs in his veins.

So, it's a shame that he doesn't even get a real ending. History says that Rothstein died in 1928. "Boardwalk Empire" Season 4 ends in 1924, and then its fifth and final eight-episode season jumps ahead to 1931. That meant the show skips over lots of real history, including Rothstein's death. He simply disappears from the series, save for vague references to his demise in Season 5.

It's even more noticeable since his legacy hangs over the show's finale. "Boardwalk Empire" Season 5 includes a fictionalized account of how Rothstein's protégés "Lucky" Luciano (Vincent Piazza), Meyer Lansky (Anatol Yusef), and Benny "Bugsy" Siegel (Michael Zegen) took over the East Coast American mob.

Rothstein's death is a pretty big missing chapter in Season 5's story, but a consequence of the larger "Boardwalk Empire" production. Looking in from the outside, "Boardwalk Empire" appears to be a show that got cut short. A fifth and final season that's only two-thirds as long as the previous ones? And which leaps past several years of story? It's hard to believe that was always the intention. It really feels like a series that ran out of runway and jumped ahead to the intended ending to resolve itself as best it could. (Mind you, Season 5 still has some great episodes.)

The often repeated narrative is that "Boardwalk Empire" cost too much for HBO for too little a return, so it had to go. It was an unavoidably expensive show that came with a lot of homework for its cast (being a period piece), costing a reported $5 million per episode. The reported episode ratings do also show a consistent downward slump across seasons. From "Boardwalk Empire" Seasons 1-4, each successive season premiere and season finale was watched by fewer people than the previous one, and by Season 4, the show was slipping below even two million viewers an episode.

Nonetheless, "Boardwalk Empire" creator Terence Winter maintained back in 2014 that ending the series was a creative call. Speaking with Time and Hitflix, Winter said he and his writers felt series lead Nucky Thompson (Steve Buscemi) was already nearing his story's end by Season 4. 1931 was chosen as the most natural endpoint because it's when Al Capone (Stephen Graham) went to prison, Luciano and Lansky began the mafia's Commission, and Prohibition was winding down. The cost was skipping over major events like Rothstein's murder, which in real life remains shrouded in mystery.

Reportedly, Rothstein owed $300,000 after a poker loss and refused to pay up, earning him a bullet to the gut on November 4, 1928. But he took his killer's identity to the grave. Rothstein's real death being unsolved would give "Boardwalk Empire" dramatic license to fill in the details. I'm confident it would've pulled it off since whenever Rothstein was onscreen, "Boardwalk Empire" became a more compelling show.

The ending of "Boardwalk Empire" Season 4 even directly teases more to come from Rothstein. He enters a business alliance with Nucky's ex-wife, Margaret Thompson (a pre-"Lanterns" Kelly Macdonald), who is working as a secretary at a New York City investment firm and agrees to slip Rothstein insider information. Instead, nothing comes of that.

Stuhlbarg deserves a mountain's worth of credit. The actor studied his character, including how the real Rothstein thought of himself as a businessman and held his conduct to such a standard, and he's said the "Boardwalk Empire" writers' room was "amiable" about implementing his own research into his character. Stuhlbarg was similarly gracious about not returning for Season 5, especially considering it wasn't even his choice to leave the show, saying during a 2014 press junket that:

"They had to act fast, and they had a lot of ground to cover. It was amazing that we all got as much coverage as we did, considering how many characters they were juggling. I had so much fun doing the show, and I had no regrets. And yeah, sure it would've been fun to have shown [Rothstein's death], but I thought what they came up with was very cool, as it was. I think if they could have, they would've shown it, but they didn't have the time."

#3487. The Top 10 Movies Right Now, According to Streaming Data

The most streamed movie in October was Steven Spielberg's Disclosure Day, but half of the month's top ten is made up of season-appropriate horror movies. This year's two most successful horror movies, Backrooms and Obsession, made the list; so did a classic (Halloween from 1978) and an art movie about the genre that Halloween created,Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Perfect double feature. Rounding out the list is the all-around-excellent Hokum. If you're not into horror, you might like Golden Arm, a comedy that refused to die, star-studded comedy The Invite, or ultimate crowd-pleaser Project Hail Mary.

Disclosure Day details the events that lead up to the revelation that aliens are among us. Meanwhile, a TV meteorologist (Emily Blunt) begins speaking in an alien language. It all sets the stage for a series of set pieces and chases leading to the biggest revelation in human history. Stream Disclosure Day on Peacock.

Based on the viral YouTube series of the same name, Backrooms tells the story of Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a store owner who discovers a labyrinthian liminal space in his furniture shop's basement. Renate Reinsve plays his therapist, who goes downstairs for a visit and does not find it easy to return. A hit with critics—Backrooms is sitting at 86% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes—and audiences, Backrooms is a delicious Halloween treat for horror fans. Stream Backrooms on HBO Max.

Director Curry Barker is still in his 20s, but his debut theatrical feature is the kind of horror film that changes the entire genre. Obsession is a classic "be careful what you wish for" story that feels fresh thanks to its talented young cast, unpredictable plot, and careful pace. Michael Johnston plays a young man too scared to tell his crush how he feels, so he wishes she'd fall in love with him instead. With the straight-laced couple's marriage on thin ice, Angela and Joe invite their more, uh, open-minded neighbors Piña, played by Penélope Cruz, and Hawk, played by Edward Norton, over for dinner. The evening unravels in hilarious ways, changing everyone's life. If you're a fan of smart, honest comedy, you will really like The Invite. Stream The Invite on HBO Max.

With Hokum, Director Damian McCarthy (Oddity, Caveat) carefully builds a suffocatingly creepy story around Adam Scott's portrayal of Ohm Bauman, a celebrity novelist and unmitigated jerk who travels to the isolated Bilberry Woods Hotel in Ireland to scatter the ashes of his parents and finish his book. Bauman soon learns that the lore of the hotel includes an ancient witch who feeds her victims to the creatures of hell, and she might be more than just a local legend. Hokum is a horror movie for fans of dreadful atmosphere and careful pacing instead of gore or jump-scares. Stream Hokum on Hulu.

With a title like this, it's not going to be a normal movie. Director Jane Schoenbrun’s I Saw the TV Glow and We're All Going to the World's Fair are two of the most fascinating, fiercely original horror movies of the last decade, and their third film follows in those strange footfalls. While it's technically a meta re-imagining of the slasher genre, Miasma goes way deeper than Scream ever could. It's a postmodern exploration of why the slasher genre's cocktail of sex, death, and subversion casts such a strong spell on interesting, weird people. Definitely see this movie. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

When Golden Arm was released in 2021, not many people paid attention—with the pandemic in full swing, people didn't seem to have room for a quirky, indie comedy about a woman's quest to win the ladies' arm-wrestling championship—but it's a new age, and you should stream Golden Arm. It's sitting on a perfect score at Rotten Tomatoes, the movie's stars, Mary Holland and Betsy Sodaro, are charming and hilarious, and you can catch Golden Arm on Fandango, a free streaming service. What's not to love? Stream Golden Arm on Fandango or Prime Video.

Grace is the only person on Earth who might know how to protect the sun from a cosmic infection that threatens all life, but he's definitely not an astronaut and doesn't see himself as a hero either. Will he rise to the occasion and learn something about his inner strength and resilience while saving us all from death? My money is on, "yeah, probably." Watch or re-watch Halloween now! Stream Halloween on Philo, AMC+, and Prime Video.

Animals is a taut, expertly directed movie that should more than satisfy fans of political thrillers. Stream Animals on Netflix.

#3486. 19 Years Later, Avatar’s Most Terrifying Episode Changed the Franchise Forever

“The Puppetmaster” gave Katara a terrifying new power — and laid the groundwork for some of Korra’s greatest villains

For much of Avatar: The Last Airbender, waterbending seems like the most limited of the four elements for one practical reason: Its wielders need access to water. Firebenders generate their own flames. Earth is everywhere, and air is even more readily accessible. On her adventure with Aang, Katara is almost never separated from her water skin for this very reason. A waterbender in the desert is about as useful as a badgermole cub in a swimming pool.

Partway through The Last Airbender’s final season, however, that limitation becomes the basis for one of the show’s most horrifying revelations. Water is everywhere. You just have to do something terrible to access it.

Nineteen years ago today, on Nov. 9, 2007, “The Puppetmaster” introduced bloodbending, which allows a waterbender to manipulate the water inside another person’s body. Along with that extreme version of waterbending, we also learned that it’s possible to draw the water out of living things, or even the air itself.

These implications would eventually supply some of The Legend of Korra’s most frightening villains with their signature bending abilities. But its most disturbing achievement is what it does to Katara. In many ways, she’s the most virtuous of Team Avatar’s members, yet under the light of the full moon, she’s forced to learn arguably the most evil form of bending in existence.

“The Puppetmaster” opens with the gang telling horror stories around a campfire at night somewhere in the Fire Nation, immediately establishing a decidedly spooky vibe. An older innkeeper named Hama soon shows up and tells them that locals have been disappearing during the full moon. She offers them a safe place to stay. The story quickly evolves into something of a smalltown murder mystery where Toph is the hardnosed detective with Aang and Sokka as her hapless sidekicks.

Despite appearing a bit creepy and suspicious, Hama reveals that, just like Katara, she’s a waterbender from the Southern Water Tribe. Given the fact that the Fire Nation hunted and imprisoned most of the waterbenders from the south, leaving Katara as the only one left, Hama suddenly becomes the mentor Katara wanted for most of her life.

Hama teaches Katara that it’s possible to draw moisture from the air and extract water from plants, but doing so kills the fire lilies she demonstrates with. It’s an unsettling but practical answer to a waterbender’s most glaring struggle. Suddenly, a resourceful waterbender with no qualms about where their water comes from becomes the most potentially dangerous among the four bending styles.

By this point, Avatar had long since established that bending’s boundaries were negotiable. Lightning offered an advanced application of firebending that few could perform. Late in Book 2, Toph escaped captivity by discovering that metal wasn’t as separate from earth as everyone assumed. These breakthroughs rewarded exceptional skill and a willingness to question conventional wisdom.

Season 1 also established that certain cosmic events can influence bending. Sozin’s Comet dramatically strengthens firebending once every 100 years. Much like the tides, the waterbenders strength also stems from the moon. (It’s a little surprising that earth and air don’t get their own cosmic power boost in the same way.) That’s important because the full moon allows Hama to employ this base concept of manipulating water inside living things to its darkest potential.

On the night of the full moon, Hama reveals that she had been imprisoned by the Fire Nation for years with virtually no water. Over time, she developed bloodbending and practiced controlling the rats in her cell like puppets before applying the technique to her captors. She’s been abducting members of the Fire Nation as a form of revenge for the years of torture. The Fire Nation nearly wiped out the Water Nation's culture, so Hama sees it as their shared responsibility to return the favor. Katara refuses, which prompts an epic fight between the two where they both have to draw the water out of their surroundings to keep going.

Katara is able to resist Hama’s use of bloodbending on her, but after Aang and Sokka show up and are put in grave danger, Katara has to use it herself on Hama out of desperation. Even with the power boost from a full moon, bloodbending requires a tremendous amount of skill. A feat like this solidifies Katara’s place as one of her generation’s greatest waterbenders and is parallel to Toph discovering metalbending. The episode ends on a downer, however, with Katara bursting into tears out of regret as Hama cackles with delight that her legacy lives on.

Decades later, during the era presented in The Legend of Korra, various advanced forms of bending become far more prevalent than they were previously. Republic City’s police force is composed of master metalbenders. Firebenders generate lightning to provide electricity to the city. And one particularly frightening crime family masters bloodbending in ways that are far beyond what even Hama could have dreamed.

Book 1’s primary villain is a masked revolutionary called Amon who has the power to strip a person of their bending abilities. At first it appears to be a feat similar to the energy bending technique that Aang uses on Ozai, but it’s eventually revealed that Amon is actually a Northern Water Tribe waterbender named Noatak who, like his brother, inherited the ability to use psychic bloodbending. That meant they could bend a person’s blood without the full moon and without the use of hand gestures. Noatak took it even further and developed a way to sever a person’s internal energy paths, thereby stripping them of their bending altogether.

Toward the end of the season, we learn that Noatak’s father, Yakone, was a deadly crime boss who hid his powers for years. After he was sentenced to life imprisonment, he used bloodbending to subdue Sokka, Toph, and even Aang. But in the ensuing confrontation, Aang used the Avatar state to overpower Yakone and strip him of his bending.

Yakone later had sons, Noatak and Tarrlok, and forced them to practice bloodbending on animals and eventually each other. Like Hama, he treats the younger generation’s potential as instruments of revenge. As adults, Noatak assumes the alias of Amon to lead an insurrection while Tarrlok secretly infiltrates Republic City leadership to eventually become the chairman of the United Republic Council. While they weren’t working together (Amon even went on to take Tarrlok’s bending away), they both used bloodbending to enact their father’s vengeance in very different ways.

Interestingly, after Amon succeeds in taking away Korra’s water, earth, and firebending, it’s Katara that attempts to restore them through healing. Decades after Hama forced the power of bloodbending upon her, she comes face to face with the worst damage it can cause. Of course, season 1 ends with one of the franchise’s most uplifting scenes as Korra finally connects with her past selves and Aang is able to restore her bending fully. But seeing the Avatar nearly powerless because of an obscure extension of bloodbending is one of the scariest and boldest narrative choices the series has ever made.

All of this stems from one observation a tortured old woman made: Water exists inside living things. That made the element typically associated with healing become a means of domination. Nineteen years later, Katara’s reaction still unsettles me more than the technique itself. We’re used to cheering when heroes level up and discover a new power. But when that power is as frightening as bloodbending, it’s enough to make you want to cry.

#3485. This X-Men-Esque '80s Sci-Fi Series Launched Courteney Cox's Career

The premise of James D. Parriott's 1985 superhero/comedy series "Misfits of Science," which featured a young Courteney Cox, will sound very familiar to fans of Marvel Comics' X-Men titles.

The series follows a human scientist named Dr. Billy Hayes (Dean Paul Martin), who has taken an interest in what he called "human anomalies," which are people who have been born with a variety of unpredictable superpowers. In the show's pilot episode, he assembles the main cast of powerful castoffs with the intention of studying them, but also helping them come to terms with their supernatural abilities.

The team was small but mighty. It included Dr. Hayes' lab partner, Dr. Lincoln (Kevin Peter Hall), who can shrink for a limited period. Additionally, Mark Thomas Miller plays "Johnny B" Bukowski, a rocker who can suck up electricity and who wears shades to cover his glowing eyes. He can throw lightning bolts.

Most strikingly, Courteney Cox, future star of "Friends" and "Scream," plays Gloria, a troubled teen with "Carrie"-like telekinetic powers. "Misfits of Science" wasn't Cox's first credit: She had appeared in an episode of "As the World Turns" back in 1975, when she was still a kid, and famously danced with Bruce Springsteen in the "Dancing in the Dark" music video in 1984. "Misfits of Science," though, was the first time Cox starred in a TV series.

"Misfits of Science" is not currently available to stream, but resourceful media hunters will be able to find episodes online easily enough. It's a whimsical, lighthearted show that prodded at the conventions of superheroes as much as it vaunted them. It's definitely worth a glance.

"Misfits of Science," it should be noted, only lasted for a single 16-episode season, so it's okay if you don't remember it.

The series does have something of a superhero legacy, as R. Timothy Kring, a.k.a. Tim Kring, wrote an episode of "Misfits of Science," and he would go on to create the hit series "Heroes," the first season of which remains a must-watch (the later seasons, though, less so). Kring's "Misfits" episode, called "Twin Engines," is about a young man (Joel Polis) who is plagued with uncontrollable visions. It's eventually revealed that he was sharing the visions of his long-lost twin brother.

Indeed, the entire show was based on a long series of super-powered shenanigans and investigations. Mostly, the protagonists get involved in run-of-the-mill spy plots. The main characters aren't costumed vigilantes, but they do seem to operate as freelance spies. Famed drummer Mikey Jones appears in the show's pilot as a character with freezing powers named Ice Man. According to Giant Freakin' Robot, that character was abandoned after Marvel Comics "raised objections" over its own Ice Man character. And speaking of Marvel, Courteney Cox's character was very similar to the X-Men's Jean Gray.

Some fun trivia: Shortly after the time "Misfits of Science" was being made, Dr. Lincoln actor Kevin Peter Hall (who played the original Predator in John McTiernan's sci-fi action classic) was in contention to play either Data or Geordi La Forge on "Star Trek: The Next Generation." /Film has previously talked about all the finalists for the roles, and Hall eventually lost the roles to Brent Spiner and LeVar Burton, respectively.

As mentioned, "Misfits of Science" was not successful. Thanks to low ratings, the series was canceled before all of its episodes could even air, leaving one of them unaired in the United States.

Courteney Cox continued to work undeterred, of course. In 1987, she appeared in the low-budget, high-profile Cannon adaptation of "Masters of the Universe," a movie so goofy, it has been subjected to a "How Did This Get Made" oral history. That same year, she began playing the recurring role of Lauren Miller on the hit sitcom "Family Ties." By 1994, she was appearing in the comedy "Ace Ventura: Pet Detective" and began playing one of the six lead roles on "Friends." "Misfits of Science" was her first starring role, but it certainly wasn't her last.

#3484. Bond 26 Director Teases The Next 007 Casting Reveal In Unexpected Moment

The director of Bond 26 almost names the next 007 before retracting his claims to reveal the new actor who will take on the role.

Bond 26 is the upcoming installment in the James Bond film series, which follows the adventures of 007, a British secret agent working for MI6. Although specific plot details remain shrouded in mystery, the movie is expected to feature a different take on the titular character, bringing the agent back to the big screen with a new face and story.

Bond 26 director Denis Villeneuve has found a humorous way to address the rumors that have been swirling on the internet regarding the iconic franchise's next actor. With Daniel Craig having concluded his five-film run as the secret agent, speculation about his successor has been spreading like wildfire. Although many insiders have claimed that several actors have auditioned for the role, Amazon MGM Studios has not confirmed any casting information about the new leading man.

According to IGN, Villeneuve poked fun at all the reports about who the next Bond was that have been surfacing on the internet. The director, best known for Dune, Dune: Part Two, Arrival, and Blade Runner 2049, was at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art's annual Art+Film Gala, where he decided to play a little joke at the expense of the studio.

IGN stated that Villeneuve unexpectedly brought up the next James Bond during the closing moments of a speech. After expressing his appreciation for Amazon, the director joked that he was about to announce the identity of the actor taking over the role. However, just as he was about to say a name, Villeneuve abruptly stopped himself. He playfully explained that revealing the information would be enough to give producer Amy Pascal a heart attack.

To express my gratitude with the blessing of my new friends at Amazon, I will reveal to you tonight who will be the next James Bond. The new James Bond is… and I will stop right now because Amy Pascal is about to have a heart attack. Thank you very much.

Although Villeneuve wasn't being serious and wasn't seriously considering revealing anything, his comments arrived during a transitional period for the franchise. The upcoming film will introduce the first new James Bond since Craig's departure in 2021's No Time to Die, which ended his run as the character after 15 years.

Recent reports have connected actors including Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O'Connor, Robert Pattinson, and Nicholas Hoult to Bond 26. However, none of these performers has been officially announced as Craig's successor, and their alleged involvement should not be interpreted as confirmation that any of them have received the role.

There is no official release date for Bond 26 at the time of this article's publication.

#3483. This Chilling Japanese Folk Horror Series Is One Of Hulu's Best Hidden Gems

If you're in the mood for a discrete dose of folk horror, Hulu recently added Adam Scott's terrifying horror "Hokum." But if you'd like to extend your trauma over, say two seasons of sheer terror, then "Gannibal" is for you. The show stars Yuya Yagira as a police officer who leaves the city to start over in a remote village. Here, he quickly discovers things aren't quite as idyllic as they seem.

"Gannibal" premiered in December 2022 but has failed to make much of an impact outside of Japan, despite arguably being one of the best horror series of the 2020s. Thus far, two seasons of "Gannibal" have been released, and had they hit Netflix in the United States, the show may well have become a big hit stateside. As it stands, this is one of Japan's best kept secrets and it's waiting to be discovered on Hulu.

Masaaki Ninomiya's "Gannibal" manga was originally serialized across thirteen volumes from October 2018 to November 2021. In October of that year, it was announced that "Gannibal" would be adapted as a TV series, with Shinzo Katayama directing from teleplays by Takamasa Oe.Thankfully, it turned out to be a worthy adaptation.

One of the best foreign horror shows streaming right now, "Gannibal" shares much in common with the South Korean horror movie with a 99% Rotten Tomatoes score "The Wailing." Both are set in remote villages and follow a police officer who becomes increasingly menaced by some terrifying ancient evil. But "Gannibal" departs from the movie with its tale of a cannibal conspiracy.

Yuya Yagira plays police officer Daigo Agawa, who after an unfortunate ordeal in Tokyo moves to the small mountain village of Kuge with his wife Yuki Agawa (Riho Yoshioka) and daughter Mashiro Agawa (Kokone Shimizu). At first, this secluded hamlet seems like the ideal refuge from the city and Agawa's fraught past. But things get off to an eerie start as Kuge's previous police officer has mysteriously vanished.

As Agawa and his family become more acquainted with the village and its people they discover the Goto family essentially run the town, and they don't seem like the most charming bunch. Meanwhile, a woman's body is found on the mountain, and while the Gotos claim she was killed by a bear, Agawa notices a human bite mark. Soon, his family's escape starts to turn into a nightmare. As such, this is not a horror TV show you can watch with the whole family. But it definitely deserves your attention regardless.

While you may never have heard of "Gannibal," the series has become a sensation in its native Japan. In April 2025, The Hollywood Reporter reported that "Gannibal" had become the most-viewed title in the country on Disney+ since its second season debuted in March of that year. The show also set new records for the streamer, solidifying its status as a bonafide mega-hit in Japan. In the United States, however, "Gannibal" mostly flew under the radar.

There are no "top critic" reviews for the series on Rotten Tomatoes, and it hasn't shown up on any "best horror series" lists since its 2022 debut. But it has managed to generate a small amount of buzz among non-Japanese viewers. One Redditor described the series as "grim folk horror" and was evidently left "completely wrecked" by it. Elsewhere on Reddit, another user described the series as "like 'Midsommar' meets 'Resident Evil 7'" and praised the "amazing actors, great cinematography, chilling and memorable soundtrack, and an absurdly dark story."

Letterboxd users are similarly impressed. "I just love it," writes one, who goes on to commend the series for its "sharp plot," "creepy characters," and "unsettling vibes," as well as the "splendid cinematography." Another also highlighted how the show is "beautifully shot and incredibly well-acted." Unfortunately, it seems unlikely there will be more to come. "Gannibal" Season 2 was released on March 19, 2025 and that wrapped up the story told in Masaaki Ninomiya's manga. Thankfully, if you are able to binge your way through both seasons of the series, there are plenty of great folk horror movies to tide you over.

So don't even try to tell anyone there's nothing on.

Horror master Mike Flanagan (Haunting of Hill House, Midnight Mass) re-imagines Stephen King's tale of teenage telekinesis, taking the story from the 1970s to now, complete with cyber bullying, smart phones, and a modern sensibility. The core of the tale, though, remains the same, as does the titular character's bloody coming-of-age. Powered by a talented young cast that includes Siena Agudong as Susan and Summer H. Howell as the title character, Carrie is a trick-or-treat for horror fans. Stream Carrie on Prime.

Based on John Steinbeck's pillar of Western literature, East of Eden follows three generations of the hardscrabble Hamilton family and the upscale Trask family, farming and ranching clans in California's Salinas Valley. The show's production is a multigenerational story too: It was written and created by Zoe Kazan, whose grandpa Elia directed the 1955 film version of East of Eden. All respect to Elia Kazan, but Steinbeck's story is so massive, it needs a seven-part mini-series. East of Eden is the kind of sprawling, melodramatic story that episodic television was made for. Stream East of Eden on Netflix.

Like Carrie, Crystal Lake reimagines a horror classic—in this case, Friday the 13th—and expands the lore even beyond the 12 films in the franchise. If you've ever wondered how Pamela Voorhees, played here by Linda Cardellini, became a serial murderer, and how her son Jason ended up a relentless, camp-counselor-killing-machine who lives at the bottom of a lake, Crystal Lake has all the answers. In a lot of ways, this show is better than all of the movies. Stream Crystal Lake on Peacock.

Apple TV's Slow Horses delivers a realistic, nuanced take on espionage by detailing the lives of the losers of British Intelligence. Instead of chiseled good guys and gals saving the world, the agents of Slough House are a team of dysfunctional, troubled souls trying to do the right thing (usually) in a morally gray world, just like real agents. Their leader, gruff, obnoxious Jackson Lamb, is played to perfection by Gary Oldman. Slow Horses has an almost perfect Rotten Tomatoes score over its first five seasons, and season 6 is setting new records. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV+.

DC's TV revamp of Green Lantern details what happens when experienced Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) trains the new guy, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), on how to wield the mysterious and powerful Green Lantern Ring. It's a reserved, neo-noir style take on the comic mythos, as the heroes investigate a series of murders tied to an extraterrestrial threat. Lanterns is pulling in a better than 90% fresh ratings from Rotten Tomatoes, so it's definitely worth a stream. Stream Lanterns on HBO Max.

Created by Jesse McKeown and starring Josh Hartnett, Charlie Heaton, and Mackenzie Davis, Below is set in a Newfoundland fishing village beset with aquatic horror. When the Canadian government offers the residents of Snooks Arm a ton of money to relocate, no one really knows why, but ice fisherman Calvin Penney (Hartnett) suspects it has something to do with the monster he saw under the ice when he was a child. If you like taut creature feature style horror, check out Below. Stream Below on Netflix.

Season four of Ted Lasso sees the title character, played by Jason Sudeikis, returning to the UK to take on a new challenge: coaching the Lady Greyhounds, AFC Richmond's second-division women's football team. This multiple Emmy Award-winning series still has all the heart, humor, and positivity of the original run. Stream Ted Lasso on Apple TV+.

The mystery that drives creepy coming-of-age drama Phony is killer: Sonny Cooke, played by Sam Nivola, is a teenager with a very close relationship to his devoted single mother Ellen, played by Connie Britton. After a freak car accident, he wakes up convinced that his mom is an impostor. She looks the same, but there's something off about her in a way that Sonny can't describe, so he sets out to solve the mystery. Phony is rated over 90% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes. Stream Phony on Hulu.

In season four of political thriller series The Diplomat, the Kate Wyler, played by Keri Russell, finds that diplomatic relations between the U.S. and the UK are starting to crumble, and so is her marriage. Meanwhile, U.S. president Grace Penn, played by Allison Janney, and VP Hal Wyler, played by Rufus Sewell, continue their conspiracy to steal a Russian super-weapon, nudging the nation toward war with our longtime adversary. In other words, it's an international mess, with a few powerful people keeping the world from descending into chaos. If you like political intrigue, this is the series for you. Stream The Diplomat on Netflix.

Who doesn't love a sprawling organized crime drama? In Mobland, the crime is being organized in Great Britain, where two warring London crime families, the Harrigans and Stevensons, are locked in a battle for underworld power. In the middle of the crossfire is Harry Da Souza, a gritty fixer played to gruff perfection by Tom Hardy. Season 2 finds Da Souza in the unenviable position of holding together the Harrigan family on the verge of civil war. If you like backstabbing, scheming, murder, and other tropes of high-stakes crime thrillers, you'll like Mobland. Stream Mobland on Paramount+.

#3481. Patrick Stewart's '90s Fantasy Movie With Neve Campbell Is Streaming For Free

An adaptation of Oscar Wilde's 1887 short story, Sydney Macartney's "The Canterville Ghost" aired on ABC on January 27, 1996, and, perhaps surprisingly, featured notable central roles for both the late legend Sir Patrick Stewart and Neve Campbell. Indeed, 1996 was a banner year for both actors, with Stewart appearing in the film "Star Trek: First Contact" and Campbell headlining two of the best teen movies of the 1990s over the same 12-month period (namely, "The Craft" and "Scream"). Stewart, of course, was already riding high professionally by that point. But for Campbell, this was the final vault before proper stardom following her breakout role on the hit series "Party of Five."

It should be noted that Wilde's original story is a light tale about a haunted mansion, and Macartney's TV movie — which is currently streaming for free on platforms like Tubi and Prime Video — affects a similarly lighthearted tone. Wilde's source material concerns the Otises, a family of two parents and three children who move into Canterville Castle, despite warnings that it is haunted. Sure enough, its ghost tries to frighten them off, but the Otises react with mere annoyance. For example, when Mrs. Otis spots a bloodstain on the carpet, she dryly states, "I don't at all care for blood-stains in a sitting-room."

Macartney's adaptation transposes the action to the modern day. In the movie, the Otises inevitably have to deal with the specter of Sir Simon de Canterville, played by Stewart. Campbell, meanwhile, plays the young Virginia Otis, and the story is told largely from her perspective. As for Sir Simon, he eventually reveals the trauma that left him in his ghostly state, which has to do with his beloved dead wife, Eleanor.

The TV movie version of "The Canterville Ghost" adds a few fun flourishes to the story. The Otis family patriarch, Hiram, is played by Edward Wiley, and there comes a scene where Virginia and the Ghost, having begun communicating, have to convince Hiram that ghosts are real. In a nod to Sir Patrick Stewart's past with the Royal Shakespeare Company, Virginia and the Ghost get Hiram's attention by staging a scene from "Hamlet" wherein Sir Simon plays the Ghost of Hamlet's Father. Fittingly enough, Stewart would later portray both the Ghost of Hamlet's Father and Claudius in a celebrated 2008 BBC production of the play opposite David Tennant.

Initially, as mentioned, Sir Simon is determined to scare away the Otis family to remain in his sad, ghostly state. Soon after moving in, however, Virginia finds a secret passageway inside the Canterville Castle leading to a chamber where Sir Simon hangs out during the daylight hours. Soon, she and her brothers befriend Sir Simon, and we learn that, despite his intense demeanor, he isn't so terrible or scary. (Virginia's brothers even startle Sir Simon with a fake ghost puppet they construct themselves.) At the same time, Virginia develops a crush on Francis, the Duke of Cheshire (Daniel Betts), a local nobleman who plays a larger role here than he does in Oscar Wilde's original story.

The central drama arises when Hiram believes Virginia is responsible for Sir Simon's shenanigans and threatens to send her back home to the U.S., where she won't be able to flirt with Francis anymore. This is basically her motivation for proving the ghost is real because, again, "The Canterville Ghost" is a fairly fanciful yarn.

There aren't a lot of professional reviews of the "Canterville Ghost" TV movie readily available. One can find a write-up on Common Sense Media by Brian Costello, who gave the film a high rating (which indicates that it's perfectly okay for younger kids). Costello also praised Patrick Stewart, writing that he brings a Shakespearean relish to his character. "[H]is performance," the review reads, "more than makes up for the dated special effects."

David Saunderson, writing for the British/Irish horror website Spooky Isles, had some mild complaints about how the TV movie strays from Oscar Wilde's original story. With weary resignation, he observed that Otises had to be made American for American audiences, despite being British in Wilde's source material. He added that the movie isn't as good as the 1944 film adaptation starring Charles Laughton in the title role and that he found the modern contrivances to be a little tiresome, despite Stewart's solid work. As he put it:

"Patrick Stewart is a fine actor, and fine actors make fine Canterville Ghosts — he's very dramatic, a bit scary, and works well with Neve Campbell [...] who plays the Otis daughter who hates that she has been brought to England but soon befriends the ghost and learns from the experience — blah, blah, blah — usual teenage angst in TV movie!"

Notably, 1996's "The Canterville Ghost" won an Emmy for Outstanding Individual Achievement in Music Composition for a Miniseries or Special, which is no small feat. Stream it now, and see what you make of it.

#3480. This New Chrome AI Feature Reads Your Gmail to Make Filling Out Web Forms Easier

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Chrome is making it easier to autofill online forms with more than just contact information and credit card numbers. For users with Personal Intelligence enabled, Gemini will now suggest items like order numbers, tracking information, membership IDs, and booking confirmations from Gmail messages when completing forms in Chrome.

Chrome's expanded autofill capabilities use Gemini to read your emails and surface suggestions, meaning you don't have to click back and forth between tabs or manually search for codes or confirmations in your inbox. When you click a form field that has a corresponding piece of data, a pop-up menu appears and indicates that an item is "Suggested by Gemini." You can click this to autofill the suggestion as well as open an additional menu to see the specific source (the original email) or remove the suggestion. The latter doesn't delete anything from Gmail; it simply dismisses the suggestion in Chrome.

As Android Police reports, Google started testing enhanced autofill in Chrome this summer using data from other connected apps like Google Photos. The feature currently rolling out is specific to Gmail and is coming first to U.S. users who have Personal Intelligence enabled on desktop as well as in the Android and iOS apps when using Gemini in Chrome.

In the blog post announcing the enhanced autofill feature, Google states that "sensitive data is encrypted" and that users can manage autofill, including enabling or disabling enhanced suggestions, via Chrome's settings.

#3479. Sebastián Lelio, Chilean Director of Oscar-Winning ‘A Fantastic Woman,’ Dead at 52

Sebastián Lelio, the humanistic Chilean filmmaker whose trans drama “A Fantastic Woman” won the Best International Feature Film Oscar in 2018, has died at age 52.

The Chilean publication Emol first revealed the news that he was found dead in his home in Santiago on Friday, November 6, amid an undisclosed health issue. His body was discovered by his partner, the actress/director Amalia Kassai, who starred in his final film, the protest musical “The Wave” from Cannes 2025. Kassai also posted a statement in Spanish on her Instagram account.

Lelio was reportedly mid-production on the feature “Chilean Poet,” adapted from Alejandro Zambra’s Viking-published 2022 novel. Along with “A Fantastic Woman,” he also directed the Hasidic lesbian romance “Disobedience” in the same year, 2017; it starred Rachel McAdams and Rachel Weisz, and helped bring the filmmaker to international prominence. In 2013, he directed Paulina García to a Berlinale Silver Bear Best Actress win with “Gloria,” a late-in-life romantic comedy about a 58-year-old divorcee starting over again. He remade his own film in 2018 in English as “Gloria Bell,” released by A24 and starring Julianne Moore in the role García originated, opposite John Turturro.

Lelio regularly collaborated with the Chilean brothers Pablo Larraín and Juan de Dios Larraín, who served as producers on nearly all of his films. They were also collaborating with Lelio on his ongoing, now-final feature. Born in Argentina, he emigrated to Chile at age two with his mother and later graduated from Chilean Film School, after which he launched his career with short films and music videos. His debut narrative feature, “The Sacred Family,” premiered at the San Sebastián International Film Festival in Spain before his follow-up, “Navidad,” premiered at Cannes in 2009. The post-Chilean-earthquake drama “The Year of the Tiger,” starring beloved Chilean actor Luis Dubó, debuted at Locarno in 2011.

His fourth feature, “Gloria,” shot digitally and with a script and dialogue developed in part with his actors, including García, received U.S. distribution from Roadside Attractions and was widely regarded as one of the best films of 2013.

Lelio directed the first Best International Feature Oscar entry to win the Academy Award with 2017’s Golden Bear-nominated “A Fantastic Woman,” an exuberantly styled drama that put trans actress Daniela Vega on the international map. As Vega consulted on the script, it’s widely seen as a groundbreaker of trans portrayals onscreen in the 21st century. And it helped reform the perception and attitudes toward transness in Lelio and Vega’s home of Chile — and inevitably, within the Academy.

Lelio’s favorite films on the 2022 Sight & Sound poll included “La Dolce Vita,” “Playtime,” “The 400 Blows,” and “Singin’ in the Rain,” and you can feel their impact across his often irreverent, at times burstingly colorful, playful body of work.

His 2017 TIFF premiere “Disobedience” received U.S. distribution from Bleecker Street, and told the story of a forbidden, transgressive romance between two Orthodox Jewish women (McAdams and Weisz) in North London. The tender, taboo drama performed well in North America, grossing nearly $3.5 million domestic during a spring-through-summer 2018 run.

Lelio, that year, deftly remade “Gloria” as “Gloria Bell” with Julianne Moore as the free-spirited divorcee being wooed by John Turturro, and weighing choices in her next chapter living as a yoga instructor in Los Angeles. Returning to filming after the pandemic, Lelio broadened his collaborative scope to adapt “Room” author Emma Donoghue’s “The Wonder,” with Donoghue and Alice Birch co-writing the script with him. Florence Pugh starred as a British nurse sent to Ireland to observe a miraculous “fasting girl,” in a film that played Telluride and streamed on Netflix to strong reviews.

His last film, “The Wave,” took a minute to get off the ground after playing out of competition in Cannes 2025. The story of an introverted music student whose passion for protest is awakened amid a growing feminist movement on campus, “The Wave” received a small release from Wolfe Video earlier this year and received positive response throughout its festival run.

The status of Lelio’s final film isn’t known right now, but we can imagine that Lelio’s sensitive approach to character — and unstable identities finding their footing, their purest expression — will carry into the new work. The Larraín brothers were also producing the film, with Lelio’s regular cinematographer Benjamín Echazarreta on board as DP.

#3478. Patrick Dempsey's Thanksgiving Horror Movie Is Worth Revisiting This Holiday Season

Eli Roth's 2023 slasher flick "Thanksgiving" follows various citizens of Plymouth, Massachusetts, as they find themselves being targeted by a killer dressed as the famed Pilgrim John Carver in the lead-up to the titular holiday. Realizing that these murders are related to a Black Friday trampling incident from the previous year (which led to three people dying), it falls to Plymouth's sheriff, Eric Newlon (Patrick Dempsey), to figure out who's been taking some Turkey Day-related revenge.

There aren't too many scary flicks centered around this particular holiday, but Roth's film has now joined the modest pantheon of Thanksgiving horror movies that includes Brad F. Grinter's schlock classic "Blood Freak," the utterly absurd "ThanksKilling," the pointed anticapitalist flick "Black Friday," and Oliver Blackburn's "Kristy." Indeed, Roth's "Thanksgiving" is the perfect horror movie to watch this November, or any November, really. Like most of his other R-rated offerings, its gore is gleefully over the top, and there's gallows humor present throughout.

"Thanksgiving" began its life as a fake trailer that Roth directed for 2007's two-in-one "Grindhouse," itself an attempt by directors Robert Rodriguez and Quentin Tarantino to recreate the experience of going to a rundown grindhouse double feature circa the 1970s or '80s. They each helmed one down-and-dirty B-movie, giving them fake film scratches and print wear to boot. The program also featured a brief reel of previews for non-existent B-movies, one of which was the gory slasher "Thanksgiving." It took Roth 16 years, but he later expanded that fake promo into a real feature film. Now, it's appointment holiday viewing.

"Thanksgiving" was, by dint of its novelty, something of a hit. On a budget of only $15 million, it made $46.6 million at the box office and, perhaps surprisingly, earned pretty good reviews. Not only that, "Thanksgiving" also has a higher critical approval score on Rotten Tomatoes than any of Eli Roth's other feature-length directorial efforts, among them the mostly well-received "The House with a Clock in Its Walls" and the critically lambasted bomb "Borderlands."

"Thanksgiving" seemingly got a lot of mileage from its creative kills. One victim, for instance, is murdered, cooked, trussed up like a turkey, and served at a table surrounded by hostages and victims. (This kill is featured in Roth's original fake trailer as well.) In addition, "Thanksgiving" features the kind of fun, splattery deaths that slasher fans crave, among them a decapitation, a disemboweling, and a trampoline stabbing.

Meanwhile, Patrick Dempsey's character is crucial to the movie's central plot, which makes sense, seeing as the actor is the film's big celebrity "get." Pop singer Addison Rae, Nell Verlaque, Jalen Thomas Brooks (aka Mateo from "The Pitt"), and Milo Manheim round out the cast, with Gina Gershon joining them in a small role.

The Black Friday trampling might make one think that "Thanksgiving" is constructed as a pointed anti-shopping satire, lampooning the bizarreness that takes place at many retail outlets the day after Thanksgiving. Roth, however, is more keen on dark humor and gooey gore than anything thoughtful. That's more of his métier. However you feel about the filmmaker, he certainly knows the power of ridiculous kill scenes.

Again, critics generally accepted "Thanksgiving" as good, silly fun. Alonso Duralde and Christy Lemire, the co-hosts of the review show "Breakfast All Day," were both positive on the film, with Duralde saying that it makes for a great movie to see with a crowd and Lemire stressing that she had a great time. They both loved the film's cast, too, with Lemire admiring that, Addison Rae notwithstanding, it wasn't just famous person stunt casting. Eli Roth even commented on the movie's casting in an exclusive interview with /Film, so he is at least astute in that regard.

Reviewing "Thanksgiving" for IndieWire, Alison Foreman gave the film an A-, writing:

"With more time dedicated to table-setting than gorging on gore, Roth and [writer Jeff] Rendell create a living-breathing corner of the United States that's actually worth terrorizing. The people populating this fictional version of Plymouth don't feel 'real,' per se, but they're toxically relatable, and the complicated relationship they have with Thanksgiving is as politically charged as it is annoyingly pointless in life."

Foreman's only issue with "Thanksgiving" was that it relies very heavily on characters checking Instagram to tell its story, and it makes a lot of references to billionaire mogul Mark Cuban (!), meaning the film will feel incredibly dated very quickly. Although, she did enjoy the soundtrack, which includes bands like the Misfits and The Waitresses.

But then, all films become dated eventually, so that's hardly a cardinal sin. If you're looking for a fun Thanksgiving movie this holiday, and you are allergic to sentimentality, then maybe "Thanksgiving" will be more your beat.

#3476. Deadpool 2's Rob Delaney Debunks Popular X-Men Fan Theory About His Character Peter

No, X-Men fans, Peter from "Deadpool 2" and "Deadpool & Wolverine" is not Peter Wisdom. Peter actor Rob Delaney confirmed this in a red carpet interview with ScreenRant, and we offer our deepest nerd condolences to anyone who may have been invested in this.

The presence of Delaney's character Peter, a supporting player in David Leitch's 2018 action/comedy "Deadpool 2," is a joke unto itself. Deadpool (Ryan Reynolds) is assembling a team of superheroes called the X-Force that he intends to employ for a skydiving-based rescue mission. Deadpool is such a non-credible deadbeat, though, that he can't afford to be too choosy about who joins his team. He recruits characters like Shatterstar (Lewis Tan), Domino (Zazie Beetz), and Bedlam (Terry Crews), but also deigns to take on Peter, a regular, kind of dorky middle-aged guy with no superpowers.

When the trailer for "Deadpool 2" first dropped, /Film theorized that Delaney could be playing Peter Wisdom, an X-Men character with deep ties to X-Force. The character was first introduced in an issue of the Britain-set X-Men comic "Excalibur," dated February of 1995, and, like all comic book characters, he underwent multiple dramatic life events in a very short amount of time. He dated Shadowcat, became the mentor for X-Force, seemingly died, returned, and became the head of a spy agency. In the comics, Pete Wisdom can absorb heat from the environment around him and channel it into magical "hot knives" that protrude from his fingers.

The character also starred in his own series of comics in 2006 called simply "Wisdom," and he likely has at least a few fans out there. For those who think he appeared in the "Deadpool" movies, though, that wasn't Peter Wisdom. That was just Peter.

The issue of Peter's identity may be a little confusing, as sources like Wikipedia list Rob Delaney as definitely playing Pete Wisdom in both "Deadpool 2" and the 2024 follow-up "Deadpool & Wolverine." On IMDb, however, his proper credit of just "Peter" is retained. In the red carpet interview, Delaney was 100% unambiguous on the matter, saying:

"Peter Wisdom is a guy from the comics. My character is not Peter Wisdom. He's just a guy named Peter. And I think maybe they arbitrarily gave him the last initial 'W,' which explains the confusion. But in fact, [he's] just Peter, created from whole cloth by the writers."

Sometimes actors in Marvel Comics-based movies have to be coy about spoilers and plot details, but it seems that Delaney is not being coy in this case. He seems to genuinely be saying he isn't playing Pete Wisdom.

The arc of Delaney's actual character is pretty hilarious unto itself. Peter is recruited into X-Force, meets a grisly fate, is saved through the miracle of time travel, and then proves to be deeply beloved across the multiverse in "Deadpool & Wolverine." Peter turns up in that film's climax, which involves hundreds of parallel-universe Deadpools pouring through an interdimensional portal to fight each other. When Peter arrives on the scene, however, every Deadpool pauses to marvel at his presence. It seems that all Deadpools have a Peter in their home dimension, and that they all hold him in very high esteem. The hundreds of Deadpools embrace Peter, and he enjoys the attention.

With a universe as long-lived and complex as Marvel Comics, of course, some fans may happily chime in with an optimistic "never say die" attitude about Rob Delaney playing Pete Wisdom. Indeed, as "Deadpool & Wolverine" proved, every character in the Marvel Cinematic Universe has an untold number of parallel doppelgängers from all across the multiverse. Even if the original Pete Wisdom is a suave British James Bond-type with heat knife powers, and the movie Peter is a dippy American everyman, there's no reason why those characters can't be one and the same across the multiverse, right?

And, heck, "Deadpool 2" made a lot of vital changes to known comic book characters, including the aforementioned Shatterstar, a.k.a Rusty. In the comics, Shatterstar is an interdimensional traveler from Mojoworld, something he does explain in "Deadpool 2." But in the movie, he doesn't become a vital member of the team. Indeed, he has an unfortunate run-in with a helicopter. Deadpool, thereafter, quips that no one is going to miss Shatterstar. Nonetheless, the character returned for a very brief cameo in "Deadpool & Wolverine."

So why not do something like that for Pete Wisdom? As of this writing, /Film has been gathering information about the upcoming X-Men film from Marvel Studios, citing a familiar line-up and keeping track of pieces of casting. (Inde Navarrette from "Obsession" has been cast as the character of Rogue, for instance.) Time will tell if the makers of the new X-Men will have enough of a sense of humor to cast Rob Delaney as Pete Wisdom.
