#3458. Apple Is About to Release a Touchscreen MacBook Pro (Plus Four More Devices)

Apple has had a busy fall. Head to the company's website, and you'll immediately be greeted by a sea of new products: the foldable iPhone Duo; the iPhone 18 Pro; HomePod mini 2; Apple Watch Series 12; the list goes on. It seems, under new Apple CEO Jon Ternus, the company is ready for a refresh of just about every product it sells. To that point, the company seems far from finished. Just this week, Apple is planning to release five brand new products, each launching on Friday. While four of these are Macs, Apple does have a new iPad in the works, as well. Here's everything new Apple is releasing this week.

Finally. For the first time, the iPad mini is about to ship with an OLED display. Apple's smallest tablet has always come with a standard screen. Despite its price tag, the iPad mini has never come with an OLED display, or even a mini-LED screen, until now. With this new model, there is no backlight. As such, each individual pixel on the iPad's display will be able to shut itself off when displaying dark content. That will benefit the content you watch on this device, as well as the overall contrast of the screen.

Beyond the new OLED panel, the new iPad mini is thinner and lighter than the previous model. It also comes with Apple's newest A20 Pro chip, the same processor the company put in its iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo smartphones. The new device starts at $699 for 128GB of storage, though there are various upgrades, including nano-texture glass (add $100) and cellular (add $150).

Good news: There's a new iMac. Bad news: Not much is different here from the previous model. The biggest change here is the new M6 chip, which Apple says is up to five times faster than the iMac with M4 and up to 12 times faster than the iMac with M1. With that M6 chip, the iMac now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Other than that, this is the same iMac you may already know: It comes with a 24-inch LED display (no OLED, unfortunately), two or four USB-C ports (depending on the configuration), and a built-in 12MP webcam. If you're looking for a new all-in-one computer, or you've been considering upgrading your older iMac, this is likely a great choice. But if you already have an M-series iMac, it's not such an obvious upgrade. (My M1 iMac may be up to 12 times slower, but it's still plenty fast for me.) Apple didn't change the price here: The M6 iMac still starts at $1,499 for two ports, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage.

Similarly, Apple's newest 14-inch MacBook Pro isn't much different from the previous model—save for the new processor. This model also comes with Apple's M6 chip, which Apple says is up to 13 times faster for AI processing than the M1 MacBook Pro. (Apple seems keen on convincing stubborn M1 users to upgrade this cycle.) Now, the company is offering this model of MacBook Pro in three chipsets, depending on use case: M6 for "entry-level" pro work; M5 Pro for mid-tier pro work; and M5 Max for the most demanding situations.

But, like the M6 iMac, this is the same MacBook Pro Apple sold before. It has a 14-inch mini-LED display with a refresh rate up to 120Hz. It comes with three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, an HDMI port, and an SDXC card slot. It, too, has a 12MP webcam for video calls. Apple's newest MacBook Pro starts at $1,999, but you can quickly ramp up that price tag with screen, chip, memory, or storage upgrades.

Apple's most exciting product launch this week is undoubtedly the new touchscreen MacBook Pros. Unlike the M6 MacBook Pro, which only comes in the 14-inch variant, Apple's first touchscreen laptop comes in both 14- and 16-inch options. Apple says this touchscreen lets you scroll, zoom, or draw on the display. That works with basic functions, like web browsing or selecting files, but also with specific workflows, like playing virtual instruments in Logic Pro, or manipulating an object in a 3D modeling app. Like the iPad mini, this laptop comes with an OLED display (Apple calls it PROLED XDR), with up to 1,000 nits of typical brightness and 2,000 nits of HDR brightness. It also brings back the backlit Apple logo, something I've missed on my last two MacBooks.

This MacBook Pro also comes with the iPhone's Dynamic Island for the first time. This replaces the "notch" that other MacBook Pros and MacBook Airs currently ship with. It can function as a basic webcam, but also as a dedicated zone for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI. This machine comes in either M5 Pro or M5 Max variants—no M6 for this model—as Apple seems to be positioning it exclusively for the most taxing situations (particularly AI). The company says the new MacBook Pro has up to 13 more hours of battery life than Intel-based MacBook Pros, and can fast charge up to 50% in 30 minutes. It's essentially a supercharged version of the existing MacBook Pro.

As such, this is Apple's most expensive laptop. The 14-inch M5 Pro version starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399. However, you can configure these machines to have outrageous price tags. The maxed-out 16-inch MacBook Pro is $14,549, roughly half of which is the 16TB of RAM.

#3457. Kevin Costner's Forgotten 117-Minute Action Thriller Is Mandatory Viewing on HBO Max

While he has been one of the biggest names in entertainment for more than four decades, Kevin Costner isn't immune to his movies getting overlooked by audiences. Just a couple of years ago, his long-awaited Western project Horizon: An American Saga totally bombed at the box office, putting the film's planned sequels on hold. Not every movie can be Dances With Wolves or Bull Durham, and a couple are going to slip through the cracks every now and again.

Such is the fate of a 12-year-old thriller that starred Costner as an international spy battling brain cancer. 3 Days to Kill, directed by Charlie's Angels helmer McG, was released in 2014 to mixed reviews and a less-than-stellar box office performance. More than a decade later, however, the thriller is streaming on HBO Max, where it is looking to capture a new audience, and remind folks of how consistently great Costner has been over the years.

When it first hit theaters back in 2014, 3 Days to Kill made just over $53 million at the global box office. That's not the worst result imaginable, considering its production was right around $28 million, but suffice it to say the film didn't really latch on with audiences. A lot of folks, even major Costner fans, missed out on the thriller the first time around, leaving it up to home media releases and streaming to help it build an audience over time.

3 Days to Kill isn't the best of its genre — not by a long shot — but it does feel like the kind of movie that would've easily found a following at Blockbusters or on cable reruns back in the day. It's very much an afternoon TNT kind of flick. Now, with streaming lineups as filled to the brim as they are, a film like this is a little harder to discover. That said, it's kind of the perfect rainy day or late night watch on HBO Max, especially with its stacked cast that will keep your attention throughout.

If you're one of the many who missed 3 Days to Kill over the years, it's the same kind of thriller you've seen a bunch of times before, but with a few fresh wrinkles and a pretty great cast. Costner stars as Ethan Renner, a CIA operative who has discovered that he's dying of brain cancer. With the sickness changing his entire outlook on life, his new focus is on getting out of the spy game and fixing his relationship with his estranged wife and teenage daughter. While spending time with said daughter, he's given a final job — a job he only takes because the payment includes an experimental drug that could potentially save his life. Renner now has to navigate the tangled web of a dangerous international conspiracy while also protecting his daughter, who is now accidentally caught up in the mess as well.

Costner was obviously the big draw for 3 Days to Kill, but he's one of several notable stars in the cast. Connie Nielsen plays his wife, while Hailee Steinfeld co-stars as their daughter. The film also stars Amber Heard as a fellow agent in the CIA, as well as Justified's Raymond J. Barry, who plays the CIA director.

#3456. Eric Bauza’s Final ‘Looney Tunes’ Performance Is ‘Daffy Season,’ Now in Theaters Ahead of ‘The Cat in the Hat’

The death of Eric Bauza in October shocked the entertainment industry. An impressively prolific voice actor, it would’ve been nearly impossible for anybody engaging with animation over the past 15 years to never come across his work. Bauza’s death came just two months after the delayed release of “Coyote vs. Acme,” the “Looney Tunes” feature once deemed unreleasable by Warner Bros. Discovery and later sold off to Ketchup Entertainment. The film, which grossed $101 million worldwide, is a true showcase for Bauza, who lends his voice to a plethora of iconic characters, including Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn, Tweety, and Porky Pig. Related Stories Box Office: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Thunders with $31.6 Million, Scoring the Biggest Debut Ever for a Live-Action, Foreign Language Film Box Office: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Roars with $6.7 Million in Previews, ‘Ramayana: Rise of a Legend’ Earns $3.5 Million

Bauza became something of the defining voice of modern “Looney Tunes” in his final years. Fans can see him give one final performance with the property in “Daffy Season,” a 7-minute animated short that plays before screenings of “The Cat in the Hat,” opening Friday from Skydance’s Warner Bros. Pictures. A representative for the studio confirmed to IndieWire that the short is Bauza’s final “Looney Tunes” movie. Bauza is also credited as providing additional voices for “The Cat in the Hat.”

“Daffy Season” centers on Daffy Duck, voiced by Bauza. He’s joined by Jeff Bergman as Bugs Bunny, Gabriel Iglesias as Speedy Gonzales, and Jeannie Tirado as Lola Bunny. The plot follows Daffy, turning his beak up at his fellow Tunes as they mindlessly obsess over the game of soccer. Todd Wilderman and Hamish Grieve are co-directors. “Daffy Season” is the first theatrically released “Looney Tunes” short since “Daffy’s Rhapsody” played before “Journey 2: The Mysterious Island” back in 2012.

Before “Daffy Season,” Bauza had already provided some voice work for a “Tunes” musical feature titled “Bye Bye Bunny,” which was canceled after some years of development and production. Other “Looney Tunes” credits from Bauza include the HBO Max series “Looney Tunes Cartoons” and the features “The Day the Earth Blew Up: A Looney Tunes Movie” and “Space Jam: A New Legacy.”

Bauza died at his home in Los Angeles on October 25 as a result of hypertensive cardiovascular disease. A group of organizers have launched a GoFundMe campaign to gather financial support for his son, Ryker Bauza, and Ryker’s mother, Jessica Borutski.

In a tribute in The Hollywood Reporter, Warner Bros. Pictures Animation producer Susan Rogers credited Bauza with playing a huge role in reviving the “Looney Tunes.”

“There wasn’t a single short he couldn’t quote or couldn’t reference,” she said. “I don’t think you replace Eric Bauza … The hole he leaves is huge. There are many talented people out there, and the franchise will move on. But there’s only one Eric Bauza.”

Prime Video has become a major destination for military action thrillers, particularly stories built around elite operators, high-stakes missions, and complicated conspiracies. The genre has given the streamer several opportunities to build franchises around recognizable characters, with audiences returning for stories that extend well beyond a single season.

That strategy has also helped Prime Video develop a growing slate of adaptations based on popular action novels. When one of those shows connects with viewers, it can become more than a one-season success — and the streamer's latest streaming numbers suggest one military thriller still has plenty of life left in it.

The series making the biggest impression is The Terminal List. According to Nielsen's latest streaming report, covering the week of October 19 through October 25, the Prime Video thriller secured the fifth spot on the overall top 10 list after accumulating 830 million minutes watched.

That's a substantial audience for the series, especially as it continues to build on the success of its first season. Starring Chris Pratt as James Reece, The Terminal List follows a Navy SEAL whose entire team is ambushed during a covert mission. After returning home, Reece begins investigating what happened, uncovering a conspiracy that reaches far beyond the operation itself.

Based on Jack Carr's novel of the same name, the series combines military action with a conspiracy thriller, giving it an appeal that extends beyond viewers who typically seek out war dramas. Its latest streaming performance is another indication that the franchise has maintained an audience even as Prime Video expands its collection of action-oriented originals.

The show's future is also looking promising. The Terminal List has recently received another major update, with a new season confirmed alongside plans involving Carr's Savage Son. That announcement gives viewers another reason to keep following the franchise, and the latest news about Chris Pratt's Terminal List future offers more details on what's ahead.

Part of the show's appeal comes from Pratt's performance as Reece, a character who is forced to navigate the aftermath of extreme violence while trying to determine who he can trust. The series also benefits from its grounded military details and willingness to make its action sequences central to the story rather than simply using them as background spectacle.

The franchise has continued to develop since its first season, with its second installment giving Reece another chapter in his story. The Terminal List season 2's Rotten Tomatoes score offers another look at how the latest episodes have been received, adding a critical perspective to the show's continued streaming performance.

Carr's work also gives Prime Video plenty of material to explore beyond Reece's story. The author has developed a larger collection of military thrillers, and viewers interested in similar adaptations will soon be able to tune in to a new detective series with a military twist called Worth in the works.

When tragedy strikes his family, grief turns to determination as he hunts those responsible, uncovering corruption that reaches deep into the military, government, and intelligence communities.

#3454. Dylan Skolnick Returning as Co-Director of the Cinema Arts Centre Following Protests and Boycotts

Dylan Skolnick is returning as Director of the Cinema Arts Centre following protests and boycotts over his firing.

In a post announcing Skolnick’s reinstatement, the Long Island cultural institution said that its board of directors had sat down for a series of meetings with an independent mediator. “Those discussions have resulted in an agreement to move forward together, and we are pleased to welcome Dylan back to the Cinema,” the announcement read.

In September, Skolnick was ousted by the CAC board of directors for “serious misconduct.” In justifying the move, the organization slammed Skolnick as a “dysfunctional” and “disloyal” manager whose freelance work as a film buyer for other indie cinemas was a conflict of interest. Skolnick and his supporters countered that the CAC board was experiencing a “hostile takeover” and said that his moonlighting as a film buyer was common practice in the business. Skolnick said he had informed an earlier iteration of the board of his work, but conceded that the current leadership was unaware of his side gig. Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson

Skolnick had deep ties to the institution, which his parents had founded in Huntington, New York more than 50 years ago, as well as strong connections to the wider filmmaking world. Major figures such as Edie Falco, Kent Jones, and Isabella Rossellini leapt to his support, while donations to the CAC dried up, and box office receipts cratered, IndieWire reported last month.

The CAC said that as part of Skolnick’s reinstatement, a new co-director will be hired in the coming months to help lead the organization and its board will invite several new members, “including individuals with backgrounds and experience in the film world.” Skolnick and his fellow co-director and and the CAC board will “undergo additional training focused on effective governance, leadership, accountability and fostering a positive workplace culture.”

In a statement, the CAC leadership acknowledged the fissures created by Skolnick’s ouster, as well as the need to repair relationships and address the non-profit’s financial challenges.

“We want to extend our deepest gratitude to everyone who spoke up, showed their support, and stood by the Cinema during one of the most challenging periods in its history,” the theater said in a statement. “Your voices made a difference, and your continued commitment to this institution means more than we can express.”

#3453. Six Fitness 'Rules' That Don't Actually Matter

I’ve learned a lot in my many years in the gym, and beginner-me would be shocked and appalled by the things present-me does during workouts. With the benefit of experience, I now do exercises I used to think one should “never” do, and I’ve broken pretty much every other rule besides.

I've already explained a bunch of things you can stop worrying about as a beginner, but I’d like to expand on that list with a few more rules that even intermediate-level exercisers can ditch without consequence.

If you can theoretically do 13 bicep curls with a certain weight, how many curls should you actually do? One common misconception is that if you don’t do all 13, you’re leaving gains on the table. The rule kind of makes sense if you have truly no clue where to start; if you go until you can’t do a single rep more, then at least you know you’re not slacking off.

But the downside is that going to failure for every set of every lift is just going to make you exhausted. On bicep curls, maybe not so much, but once you’re squatting pretty heavy weights, you’re going to feel spent if you do every single set to failure, and that fatigue will get in the way of getting a good workout in consistently. What’s better is to follow a program that advises you on when to hold back and when it’s a good time to really push your limits. You’ll find that most of the time, you stop a set at least 2-3 reps shy of failure, and sometimes even more.

Rest days are a convenient tool for making sure you’re not overworking yourself, but that’s all. Organizations like the American College of Sports Medicine recommend leaving 48 hours between intense strength-training sessions for a given muscle, but if you look at where they get that number, it’s meant to be a general recommendation for beginners and for people who are exercising just to stay healthy. Once you’re talking about athletes or enthusiasts, the ACSM acknowledges that training most days of the week is fine if your program manages fatigue effectively. That may mean alternating between heavier and lighter days, rather than taking complete rest days.

The “10% rule” is a not-terrible guideline for figuring out how quickly to ramp up your training. But like many of these other myths, it’s a suggestion, not a commandment to be strictly obeyed.

As running coach Jason Fitzgerald told Lifehacker, “While the adage is to only increase weekly mileage by 10%, this may be either too conservative or even too aggressive depending on where you start from.” When you’re coming back from a short layoff, you can probably increase mileage a lot faster. Same goes if you’re a beginner and your mileage is overall very low; if you took the rule literally, you wouldn’t be able to increase from zero to any other number.

Meanwhile, serious running programs—once again, a program is a wonderful thing—may give you a bigger increase for a few weeks in a row, then cut back and decrease your mileage temporarily before ramping up again. Or they may keep you at the same mileage for weeks at a time before venturing a larger increase. If you were to stick to the 10% rule, you would miss out on the advantages of programs that work this way.

There are pros and cons to lifting before cardio, and to doing cardio before lifting. It’s more of an “it depends” than a rule. So here are some of the ways to decide which makes sense.

Your lifts tend to suffer when you’re fatigued, and doing them fresh is important to you

Cardio is your top priority, and you want to have more energy for it

Your lifts are the kind of thing that can get done even when you’re fatigued

Or you only intend to do a small amount of cardio before lifting

So a cyclist may prefer to do a strength workout after hopping off the bike, but a powerlifter would probably rather get their conditioning in after finishing squats for the day. Either is fine if you don’t care, or if you prefer to mix it up.

There are a few supplements that can help you in your fitness journey, but none of them are necessary. Creatine is one of the best-known muscle-building supplements. It’s understood to be effective, but here’s the thing: Just because it does something for most people doesn’t mean it does very much. If you decide it’s too expensive or just that you would rather not have another thing to remember to take every day, you’re not missing out on any substantial amount of gains.

Likewise, protein powder is a helpful way to get more protein in your diet, but you don’t need to use a supplement; you can just eat more protein-containing foods.

And finally, pre-workout drinks can give you more energy in the gym (it’s mostly caffeine), but the idea that you need it is a very recent development. Even ten years ago, it wasn’t really a thing. People showed up to the gym with a coffee or a coke or with no caffeine at all in their stomach, and worked out just fine.

Look, people have been exercising successfully for millennia, but all of our apps and devices weren't even a thing until the 2000s. Tracking every minute, every step, or every mile of your routine is not actually necessary. You’re still a runner even if you don’t have an app that knows how many miles you ran. You don’t even have to track your sets and reps in your lifting journal if you don’t want to. Your body is what knows how much work you put in, even if your phone were to get wiped overnight.

Use this beginner-friendly plan to cut your risk of all-cause mortality by 45%

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It’s an age-old conundrum faced by beginners and experienced exercisers alike, assuming you can’t improve one without undermining the other.

But hybrid training, the increasingly popular practice of developing strength and fitness side-by-side, flips this principle on its head.

New research suggests doing both could even add years to your life.

According to an observational study following 147,000 health professionals over three decades, mortality risk was lowest among participants who trained cardio and strength.

Compared with doing neither, combining one to two hours of resistance training with a hearty dose of aerobic activity (30-45 MET-hours per week) reduced mortality risk by 45%.

For context, 30 Metabolic Equivalent of Task (MET) hours per week is roughly three times the minimum physical activity guidelines for Americans, equating to several hours of brisk walking, running or other moderate-to-vigorous activity.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Strength training alone was also associated with a strong reduction in all-cause mortality (13%). As was aerobic exercise. But combining both led to the greatest results.

That’s no surprise to Charlie Marchon, Co-Founder and Head of MARCHON Training, who specializes in the field of hybrid training and devised this accessible seven-day plan.

“At MARCHON, hybrid training means developing multiple performance qualities side-by-side. Put simply: strength and conditioning,” he tells Tom’s Guide.

“The science lies in managing the interference effect, so that strength and endurance training don't get in each other's way.”

That, he explains, comes down to how sessions are ordered, how hard each one is, and how much recovery sits between them. “At beginner level the interference effect is small and sensible amounts of each will improve both.”

Here, you’ll find Marchon’s seven-day hybrid training plan, plus advice on how to measure improvement and progress the plan over the course of six weeks.

Charlie Marchon is Co-Founder and Head of MARCHON Training, the training app built around structured, coach-designed programmes for strength, conditioning and hybrid racing. A Strength and Conditioning coach with 10 years of experience, he has programmed for everyone from complete beginners to competitive athletes.

How to use this hybrid training plan to build strength and cardio

To complete this plan, you’ll need two pairs of dumbbells—one lighter for pressing movements and one heavier for squats, hinges and rows.

The week is divided up into three types of sessions:

While suitable for beginners, exercising six days per week will be a big jump if coming from a standing start.

If you’re short on time or would rather ease in slowly, Marchon recommends stripping it back to just the Monday strength workout, Thursday intervals and Saturday hybrid circuit.

“That three-day version still covers strength, harder running and the hybrid link,” he says.

2B Dumbbell floor press (or bench press if available)

Take five to 10 minutes to warm up. Do a three-minute brisk walk or jog to raise your temperature, three minutes of bodyweight lunges, inchworms and glute bridges, then two lighter sets of your first superset before your first working set. For each superset, perform exercise A, rest for 30 seconds, then exercise B, rest for 60-90 seconds.

Marchon says: “A squat and a pull, then a hinge and a push. Every major muscle group gets worked without two exercises fighting for the same muscles back to back.”

20-40min run at an easy pace (3-4 out of 10 RPE)

Warm up with a brisk three-minute walk or easy jog. Swing your legs forward and back then side to side for 10 reps. Do 10 walking lunges, 20 small pogo hops on the balls of your feet, 20m of high knees and 20m of heel flicks. Then you’re good to go. Once complete, walk for five minutes then gently stretch your calves and hips.

Marchon says: “Easy running builds your aerobic base and lets you recover from Monday. The pace will feel slow. Don't try to chase intensity. Hold a conversational pace throughout, meaning you can speak in full sentences without pausing for breath. If you can’t run that long yet, alternate two minutes of running with one minute of walking.”

Warm up and cool down as per Monday’s strength workout. For each superset, perform exercise A, rest for 30 seconds, then perform exercise B, and rest for 60-90 seconds.

Marchon says: “This session swaps in single-leg and overhead work, so you're challenged in different positions to Monday.”

Warm up as per Tuesday’s run, finishing the 10min easy jog with three 10-second sprints to get ready for faster running. The intervals should feel comfortably hard, meaning you can utter a few words at a time, no more. Let your breathing settle during the two-minute recoveries before each next effort.

Marchon says: “The one harder run of the week. Short efforts improve your speed and your heart's capacity without the strain of a long hard run. Aim to run every effort at the same pace. If the last one is much slower than the first, you started too fast.”

Walking, mobility, or a gentle yoga class is fine, but keep it light.

Marchon says: “Recovery is where the adaptation happens, so take this day seriously.”

Warm up as per Tuesday’s run, then perform one easy practice round of the stations above with light dumbbells before you start. Aim to complete four rounds, resting one minute between rounds. Use moderate weights. This is about moving continuously, not lifting heavy.

Marchon says: “This hybrid session ties the week together. You run, then lift, then run again while you're still a little tired, which builds the ability to keep moving well under fatigue. Treadmill users can do the runs indoors. Outdoors, run an out and back route of 90 seconds each way and leave the dumbbells at your starting point.”

30-40min run at an easy pace (3-4/10 RPE)

Warm up and cool down as per Tuesday’s easy run. Set a pace that means you finish feeling like you could have gone further.

Marchon says: “This long easy run is optional in week one; it becomes a key session as the plan progresses. You can use run-walk intervals if you need. If your legs feel heavy from the week, swap in a brisk walk for 45 minutes.”

This week-long hybrid training plan sets the template to build both strength and cardio in parallel. Marchon recommends sticking with it for a minimum of six weeks.

“Think long term,” he says. “The real aim is a lasting training habit that keeps improving your strength, fitness, health and longevity.”

That means challenging yourself with slightly heavier weights, running for slightly longer, or repeating an extra few reps, sets, or intervals as your strength and fitness improves.

If your sleep starts to suffer, you still feel sore 48 hours after a session, or something hurts rather than just feels worked, Marchon suggests repeating the week rather than moving on.

“Progress that holds beats progress that breaks,” he says.

After six weeks, Marchon suggests repeating the six-week plan starting with your new weights and run times.

“Minimal kit will take you a long way, but in time you'll need heavier weights and more structured training to keep challenging yourself.”

#3451. Forget John Wick, HBO Max's 96-Minute Action Thriller Is Still Undefeated

If you asked someone what their favorite action movie is, John Wick would probably top the list. Chad Stahelski and David Leitch turned years of stunt experience into a bloody, gripping action movie that helped reinvigorate Keanu Reeves' career. John Wick is also notable for its deep themes of grief, as its protagonist mourns the loss of a dog meant to help him cope with the loss of his late wife. Long before John Wick hit theaters, another action thriller about a normal man trying to escape his violent past gripped audiences, and it's now streaming on HBO Max.

That movie is A History of Violence. Based on the DC Comics/Vertigo graphic novel by John Wagner and Vince Locke, A History of Violence is a pitch-perfect take on its source material, thanks to director David Cronenberg and lead Viggo Mortensen. Mortensen plays Tom Spall, a mild-mannered man who runs a local diner with his wife Edie (Maria Bello) and his two children. When two criminals attempt to hold up the diner, Tom kills them with ice-cold precision. This makes him a local hero, and reveals secrets from his past that he's tried hard to bury. What follows is a gripping thriller that will hook viewers from beginning to end.

To say that A History of Violence is . . .well, violent, is an understatement. The scene where Tom takes out the two robbers in the diner is a key example, as he slams a coffee pot into one's face and blows the other's brains out when he gets stabbed. What makes it so surprising is that the movie was a departure for its director and leading man. Cronenberg was best known for truly disturbing horror movies like Scanners and Videodrome, while Mortensen was coming off of the massive success of the Lord of the Rings trilogy. No one was expecting them to make a gritty crime thriller, and yet that's part of the draw of A History of Violence. Mortensen's mild-mannered demeanor as Tom makes the violence hit all the harder, while Cronenberg uses his horror experience to ramp up the tension leading to firefights.

A History of Violence also takes the time to explore what living a life full of violence does to a man, as it's slowly revealed that Tom was once a mob enforcer named Joey Cusack. Not only does his brother Richie (William Hurt) want him back in the "family buisness", but the revelation puts a strain on his marriage and arguments with his son about getting into fights. Cronenberg would even talk about how he wanted to explore the consequences of violence, and how he wanted his audience to think about those consequences:

"In this movie, we've got an audience that's definitely going to applaud these acts of violence, and they do because it's set up that these acts are justifiable and almost heroic at times. But I'm saying, "Okay, if you can applaud that, can you applaud this?" because this is the result of that gunshot in the head. It's not nice. And even if the violence is justifiable, the consequences of the violence are the same."

A History of Violence is still held in high esteem, to the point where it's considered to be one of the best movies released in the 21st century. It wouldn't be the last time that Viggo Mortensen and David Cronenberg worked together, as the duo reunited for two more movies. Eastern Promises stars Mortensen as a Russian enforcer forced to confront the evil his employers take part in, mirroring the conflict Tom finds himself in during A History of Violence. A Dangerous Method took a different approach, as Mortensen portrayed Sigmund Freud while exploring more of the famed psychologist's personal life.

Most crime thrillers thrive on a buffet of blood and violence, but A History of Violence is the opposite. It stays with its audience long after the credits roll, thanks to a stellar performance from Viggo Mortensen and David Cronenberg's taut, thoughtful approach to the material.

#3450. Box Office: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Thunders with $31.6 Million, Scoring the Biggest Debut Ever for a Live-Action, Foreign Language Film

The year of unlikely box office smashes continues as “Godzilla Minus Zero” opened to a thunderous $31.6 million, shattering records to become the biggest North American debut for a live-action foreign language film in history. It easily toppled the previous benchmark established in 2002 by the wuxia epic “Hero,” which kicked off with $17.8 million. Globally, “Godzilla Minus Zero’s” haul stands at $63 million.

And it comes on the heels of a string of films that have defied conventional wisdom to resonate with moviegoers. Yes, the box office is still dominated by sequels and comic book movies like “Toy Story 5” and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” but there’s been a lot more variety. Audiences have turned out in force for an original sci-fi adventure (“Project Hail Mary,” $684.6 million worldwide); a pair of low-budget horror films from 20-something auteurs with YouTube pedigree (“Obsession,” $524.3 million worldwide; “Backrooms,” $400.6 million worldwide); an adaptation of a Greek epic we were all forced to read in school (“The Odyssey,” $1.8 billion worldwide), and a three-hour documentary about a Silicon Valley cheat (“You Can See Everything,” $73.7 million and counting). Clearly, people are looking for something different. Related Stories Dylan Skolnick Returning as Co-Director of the Cinema Arts Centre Following Protests and Boycotts Eric Bauza’s Final ‘Looney Tunes’ Performance Is ‘Daffy Season,’ Now in Theaters Ahead of ‘The Cat in the Hat’

In the case of “Godzilla Minus Zero,” it helped that the first film, 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One,” was an unexpected sleeper hit, grossing an impressive $57.1 million. But the first “Godzilla” opened to a mere $11.4 million, showing that the audience for the first monster movie grew on home entertainment. “Godzilla Minus Zero” is poised to bypass its predecessor to become the highest-grossing live-action Japanese movie in history. Once again, the film was directed by Takashi Yamazaki, who also worked on the special effects, produced by Japan’s Tojo, and distributed in the U.S. by GKids.

The success of “Godzilla Minus Zero” also demonstrates that subtitles are no barrier to box office success, something that Netflix and other streamers discovered with the popularity of local-language programming like “Squid Game,” “Money Heist,” and “Lupin.” The story at multiplexes is no different. U.S. audiences have filled auditoriums to watch “Parasite” ($53.8 million domestic), “Ne Zha 2” ($23.2 million domestic), and “Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba – The Movie: Infinity Castle” ($136.9 million domestic). The outsized grosses for “Godzilla Minus Zero” probably mean we haven’t heard the last of the fire-breathing Kaiju.

The monster movie made quick work of its main competition, Warner Bros. Animation’s “The Cat in the Hat,” which stumbled with $20 million domestically and $30 million globally. The family film cost $92 million to produce and extends a string of misses for Warner Bros., which was recently purchased by Skydance. Insiders say that the studio has lost hundreds of millions of dollars on bombs like “Digger,” “Supergirl,” and “The Bride!” and “The Cat in the Hat” won’t do much to mop up all that red ink.

At this price, it's an affordable way to bring 4K streaming to an older television or give a sluggish smart TV a performance upgrade. And because this streaming stick measures just 3.6 inches and draws power directly from your TV's USB port using the included cable, it can sit out of sight behind your screen without taking up another wall outlet.

Despite its small size, it supports 4K streaming over Wi-Fi 6, along with HDR10, HDR10+, and HLG for improved contrast and color on compatible televisions. What you don't get is Dolby Vision or Dolby Atmos audio. If either is important to your home theater setup, the Fire TV Stick 4K Plus, currently $39.99, is worth considering for the extra $15. Otherwise, there's little to complain about when it comes to performance, with PCMag reporting that apps respond almost instantly and 4K streams load quickly with almost no blurry, low-resolution moments.

The redesigned Alexa voice remote is another improvement, with a more comfortable shape, an easier-to-find home button, and dedicated shortcuts for major streaming services. You can also use Alexa to search for shows, launch apps, or control compatible smart home devices. The software experience is less impressive, with advertisements and recommendations dominating the home screen, leaving relatively little room for your actual apps. There's also no support for Apple AirPlay or Google Cast, so sharing content directly from your phone isn't particularly convenient. Still, if you're comfortable with Amazon's interface and don't need the missing Dolby formats, the Fire TV Stick 4K delivers responsive streaming and a useful remote for just $25.

#3448. At Last, The MCU Is Officially Setting Up The Best Doctor Doom/Scarlet Witch Story

Marvel Studios is preparing for the debut of Robert Downey Jr.s Doctor Doom in Avengers: Doomsday, which is set to release at the end of this year. However, an exciting new theory suggests Doom's arrival in the MCU may also involve the return of The Scarlet Witch.

Played by Elizabeth Olsen, Wanda Maximoff's Scarlet Witch has been absent from the main MCU continuity since 2022's Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, which saw Wanda controversially being corrupted by the Darkhold in a bid to reunite with her sons from a different reality (no matter the cost). Eventually, Wanda was shown how far she'd fallen, prompting her to sacrifice herself by bringing down Mount Wundagore, destroying every copy of the Darkhold in the process.

That said, many fans have never stopped believing in Wanda's eventual return to the MCU, especially with the rest of her family still having such prominent, ongoing roles. Between the new VisionQuest series on Disney+ and the reveal of mysterious mystical characters beyond Victor von Doom in Avengers: Doomsday, there's plenty reason to suspect that Marvel Studios has secret plans for the Scarlet Witch (which may involve Doctor Doom himself).

Beginning with 2021's WandaVision, Wanda's grief losing Vision (Paul Bettany) in Avengers: Infinity War led to her inadvertent creation of a massive hex over the town of Westview, transforming it into her TV-perfect happy ending, while also manifesting a new Vision and their twin boys from the comics, Billy and Tommy. By the end of WandaVision, Wanda undid the hex despite the fact it meant losing Vision and here boys. This is what ultimately led to her corruption by the Darkhold trying to get her boys back via another reality and subsequent death at Mount Wundagore in 2022's Multiverse of Madness.

However, the story of Wanda Maximoff's family has very much continued even without Wanda herself. In 2024's Agatha All Along, it was revealed that Billy used his magic to transfer his soul into the body of teenager William Kaplan (Joe Locke) before the Hex was being undone. He then did the same for Tommy's soul with Thomas Shepherd (Ruaridh Mollica), a key parallel to their origins from the comics.

While Agatha All Along ended with Billy/William and the ghost of Agatha Harkness searching for Tommy/Thomas, we now have 2026's VisionQuest starring the original Vision (rebuilt by SWORD at the end of WandaVision), as well as Tommy himself who's gradually been learning from his synthezoid "father" about Wanda, the events of Westview, and their family.

With VisionQuest just days away from its finale, Vision and the Maximoff twins finding each other again feels increasingly likely. Combined with Vision starting to regain the humanity and emotion he temporarily lost after being reactivated, nearly all of the pieces are in place for a major Maximoff family reunion in the MCU's future except one: Wanda.

While she seemed to have died under the collapse of Mount Wundagore, The Scarlet Witch is one of the most powerful beings in the entire Marvel Universe. As such, it's not much of a leap in logic to suggest that she could have survived (or was perhaps even rescued by someone seeking her power...)

Beyond what's been happening on the small-screen for the surviving Maximoffs, the ambiguity and hopes about Wanda's return have never been higher thanks to Avengers: Doomsday and its masked "Latverian Witches" who will apparently be serving Doctor Doom.

Their exact identities and purpose of these witches in the upcoming MCU crossover have yet to be confirmed, and they may very well just be generic servants of Doom (a master sorcerer in his own right). However, they've notably been shown wearing different colored robes including green, purple, orange, and red, leading many to wonder if established magical characters like Sylvie, Agatha, Clea, or Wanda herself could be under Doom's influence.

Thinking about Wanda in particular, Doom would have certainly had the power to secretly intervene to save Wanda at Mount Wundagore, perhaps in a bid to bring her into his service and plans for the multiverse at large. There's also some key comics precedent for this idea as well, as seen in Marvel's classic "Children's Crusade" storyline.

In "Children's Crusade", Doctor Doom secretly takes in an amnesiac Wanda from Mount Wundagore after her major breakdown that resulted in her magic triggering the near-genocide of mutantkind (House of M). Hoping to marry Wanda and use her power for his own ends, the intervention of Wanda's boys, their fellow Young Avengers, and several Avengers and X-Men alike prevented Doom from taking full control of the Scarlet Witch's power and her memories being restored.

While none of this confirms that the MCU's Wanda Maximoff is indeed one of these Latverian Witches in Doomsday, being onee of the masked magic wielders would provide a very natural way for the MCU to kick-off a new storyline inspired by "Children's Crusade", perhaps even one that continues beyond the Multiverse Saga itself.

The basic premise of "Children's Crusade" feels remarkably perfect to the MCU's future. While VisionQuest can bring Billy and Tommy together with Vision, Avengers: Doomsday can establish Doom's true purpose for these Latverian Witches, and whether one of them is indeed Wanda Maximoff. Perhaps the reveal will even saved for the end of Doomsday or even in 2027's Avengers: Secret Wars to then kick off a substantial project in the MCU's next major saga.

Most importantly, this major MCU thoery would go a long way to redeem the events of Multiverse of Madness and Wanda's controversial (and underveloped) turn to the darkness. Likewise, throwing Doctor Doom into the mix even just to start would not only keep the Maximoff Family's story tied to the greater events happening in the MCU, but would also provide the perfect narrative launchpad by adapting the basic elements from "Children's Crusade".

It may be some time before we get it, but the twins' reunion more than likely approaching and Doctor Doom's mysterious magical followers definitely makes it feel like a solid foundation is being formed for Wanda's long hoped-for return in the MCU.

The finale of VisionQuest begins streaming November 10th on Disney+. Avengers: Doomsday releases in theaters on December 18th from Marvel Studios.

#3446. Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Hits $80 Million, Becoming A24’s Third-Biggest Domestic Release

“You Can See Everything,” an intimate look at Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, has earned nearly $80 million at the domestic box office, becoming A24‘s third-highest-grossing release in North America. It bypasses “Everything Everywhere All at Once” and its $77 million haul to take its spot on the indie studio’s chart, and that film won the Oscar for Best Picture.

With $79.8 million stateside, “You Can See Everything” sits behind the summer blockbuster “Backrooms” ($197 million) and 2025’s “Marty Supreme” ($96 million) on the list of A24 releases. Other A24 films made more globally, with “Backrooms” earning more than $400 million, “Marty Supreme” grossing $192.4 million, and “Everything Everywhere All at Once” netting $147.9 million. Related Stories Box Office: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Thunders with $31.6 Million, Scoring the Biggest Debut Ever for a Live-Action, Foreign Language Film Dylan Skolnick Returning as Co-Director of the Cinema Arts Centre Following Protests and Boycotts

However, “You Can See Everything” has yet to be released in most international markets. It’s unclear if Holmes’ fraud will resonate with moviegoers so far from Silicon Valley. It doesn’t matter if it doesn’t connect, because with a budget of $7 million, “You Can See Everything” is already wildly profitable. Its success means that Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, the directing duo behind the doc, are now in high demand.

“You Can See Everything” also jumped ahead of “March of the Penguins” ($77 million) on the list of highest-grossing documentaries in North America. Variety reports that makes it the second highest-grossing doc behind Michael Moore’s “Fahrenheit 9/11,” which earned $119 million domestically. That doesn’t account for music documentaries like “Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour” ($267.1 million) and “Michael Jackson’s This is It” ($268 million), which were far more popular.

A24 is on a hot streak. In addition to “Backrooms,” the indie studio has released hits like “The Drama” and “Primetime.” Its latest film, “Club Kid,” grossed an impressive $390,583 this weekend when it opened on six screens in New York and Los Angeles. That’s a per-screen average of $65,097. A24 acquired the drama about a hard-living gay man and his son out of the Cannes Film Festival, where it debuted to raves. The studio hopes to position the film and its writer, director, and star Jordan Firstman in the Oscar race.

The Steam Deck is one of the best purchases I’ve ever made. Valve’s handheld PC can play so many games with ease. However, with the Steam Machine and Steam Frame now available, the Steam Deck is still one of the best handhelds for retro gaming in 2026.

I’ve always been a retro gamer. I grew up with Sonic the Hedgehog, Tomb Raider, Metal Gear Solid, and others. I’ve carried a PS Vita in my backpack for years so I could play titles from each of these series, and more, on the go. Granted, recent remasters mean I haven’t needed to use the Vita as much, but plenty still hasn't appeared on modern systems.

It’s why the Steam Deck fills that gap. Not only can I play DRM-free games via GOG and many Steam games that haven't been updated in years, but I can also use many emulators, giving me access to titles that have next to no chance of appearing anytime soon. With that in mind, here’s how you can set up your Steam Deck as a powerful retro handheld.

Although the Steam Deck OLED is almost 3 years old as of this writing, it’s still powerful enough to play plenty of games from the PlayStation 3 era. Games like Star Wars: Rogue Squadron II and Dead or Alive 3 run at full speed thanks to Dolphin and Xemu, respectively.

But setting up all these emulators can be a hassle, which is where EmuDeck comes in. In less than 10 minutes, you can transfer games from your PC or Mac to your Steam Deck via its ROM Manager, and start playing games from your childhood. Better yet, EmuDeck works with SteamOS, so any titles you transfer will sit alongside your Steam library.

You don’t have to install every emulator, perhaps a few, just to save space on your Steam Deck. EmuDeck gives you plenty of control over your games and BIOS files, as well as how they look on the handheld’s display. The app is a fantastic way of playing games from your past without much hassle.

If you own a Steam Deck but have been tempted to play The Legend of Zelda: Wind Waker HD or Tekken Tag Tournament, EmuDeck will make it happen. But something else has been making the Steam Deck an essential retro gaming machine that doesn’t run via emulators.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

2026 will be known as the year when decompilations exploded, and for good reason. For anyone unaware, decompilations reverse-engineer games into source code, meaning long-standing bugs can be fixed and new features can be added. For example, Harbour Masters has released decompilations of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, Banjo-Kazooie, Star Fox 64, and more.

You can play these on the best Windows PCs or Macs in native widescreen, with quality-of-life features and more benefits. But you can play plenty of others right now. The decomps subreddit mostly keeps track of what’s in development - with many of them not made by AI.

Wes Fenlon has a fantastic, frequently updated overview of decompilations and recompilations of classic games, and it also means many of these re-releases can be played on Steam Deck. Many, like Harbour Masters, offer a Linux version, so it’s a matter of installing the file and following a few steps to get it up and running.

It’s another way to preserve certain games that run even better than emulation. It’s also better for battery life on the Steam Deck, since these are native ports, meaning the CPU and GPU use less power to run the game. When you consider the native display resolution and graphical settings for these decompilations, it makes these games feel like they were meant to be played this way on the Steam Deck.

Game preservation is in a state of interesting flux. Emulators are now running games as originally intended, with no major graphical glitches or slowdown on devices from the Raspberry Pi to the Steam Deck. New emulators for PS4 and PS5 are already beginning to appear, which means games like Astro Bot and Marvel's Wolverine could someday be playable on a future Steam Deck handheld.

But there’s also the matter of decompilations. Plenty of AI-vibe-coded ones have recently appeared, to the detriment of others that have passionately reverse-engineered classic games with care and determination. You can keep track of others that are close to being fully decompiled at decomp.dev, with titles like Silent Hill, Starfox Adventures, and Super Smash Bros. Melee that could have the same benefits as Harbour Masters’ The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time decompilation someday.

Nevertheless, this is all good news for your Steam Deck. Emulation and decompilations give your handheld another way to play your favorite games on the go, including eras like the Game Boy and PlayStation 3. As things stand, it looks like there are plenty more decompiled titles to look forward to playing on it.

#3444. The Out of Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Does 'Code Rot' Mean?

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's Out-of-Touch guide takes a look at a phenomena that's probably going to define the lives of generations of young people: Code rot—both actual computer-style code rot, and the more elusive cultural kind. I'm also taking a look at the fake controversy over the "cancellation" of Freddy Krueger, and finally, bringing things home with viral videos of boyfriends dancing.

Expect to hear young people talking about code rot for awhile, maybe for the rest of their lives. It's a concept that's going to affect them more than any previous generation. Code rot, or software rot, describes what happens to a computer program when the hardware and operating system it runs on advance. If older programs aren't updated, they become less stable and glitchy until they eventually become unusable.

The idea of code rot has really caught on in the young people's popular imagination, probably because they're going to spend a lot of their lives dealing with it. They've even taken the idea of code rot into life, and use the phrase to describe anything that is worn out or malfunctioning. If the ice cream machine isn't working at McDonald's, it's code rotted. Bad grades on a report card? Code rot.

Kids are making videos where they demonstrate actual code rot:

or point out physical things that are code rotted, like a cat:

Interestingly, a lot of the online discourse around code rotting concerns the massive video game platform Roblox. Because Roblox games there are made by users, there's often not a lot of incentive for the creators to keep the games current with the platform's changes, so a lot of Gen Z's childhood memories of playing games are sinking into code rot. Here's a video about it:

Another interesting wrinkle is the tone these videos take. Code rot is seen as apocalyptic. While it's mostly hyperbole, I think part of it is the realization that the entire world is code rotted. The old programs that used to run within the "Western Culture" operating system no longer apply and everything is starting to glitch out.

The meaning of "PDF file" depends on the context. If you're at work, it refers to a Portable Document Format file, a format created by Adobe that is famously hard for older people to open. In slang, though, PDF file is algo speak for "pedophile." Because that word is flagged by moderation software online, people say "PDF File" to skirt the censorship.

The run-up to Halloween brought a lot of online discourse about Nightmare on Elm Street villain Freddy Krueger. The supernatural serial murder/PDF File was supposedly cancelled online by overly woke, Gen-Z Tiktokers outraged that he is a child predator. The controversy started with a post from Entertainment Industry Reporter that points out how strange it is that in the '80s and '90s, Freddy Krueger, depicted in 1984's A Nightmare on Elm Street as a child murderer so driven by bloodlust he transcended death, was featured on dolls, board games, and lunchboxes aimed at children. It's a good point, but not a call for "cancellation."

Although the article does say that "Freddy Krueger lunchboxes shouldn’t exist," and that parents "shouldn’t have been buying their kids action figures of a child murderer," this is not a call to action. It's not suggesting cancellation of any kind, and it's hard to even conceive of what cancellation of a fictional character in an old horror franchise would even mean. The article is actually an observation about how merchandising (and low-quality sequels) change the meaning of art. But people online missed the point entirely and invented a scenario where "woke" young people are calling for the cancellations of a fictional villain for doing bad things.

I've been scouring TikTok, looking for even one video where someone is calling for "canceling" Freddy Krueger, and I can't find any, but there are hundreds, maybe thousands of videos like this:

In these videos, people point out how enraging it is that the woke people are calling for Krueger's cancellation and vowing that they won't let it happen. Even though it is not happening. There are even levels to the myths about woke mobs canceling Freddy. Supposedly, younger users were unaware that Krueger is depicted as a "PDF file" as well as a murderer in the 2010 reboot of the franchise, so there are online arguments about whether that's the reason he's being canceled. Even though no one is canceling anything. These anti-woke folks are, ironically, defending a fictional villain from cancellation by creating another fictional villain, the shadowy woke mob that's ruining horror movies. Meanwhile, the real villain is a lack of media literacy. Saying "wow, it's crazy that previous generations made a comedy mascot of such a terrible character and marketed him to children" is not the same as cancellation.

This week's viral videos are of boyfriends dancing. The newest thing on the TikTok is young women sharing video of their boyfriends getting down accompanied by a clip from the song "gay alligations fr. my girlfriend" by TikToker OH MICKEY. Like this:

It's a simple, silly template that maybe doesn't mean a whole lot, but this generation of young men are so messed up when it comes to relationships and masculinity, I'm always happy when a meme becomes popular that indicates that young women want goofy dudes, dudes who know how to dance, and dudes who act silly as boyfriends more than they want red-pilled, manosphere, looksmaxxing types. I don't know if these kinds of messages ever really "break through" to the underground of internet incels, but I like to hope they do, because a lot of young men are not OK.

#3443. 6 Romance Books That Are a Masterclass in Yearning

No matter what tropes you prefer, there will be a number of romance books out there that meet the criteria of what you're looking for. From older romance books to modern ones, there are so many excellent romance books across subgenres. The best romance books have strong characters that readers can get attached to. Both of the lead characters are well-written and have their own lives and wants outside each other, but their scenes together are the heart of the book.

One thing that most romance readers tend to look for is an element of yearning. It is especially exciting to see one or both leads pine after the other for a long time, even when – and especially when – they don't know they're doing it. Romance books with excellent yearning might see the characters fighting to be together despite impossibly high stakes, or secretly harbor feelings for each other for years. These are amazing romance books that are a masterclass in yearning.

Before it was a hit Netflix rom-com, People We Meet on Vacation was an amazing romance novel by Emily Henry. The book follows Poppy Wright and Alex Nilsen, two polar opposites who have been best friends ever since they roadtripped back to their shared hometown together for a college break. Ever since, Poppy and Alex have gotten together once a year for a week-long summer vacation, where they visit a different place together every time. The book moves back and forth through time to tell this story. In the present day, Poppy and Alex haven't spoken in two years after a mysterious falling out. As a professional travel writer, Poppy goes on vacation for work now, and she decides to invite Alex with her this time to try to start their old tradition back up. She'll also be going with Alex as his date to his brother's wedding that same summer.

In the past, People We Meet on Vacation follows Poppy and Alex's other trips together, showing how their feelings for each other have been building up since the very beginning of their friendship. Every time their friendship starts to become something more, an obstacle gets in the way, from work to other people. The past timeline builds up to their final trip where their friendship ended, while they avoid talking about their falling out and just try to rebuild their friendship on their present-day trip. People We Meet on Vacation has amazing yearning from both Poppy and Alex, especially because Poppy doesn't fully understand what she's feeling for most of the book. Over the course of their past vacations, Poppy and Alex's feelings build for each other while they both try to ignore them and prioritize the friendship. In the present, there's an even deeper aspect to the yearning, as the two long for their old friendship while still harboring hopes of something more.

Atmosphere by Taylor Jenkins Reid is a historical fiction romance novel set in the 1980s. The book starts with a flash-forward to December 1984, where astronaut Joan Goodwin is working from the ground to navigate a malfunctioning NASA space shuttle back to safety. Three of the astronauts on the shuttle have already died, one is unconscious, and only astronaut Vanessa Ford is left to work with Joan to get the shuttle home. The story then rewinds all the way back to 1980, where Joan joins NASA's Space Shuttle program and meets the rest of her class, shortly after the program started to include women. Joan's class is made up of the astronauts who will later be on that shuttle four years later, including Vanessa, with whom she strikes an instant connection.

Joan has never been in love before, but about a year into the program, she realizes that that's what she feels for Vanessa. The two would lose their jobs if anyone found out that they were lesbians, though, so they have to keep their relationship a secret from everyone in their lives. Atmosphere features a different depiction of yearning, because Joan and Vanessa are together for most of the book. All the while, they long to be able to be together publicly, and to get to experience everything that the straight couple in their class gets to. In the present day, Joan is stuck on the ground trying to get the woman she loves to safety, all while the two have to hide their love for each other during their monitored communication. Atmosphere is a beautiful, heartbreaking novel that sees Joan and Vanessa risk everything to be together, all while trying to still find a way for both of them to continue to pursue their dreams of going to space.

Red, White & Royal Blue, the extremely popular romance novel that was adapted into a hit rom-com for Prime Video, is one of the best depictions of yearning of any romance book. The book follows Alex Claremont-Diaz, the college-age son of the first female President of the United States, Ellen Claremont. Ellen is nearing the end of her first term, and tensions are high as she runs for re-election. Alex has a passion for politics and wants to help, especially because he's now in his final year of college. At a wedding thrown by the British royal family, though, Alex makes his mother look bad when he gets into a public altercation with his longtime rival, Prince Henry.

For the sakes of both their families and countries, Alex and Henry then have to do damage control by pretending to be friends. They start meeting up over the course of the following months for staged hangouts where they know they will be photographed. Along the way, though, Alex and Henry start to really get to know each other, and they realize they were wrong about each other. They start talking to and messaging each other all the time, and they soon become best friends, which turns romantic at a New Year's Eve party. Alex and Henry cannot actually be together, though, because of their respective titles. As such, they try to compartmentalize their feelings for each other, but they ultimately can't help but fall in love with each other. Red, White & Royal Blue is full of intense yearning throughout the book, and Alex and Henry also just have phenomenal chemistry and banter. It's easy to root for them no matter the odds stacked against them, and their pining for each other jumps off the page through every one of their conversations and emails.

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of you.

You do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most durable way anybody has found to do this.

You want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the relationship easier.

The intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

You do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

I've Got Your Number by Sophie Kinsella follows an unlikely romance that develops between two polar opposites who get temporarily stuck with each other for the sake of convenience. Poppy Wyatt is happily engaged to be married, but she finds herself in a messy situation when she loses both her cellphone and her engagement ring on the same day. Luckily, Poppy finds a discarded cellphone in the trash, so she gives out the number in case anyone finds the ring. The only problem is, the phone is actually the work cell of Sam Roxton, a no-nonsense business executive who is frustrated by this inconvenience.

Still, Sam agrees to share the phone with Poppy until she finds her ring. Through sharing the cellphone, Poppy and Sam get daily glimpses into each other's lives. They also start to become friends by talking to each other all the time in order to coordinate their shared usage of the phone. Poppy and Sam start to get used to their arrangement and even depend on each other, but it's just temporary. Eventually, Poppy will find her ring and get married to her fiancé, Magnus, and Sam will get his phone back to himself. While Poppy spends most of the novel in denial of her growing feelings for Sam, Sam's yearning for her is apparent from early on. Each of their interactions is charged, as the two long to be more than what they are, relegated mostly to virtual interactions while still becoming involved in nearly every aspect of each other's lives.

The Flatshare by Beth O'Leary, which was adapted into the romance miniseries of the same name, follows the growing romance of two people who have never met. After a bad breakup, Tiffy Moore is in a rush to find a new place to live that she can afford, so she winds up in an unconventional arrangement. Leon Twomey is a hospice nurse who works nights and sleeps during the day, so he rents the apartment to Tiffy half the time. They share the space and its single bed, but their hours never overlap, so they become roommates who have never met each other.

Tiffy and Leon use post-it notes to communicate with one another, starting out with practical back-and-forth about their living arrangement and slowly getting to know each other through these notes. Over the course of The Flatshare, Tiffy and Leon fall in love through their post-it notes, while still working vastly different hours and never meeting in person. The yearning between them is beautiful as they both become more reliant on their post-it note system over time, while trying to determine whether what they have is worth risking by finally meeting each other.

Before it was a massively popular TV show, Heated Rivalry was the second book in Rachel Reid's Game Changers series. The romance novel tells the love story of rival NHL players Shane Hollander and Ilya Rozanov over the course of about a decade. The novel starts with a flash-forward that shows Shane and Ilya carrying on a secret fling, before then going back in time to show them meeting in their rookie year. For years, the two regularly hook up in secret, compartmentalizing their feelings for each other because they know that they could never actually be together.

Shane and Ilya's careers are everything to them, and they would likely lose it all if anyone every found out about them, due to both rampant homophobia in the NHL and their status as professional rivals. Still, they can't fight their growing feelings for each other. No matter how many times either one of them tries to end things, they just keep finding their way back to one another. Both Shane and Ilya's yearning for one another is very clear throughout the book, even as neither of them knows just how deep their own feelings run, until they ultimately have to face these feelings and decide what to do about them.

Heated Rivalry centers on two hockey stars whose fierce competition transforms into a complex relationship as they navigate conflicting feelings and the sport’s demands. As they attempt to balance personal emotions with professional ambitions, their unexpected bond challenges traditional expectations in the world of competitive hockey.

#3442. ‘You Can See Everything’ Sweeps Critics Choice Documentary Awards

“You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim‘s phenomenally successful documentary about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, swept the Critics Choice Association‘s documentary awards tonight, winning each of its five categories — including Best Documentary Feature. Ava DuVernay’s “14th,” which headed into the night with the most nominations (six), went home empty-handed.

In addition to the top prize, “You Can See Everything” won Best Director (Fielder and Oppenheimer), Best Cinematography (David Bolen), Best Editing (Adam Locke-Norton), and Best Music Score (Ari Balouzian).

Whether or not this is a harbinger of the film‘s Oscar chances is anybody’s guess. A24 is aggressively campaigning for “You Can See Everything” to score both Best Documentary and Best Picture nominations. If the film receives the latter, it would be the first documentary ever to do so. The CCA sweep certainly doesn’t hurt its prospects, but it’s not necessarily a predictor either — in the last 10 years, the CCA and Academy have only agreed on the best documentary twice (with “O.J.: Made in America” and “Summer of Soul”). Other winners tonight included David Greaves’ “Once Upon a Time in Harlem,” which took home awards for Best First Documentary Feature, Best Historical Documentary and Best Archival Documentary, and Alex Gibney’s four-hour “Musk,” which won Best Biographical Documentary. John Wilson scored an award for Best Narration for his work as writer and performer on “A History of Concrete,” and Baz Luhrmann’s maximalist “EPiC: Elvis Presley in Concert” won Best Music Documentary.

The movie currently favored by many awards season pundits to take home the Best Documentary Oscar, “Naza,” won Best Political Documentary, and Best Science/Nature Documentary went to “Nuisance Bear.” Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin’s widely acclaimed “Everest: The Other Side” was awarded Best Sports Documentary.

#3441. Stephen King’s Supernatural Sci-Fi Series Is Officially Back, And It’s The Perfect Carrie Follow-Up

Mike Flanagan's Carrie became the biggest Stephen King hit of the year, and it is all set to be followed up with season 2. However, it will be a while before Carrie season 2 sees the light of day. While waiting for its release, horror fans can now watch another ongoing TV adaptation of a Stephen King book, which has officially returned in 2026.

The show in question, The Institute, has a lot in common with Carrie, and these parallels between the two Stephen King stories will now be even more evident.

Carrie marked Stephen King's literary debut. The Institute, in contrast, ranks among the King of Horror's more recent books as it was published in 2019. Its first TV adaptation of the same name landed on MGM+ and garnered a more mixed reception compared to recent shows like It: Welcome to Derry and Carrie. Still, MGM+'s The Institute performed well enough to be renewed for another season.

Interestingly, The Institute season 1 exhausted the story from the original Stephen King novel. Owing to this, its second season is now expanding the source material's lore. After season 1's developments and season 2's opening arcs, The Institute is already starting to look like the perfect follow-up to Stephen King's Carrie. The two Stephen King stories also share some hidden connections.

Carrie was the first breakout horror novel in which Stephen King used telekinesis as a narrative device to highlight the impact of abuse on a young adult. The Institute not only riffs on the same themes but also significantly raises the stakes. Instead of featuring only one character with the "Shine," it shows how multiple children are gifted with telekinesis (TK), telepathy (TP), and precognition.

The characters in The Institute, however, are subjected to explicit institutional abuse after being abducted from their homes and subjected to immoral experimentation. It almost feels like a sequel to Carrie where the White Commission has realized that more children like Carrie White exist. Now, they have started an "institute" to exploit their powers.

The Institute season 2's episode 1 further leans into these overlaps. It shows how entire systems have been built to exploit children with superpowers. The episode introduces older test subjects who use their abilities to help an organization serve a perceived greater good. This introduction of older subjects suggests that humans with TK and TP have been around for a very long time.

Its origins can probably be traced back to Carrie White.

Season 2's episode 1 also reveals how the overarching corporate-backed project is trying to develop an AI that could replace humans with precognition, TK, and TP. However, AI is just not as effective as humans. Mike Flanagan's Carrie also ends with the titular character surviving, paving the way for season 2.

It is hard not to see how her story will be similar to the young characters from The Institute who are struggling to escape the clutches of a powerful shadow organization.

Stephen King never draws any explicit connections between The Dark Tower, Carrie, and The Institute. However, it is hard not to notice many clear overlaps between all three. For instance, in The Dark Tower universe, all psychic abilities are manifestations of a single cosmic force called the "Shine."

In The Dark Tower book series, specifically in Wolves of the Calla and The Dark Tower, characters with psychic powers are called are held captive by the Crimson King and referred to as Breakers. The Breakers are collectively expected to use their powers and chip away at the Beams of reality. Even the characters in The Institute are expected to do the same through quantum manipulation.

Put simply, in the grand scheme of Stephen King's larger horror universe, Carrie tells the foundational story of young adults with superpowers. The Institute and Firestarter step things up by featuring organizations that exploit these powers. Finally, The Dark Tower walks through the cosmic purpose of these powers, revealing why those with the "Shine" are so sought after in every Stephen King story.

Carrie serves as the first step for Mike Flanagan to establish a larger Stephen King universe on the small screen. He will double down on these connections and overlaps in Carrie season 2 and his highly-anticipated Dark Tower adaptation.

The Institute, released in 2025, follows 14-year-old genius Luke Ellis, who is kidnapped and wakes up at a mysterious facility filled with children possessing unusual abilities. Meanwhile, Tim Jamieson, a former police officer, seeks a fresh start in a nearby town, inevitably intertwining his fate with Luke's.

The winter air-drying rules that actually cut your laundry drying time in half

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When cold, wet weather rolls in, drying laundry indoors without a clothes dryer often turns into a multi-day ordeal. Piles of damp fabric draped across clothes airers bring chilling humidity into your living space, leaving garments smelling stale and walls prone to condensation and mould.

The secret to slashing indoor drying times lies not in cranking up the central heating to full blast, but in mastering air movement, extraction, and strategic placement. Here is how to dry your clothes indoors quickly and cleanly this winter, without inviting damp, mold, or musty smells into your home.

The single most effective shortcut begins before your clothes even leave the washing machine drum. Most spin cycles leave substantial moisture trapped deep inside thick cottons, heavy jeans, and knitwear.

Running a dedicated second spin cycle at your machine’s maximum spin speed pulls out surprising amounts of excess water without adding heat or risking fabric damage.

Shaking each item out vigorously immediately after unloading loosens compacted fibres and opens up airflow pockets that otherwise trap dampness for hours.

Where and how you hang wet laundry makes the difference between fresh clothes in hours and musty garments after two days. Cramming items closely onto a clothes drying rack restricts air circulation, trapping damp air directly between layers of fabric.

If you can, space each garment across two rungs rather than one, or slip button-up shirts and tops onto sturdy coat hangers suspended along the outer frame to keep fabrics exposed to circulating room air.

Moisture evaporates only as fast as the surrounding air can absorb and carry it away. Trapping a full airer in a closed, cold room creates a humid microclimate that halts evaporation entirely.

Positioning your clothes airer roughly a foot away from a heating duct, never draped directly in front of it, which blocks heating efficiency and risks scorching fabrics, paired with an oscillating fan on its lowest setting forces air constantly across the textiles.

If your home struggles with persistent condensation in late fall and winter, running one of the best dehumidifiers directly beneath or alongside the rack draws pints of moisture straight out of the wet fibres while blowing warm, dry air back through the load.
