Microsoft’s flagship development tool, Visual Studio Professional 2026, reduces much of the friction that used to come with large projects, and it’s on sale for just $29.97 on StackSocial right now, which is far less than what most developers expect to pay for a professional-grade IDE.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a desktop-only Windows product built as a 64-bit application, designed for people working on real-world codebases. Think multi-project solutions, long build times, and code that’s touched by more than one person. In day-to-day use, the biggest benefit is the context the software provides while you work. Visual Studio 2026 supports C#, C++, .NET, ASP.NET, Blazor, and .NET MAUI, so you can move between desktop, web, and cross-platform projects without switching tools. You also get Hot Reload, which helps reduce rebuild time by letting you edit code in .NET and C++ apps and see changes immediately. The software’s AI-powered IntelliCode suggestions also feel more restrained than flashy. They tend to fill in logical patterns based on your existing code. System requirements are also worth noting: While it can technically run on 4GB of RAM, 8GB or more is far more realistic, especially for larger solutions, and storage needs can balloon depending on workloads, reaching well over 100GB in some setups. Also, it doesn’t support 32-bit systems and won’t run on mobile devices or Chromebooks. For developers already working in the Windows ecosystem, this is a solid long-term license. For everyone else, those limitations can be deal breakers.

#3436. Netflix's Unhinged Alan Ritchson Thriller 'War Machine' Is Officially Best of the Year

The breakout movies and TV shows of 2026 are putting certain actors in the spotlight. Tom Holland became summer's biggest star thanks to the one-two punch of Spider-Man: Brand New Day and The Odyssey. Inde Navarrette's breakout role in Obsession led to her snagging the role of Rogue in Marvel Studios' upcoming X-Men reboot. It's Alan Ritchson, though, who's had the biggest surprise. While Ritchson's best known for playing the title role in Reacher, he also starred in a gritty sci-fi/action thriller that quickly became one of Netflix's biggest movies.

That movie is War Machine, which is directed and co-written by Patrick Hughes (The Hitman's Bodyguard.) War Machine centers on a unnamed soldier (Ritchson) who is currently training to join the Army Rangers. The soldier, given the designation "81", is about to complete the test known as the "Death March" where he and other soldiers destroy a prototype aircraft. It turns out that the aircraft they're meant to destroy is a highly advanced alien machine that starts picking off soldiers left and right. What follows is a blood-soaked, adrenaline-fueled story that's been described as "The Terminator meets The Hurt Locker," and it wouldn't work without Alan Ritchson.

War Machine takes its time building up to the reveal that its protagonist is fighting an alien machine, which makes the carnage hit that much harder once it begins. The real meat of the movie's story lies in exploring 81's emotional state. At the opening of the movie, he loses his brother (Jai Courtney) during a firefight; the lingering guilt and grief lead him to take greater risks and have his superiors questioning him. It isn't until the machine attacks that 81 is forced to rely on his fellow soldiers, even taking the leadership position he kept denying.

Ritchson helps give War Machine an emotional core through his performance. Over time, he showcases a slowly defrosting exterior, going from a tortured soldier to a bona fide leader. It doesn't hurt that he has a great supporting cast to bounce off, whether it's Stephan James as fellow Ranger trainee 7 or Dennis Quaid and Esai Morales as his superior officers. Unlike Reacher, which has settled into a predictable but reliable formula, or Motor City, which prioritized its no-dialogue gimmick over an actual story, War Machine develops its characters while still delivering the action you'd expect from Army men taking on alien machinery.

While War Machine drew mixed reviews, it was a hit for Netflix and still holds a spot on the streamer's Top 10 list of most popular movies. That puts it among other Netflix breakouts, like KPop Demon Hunters and Ryan Reynolds' time travel epic The Adam Project. Ironically, War Machine wasn't developed as a Netflix movie. Patrick Hughes originally meant to release the movie theatrically until Netflix partnered with Lionsgate. Hughes also told Decider that War Machine was part of a larger story he wanted to tell if given the chance.

“I know exactly where I want to take it, and what that broader story is...We absolutely love the character of 81. For me, I wanted to tell a film that started with the micro, and ended with the macro. And I thought that was a really unique take on the genre that we were working in. Let’s see what happens.”

Hughes is about to get his chance as Netflix greenlit a sequel to War Machine, appropriately titled War Machines. Details are scarce, but the sequel is more than likely following up on the end of War Machine where it's revealed that more alien machines have touched down on Earth — and 81 is the sole man who knows their weakness. Alan Ritchson is also continuing his working relationship with Netflix, as he's set to star in the upcoming action thriller Malestrom. The smash success of War Machine proves Ritchson has a future outside of Reacher, and that sci-fi remains Netflix's most successful genre for original projects.

#3435. 34 Years Ago, Marvel's Best Creators Rebelled Like Never Before

Back in 1992, a crew of Marvel Comics' best artists dramatically left to start their own venture; that decision would end up having a colossal impact on the comics industry of today. Image Comics is nowadays known as a powerhouse unto itself, historically publishing major works like Spawn, The Walking Dead, and Savage Dragon. Meanwhile, Robert Kirkman's Invincible has been adapted into what's arguably the 21st Century's best animated superhero series so far.

Despite a slew of top-tier material, what makes Image Comics a particular standout in the history of comics is the publisher's fraught origins. Nestled within its founding and the early years when Image defined '90s comics is a story of independent comics, creators' rights, and more that connects back to creators' disillusionment with Marvel for decades. Image Comics just happened to have the right combination of things to make a true creators' rebellion work.

Image Comics was born from what was effectively an exodus of Marvel's hottest talents of the time: Todd McFarlane (Spider-Man), Rob Liefeld (X-Force), and Jim Lee (X-Men), all of whom had broken sales records—Lee's X-Men #1 remains the best-selling comic of all time. This wasn't something that Marvel rewarded. For Marvel, brand identity was the most important thing—over and above the personalities working on the comics, themselves. Comics were effectively written freelance as work-for-hire, meaning that creators themselves were—and often still are—disposable.

This had two effective consequences for breakout stars working under the Big Two. The first, for some creators like Liefeld, was the feeling that their stardom made them disposable; creators with star power presented a risk to the brand-centric paradigm. The second, for other creators, was a feeling of being undervalued: because they worked as freelancers, they had no actual rights to things like royalties for merchandise based on their work.

While Invincible enjoys its well-deserved place in the spotlight today, it’s worth remembering the groundbreaking work done 24 years earlier.

All of this should also be understood in the context of a tide-shift in the industry, generally. More and more independent and creator-owned publishers were cropping up, with varying levels of success. Creators' rights had always been a major concern in the industry: milestones included the 1978 formation of the Comics Creators Guild (featuring huge names like Neal Adams, Frank Miller, Chris Claremont, and more). Todd McFarlane had made efforts to unionize creators at Marvel prior to Image Comics being established.

For the Image Comics exodus in particular, the minutiae were well documented in Michael Dean's four-part series "The Image Story" for The Comics Journal, charting the history of Image Comics up to its publication in 2000. What the deep-dive shows isn't an organized group of rebels but disgruntled artists with variable motivations and wavering commitments simply seeking to own the works they create if they were going to stay in the comics industry.

Image Comics was the end result of a long process through which Liefeld found other options—it was Liefeld who would bring Marvel's top artists together, and it was Liefeld who went to Malibu Comics and probed into whether they would publish black-and-white lines from Marvel's biggest names. Liefeld would go on to recruit McFarlane, Lee, Erik Larsen, Jim Valentino, Marc Silvestri, and Whilce Portacio as a united front to bargain with Marvel for creative control.

The triumphant Image Comics rebellion doesn't start with an exodus, but with an ultimatum given to Marvel Comics' president by Liefeld, Lee, and McFarlane in December 1991: that they would continue working at Marvel on their own creator-owned lines, or they would leave to publish elsewhere. The outcome was perhaps predictable, and the artists left with intentions to defect completely.

In 1992, Image Comics was officially established. The underlying principle of creators owning their own works wasn't new, but Image's managerial structure was relatively novel; Image would act as infrastructure for the studios and partners working under its umbrella, and no partner could interfere with another partner's work. Malibu Comics played a critical role in realizing those principles, willing to take on the Marvel talent at face value and provide essential early support with marketing, publication, and distribution.

Through a combination of luck, timing, and star power, Image would become a massive hit, even briefly overtaking DC's market share with record-breaking titles like Liefeld's Youngblood, McFarlane's Spawn, and Larsen's The Savage Dragon. To this day, many of Image Comics' best series can be traced to the company's first year. By 1993, Image was successful enough to leave Malibu entirely and become independent.

The Youngblood franchise returns and expands this summer and ScreenRant is proud to offer an exclusive first look at two exciting variant covers.

The following year, more non-partners would start publishing under Image with titles like Alan Moore, Steve Bissette, and Rick Veitch's 1963 and Larry Stroman's Tribe (which would become the best-selling African American comic from an African American creator of all time).

To an extent, Image's structure would also become its undoing for a while. The surrounding hype combined with its creators' failures to deliver books on time would arguably play a considerable role in comics' speculative bubble bursting in 1993. The same varied motivations that birthed Image Comics would pave the way for intense disagreements, tension, and poaching between founders—Liefeld would officially resign in 1996, right before a meeting where he would have been ousted. (He would later return as a creator, not a partner, in 2007.)

Despite everything, though, Image Comics eventually righted the ship, steadily expanding their line of comics and eventually bringing on a new partner, Robert Kirkman. Today, Image stands as an emblem of independent comics publishing in general: independent studios can not only survive and thrive in an ecosystem dominated by the Big Two, but they can become enough of a force to compete with them.

This is despite unglamorous origins in an often understated history of creators' rights in comics that, ironically, found a major watershed at Marvel itself when the legendary Jack Kirby, co-creator of many of the brand's biggest characters, started to publicly criticize Stan Lee and the company over rights, royalties, authorial credit, and the work-for-hire model in the '70s and '80s.

The MCU Slump is still at the front of fans' minds, and 1 Marvel creator says the dip is happening on comics for the same reason.

In other words, the stardom that would propel Image to success was latent in Marvel's own machinery. Image stands as a spiritual win for creators' rights in comics. But its huge success also meant it could provide a truly commercially viable platform for independent creator-owned works that could stand up against the Big Two—the lack of which creators had been circling for years before.

The history of Image Comics is fascinating precisely because it's rocky. There was no golden origin, and the reality is that the bedrock was there for something like Image Comics to emerge eventually—the industry had been setting up for a creator-focused behemoth that could actually contest the Big Two for decades. But Image Comics is what emerged, and through the rebellion of seven disgruntled Marvel artists, the company now stands as a beacon for the stories mainstream publishers might not want to tell.

#3434. How to Try 'Audio Intelligence' on Your Apple Watch Early

It has been a big year for Apple. There's a new CEO, prices have increased across the board, and there's been a seemingly endless rollout of new devices, including two new Apple Watches: the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. All things considered, these watches offer only minor upgrades over the previous models, shipping with new heart rate monitors and the latest S11 processor. But one of the biggest new watch features, "Audio Intelligence," is also the most controversial—and it's rolling out in beta today.

Audio Intelligence is Apple's branding for a new set of features exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4. These features use the new Apple Watches' hardware, along with on-device and cloud-based AI, for tasks like sound and music identification as well as dictation. "Sound Recognition" can alert you to important sounds, like alarms and doorbells, while "Music Recognition" can automatically display songs playing around you—but these aren't the features you'll hear talked about in discussions of Audio Intelligence.

Rather, everyone is up in arms about "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap." These Audio Intelligence features passively "listen" to your conversations throughout the day, and, using AI, deliver summaries of what was said. When you double-click your Apple Watch's crown to use Live Rewind, you'll get a loose transcript of the last 15 seconds of conversation it overheard, while Siri Recap can show summaries of all your in-person chats throughout the day. You can even configure a schedule for when your watch is "listening" for recaps—e.g., only run during work hours. Apple suggests each is intended to help jog your memory; maybe you use Siri Recap to remember important discussions you had that morning, while Live Rewind is meant for moments where you forget what someone just said. (As opposed to asking them to repeat themselves, I suppose.)

Apple's claims may or may not assuage your fears, but it seems the company is pushing on ahead regardless. Apple is releasing Audio Intelligence as part of iOS 27.3, which launches in beta on Tuesday. If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, you can try it out today, assuming you enroll in Apple's latest beta version.

To do so, you'll need to sign up for the Apple Developer program, since iOS 27.3 is rolling out first for devs. This program used to require a $99 fee, but you can skip it now if you opt for the free account. Once you enroll your Apple Account in this program, you can open your iPhone, head to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, and choose "iOS 27 Developer Beta." Go back one page, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install iOS 27.3 when it's available.

The Salomon Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX is a waterproof running shoe designed primarily for gravel, but it’s also very capable on roads and other light trails. It will suit some runners’ needs perfectly, but the waterproof upper can run hot.

Comfortable midsole with good energy return

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

For those of us in the Northern Hemisphere, the cold, wet days of winter are approaching fast, and if you plan on running through the season, there are some benefits to buying a specialist set of running shoes for it.

The two features I look for in the best running shoes for the winter are an outsole that grips well in wet conditions and a water-repellent or waterproof upper.

Both boxes are ticked by the Salomon Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX, which has a Gore-Tex membrane in the upper, is fully waterproof, and has a gravel-ready outsole that works well on a wide variety of terrain.

I’ve used the shoe for a mix of runs on roads, light trails and grassy hills and it’s impressed me as a winter-ready daily trainer. If you don’t need its waterproof upper or versatile outsole, though, you’ll get a better ride from some lighter, bouncier road options like the Asics Novablast 6.

The Salomon Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX launched in fall 2026 and costs $160 in the U.S. and £145 in the U.K., which is $20/£20 more expensive than the standard model of the shoe without the Gore-Tex upper.

Salomon also released the Aero Glide 4 GRVL in its line-up, which is a slightly softer and more cushioned option than the Blaze, which some runners might prefer for easy long runs in particular.

The Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX is currently available in four colors, including Vanilla Ice, the model I tested for those who want to show off the dirt they run through, and an all-black design for those who don’t.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

My US men’s size 10 weighs exactly 10oz, which is light for a shoe with a thick outsole, waterproof upper, and tall stack of foam in the midsole.

The stack height is 37mm at the heel and 29mm at the forefoot for an 8mm drop, which is a little lower than the stack on the Aero Glide 4 GRVL.

I found the shoe fit me well in my normal running shoe size, and the Gore-Tex upper wasn’t stiff or uncomfortable during my testing.

The Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX uses a mesh upper with Gore-Tex lining and padding on the tongue and around the collar.

During my testing, I was able to run in heavy rain and splash through puddles without my feet getting wet, and I also like that it’s quick and easy to clean the waterproof upper after muddy runs.

However, the drawback is that it’s not the most breathable material, and when running in warm conditions or using the shoe for walks, my feet got sweatier than normal.

Rather than traditional laces, it has Salomon’s QuickLace Neo system so you can loosen and tighten the fit quickly with the pull toggle, which you can then tuck under an elastic band so it doesn’t bounce around on the run.

The Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX uses a supercritical TPU foam called OptiFoam Squared in its midsole, with a mild rocker shape helping to roll you from heel to toe with each stride.

I’m a fan of this foam, which is also used on the Aero Glide 4 GRVL. It’s soft enough to be comfortable without being overly squishy, and it gives a good amount of energy return when you hit faster paces.

The rubber outsole on the shoe has 2.5mm deep, chevron-shaped lugs that are built to grip on gravel tracks but also work well on roads and other light trails.

This outsole is a star feature on the shoe because it allows you to tackle such a wide variety of terrain with confidence, even in wet conditions.

The Salomon Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX proved to be an enjoyably versatile shoe in my testing. I used it as my main daily trainer, tackling easy, steady-paced runs mainly on the road and forest trails.

I also used it for one run on slightly more technical trails with rocky and grassy sections, and throughout all my testing, the grip was impressively reliable, even in very wet conditions. It’s not a good option for deep mud, but can handle most other trails well.

That versatility extends to the paces the Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX can handle. The midsole has a responsive feel at faster paces while soft enough for long, easy runs — it felt good at all the paces I’d run at outside dedicated interval workouts.

The waterproof upper does its job on rainy days well, and also helps keep your feet warm on easy runs in cold conditions.

However, this upper did limit me because it can be a bit too hot at times. My feet got very sweaty on longer runs on dry days, and if you’re a runner who uses one shoe for everything, a fully waterproof sneaker like this probably isn't the best buy.

The Salomon Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX does a great job in the role it’s built for. The waterproof upper is great on wet, cold days; the outsole grips well in wet and dry conditions on both the road and light trails, and the midsole is enjoyably energetic.

If that all sounds good but you want something a little softer and more cushioned, the Salomon Aero Glide 4 GRVL also comes in a Gore-Tex model, and Salomon also has non-GTX models of both shoes, and road versions with less substantial outsoles.

There are a lot of choices in the line-up, and I’d say all are good shoes thanks to the OptiFoam Squared midsole at the heart of them, so you can tailor your Blaze or Glide to suit your needs and preferences.

If you’re sticking to the roads during your winter runs, I’d also consider the Adidas Adizero Evo SL ATR, which has a water-repellent upper and small lugs on its outsole. It’s a good option if the full waterproof upper and thick outsole on the Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX is overkill for your needs.

#3428. 7 Perfect Sci-Fi Movies That Hooked Me From the First 10 Minutes

The brilliance of science fiction lies in its ability to blend thrilling, out-of-this-world spectacle with explorations of human fears, ethics, and big ideas rooted in science. Through wonder and escapism, these films transport us to strange new worlds, futuristic cities, or deep space, giving our brains a moment of reprieve. Whether robots, clones, aliens, or artificial intelligence, these stories often mirror our mortality, isolation, and capacity to be human.

A good flick will sustain and entertain, but a brilliant sci-fi film will hook you immediately. Though incredible sci-fi movies exist throughout cinema history, these seven hook you within the first ten minutes. From a thrilling chase to a scrolling exposition that establishes an entire galaxy, these movies capture you instantaneously, leaving an impression that lasts far beyond the final credits.

Based on Philip K. Dick's 1968 novel, Blade Runner is a cyberpunk neo-noir science fiction thriller set in a dystopian Los Angeles in 2019. Retired police officer Rick Deckard (Harrison Ford) is forced back into service as a blade runner to "retire" bioengineered synthetic humans known as replicants. The film uses its narrative to question the boundary between human and machine.

Through visual overload, the film opens on a sweeping industrial city landscape, seemingly foreign to our modern eye, where fire-belching smokestacks, flying cars, and neon lights dominate the skyline. The camera then cuts to an extreme close-up of a human eye reflecting the cityscape, establishing the core themes of vision, surveillance, and the blurred line between what's natural and what is manufactured. From there, the audience is plunged into Dave Holden's (Morgan Paull) high-stakes Voight-Kampff interrogation of Leon (Brion James), a Nexus-6 replicant. With the world established, our hero, Deckard, is introduced, sitting on a rainy, grimy street as his mission is about to begin.

In Alfonso Cuarón's dystopian action thriller Children of Men, the planet is experiencing global infertility as humans have mysteriously lost the ability to procreate. As civilization crumbles, plagued by suicide, despair, and terrorism, the United Kingdom stands as one of the last functioning governments, turning into an authoritarian regime that rounds up, detains, and deports "fugees." Theo Farron (Clive Owen) is tasked with transporting Kee (Clare-Hope Ashitey), a miraculously pregnant refugee, to the Human Project.

The film's opening scene masterfully hooks you through abrupt worldbuilding, sensory shock, and a complete subversion of the genre. In total darkness, a bleak news broadcast drops key information about the dystopian stakes. When the visuals kick in, the camera tracks Theo as he pushes through a grieving crowd watching the news. The action kicks in when the coffee shop he just left explodes violently. The audio drops, mirroring the ringing tinnitus and capturing our protagonist's temporary deafness as a striking image of a bleeding woman holding her severed arm is seen. The sudden, visceral violence shatters all sense of safety as Cuarón's continuous, unbroken shot forces you to experience the event in real time.

In Doug Liman's military sci-fi action film Edge of Tomorrow, Major William Cage (Tom Cruise), a military public relations officer with no combat experience, is thrust into a time loop during a desperate human war against an alien race known as mimics. As the war rages on, Cage wakes up the next morning before the battle, only to find the loop resets to the same day every time he dies. He teams up with Rita Vrataski (Emily Blunt) as they train, die, and investigate the mysterious alien hivemind.

Within the first ten minutes, the film becomes a masterclass in efficient, high-stakes storytelling. Through an aggressive montage of real-world and fictional news footage, you're caught up on years of lore before meeting Cage, a smarmy PR slickster who desperately avoids the battlefield. The tension spikes when he is unexpectedly dropped on the front lines of a suicide mission beach invasion. Liman captures claustrophobic dread as Cage, strapped into a massive, lethal, weaponized suit, has no idea how to maneuver. Edge of Tomorrow establishes a terrifying world where death seems imminent.

All it took was a scroll to change the galaxy. In Star Wars: Episode IV—A New Hope, the first film in George Lucas' long-running franchise, a classic hero's journey unfolds during a galactic civil war against the tyrannical Galactic Empire. The Rebel Alliance steals the architectural plans for the planet-destroying superweapon, the Death Star. Luke Skywalker (Mark Hamill) joins Obi-Wan Kenobi (Alec Guinness) and hired smuggler Han Solo (Harrison Ford) to rescue Princess Leia (Carrie Fisher) from Darth Vader's (James Earl Jones) clutches.

Star Wars hooks you immediately with John Williams' fanfare and the epic yellow text crawl that sets up the entire story. Without lecturing or boring the audience, the rolling text throws you into the fray at warp speed. From there, an endless Imperial Star Destroyer roars overhead as C-3PO and R2-D2 bicker through the chaos, giving you characters to latch onto instantly. As the smoke clears, the greatest sci-fi villain emerges, and terror is born without a lengthy introductory monologue. The iconic opening became a franchise staple, exciting fans for generations.

The scores below reveal how the Force sees you. Your highest number is your true alignment. Read on to understand what that means — and what it will cost you.

Disciplined, compassionate, and deeply attuned to the living Force, you have walked the path long enough to understand its demands — and accept them. You lead not through authority alone, but through example. You have felt the pull of the dark side and chosen otherwise, every time. That is not certainty. That is courage.

You are earnest, powerful, and brimming with potential — and you know it, which is both your greatest asset and your most dangerous flaw. You act before you think, trust your gut over your training, and sometimes confuse impatience for bravery. The Masters see something in you, though. The question isn't whether you have what it takes — it's whether you'll be patient enough to find out.

You are not simply dangerous — you are certain, and that is worse. You have decided what the galaxy needs, and you have decided you are the one to deliver it. Your power is genuine and formidable, earned through sacrifice that would have broken lesser beings. But examine your victories carefully. Every Sith believed their cause was righteous. The dark side's cruelest trick is that it agrees with you.

You were forged in fire and reshaped by those who found you at your lowest. You serve, because service gave you structure when you had none. Your allegiance is not to an ideology — it is to survival and to the master who gave you purpose. But there is something buried beneath the conditioning. The Jedi you hunt? You recognize them. Because you remember what it felt like before the choice was taken from you.

You have looked at the Jedi Code and the Sith Code and found both of them incomplete. You walk the line not out of indecision but out of conviction — you genuinely believe both extremes miss something essential. The Jedi don't fully trust you. The Sith think you're wasting your potential. They're both partially right. But so are you.

Written and directed by the Wachowskis, The Matrix follows computer hacker Neo (Keanu Reeves), who discovers that human reality is a complex computer simulation known as The Matrix. Rebel leader Morpheus (Laurence Fishburne) and his partner Trinity (Carrie-Anne Moss) contact him and see him as "The One" with the power to bend and manipulate the Matrix's physical laws and fightthe computer programs that police the simulation.

A high-octane philosophical wonder, The Matrix establishes mystery and breaks the laws of physics as it introduces an immediate, high-stakes threat. The film opens with glowing green computer code shifting across a black screen, establishing the cyberpunk atmosphere, with the only explanation being the voice of a woman discussing the mysterious "Neo." Espionage and curiosity arrive as Trinity is cornered by a police squad, and bang! The infamous bullet time is revealed. The groundbreaking effect comes as a cinematic, mind-bending shock.

A brilliant product of its time, James Cameron's The Terminator set the tone for sci-fi action films in the decades that followed. The first film in the franchise follows a T-8000 cyborg assassin (Arnold Schwarzenegger) sent back in time from a post-apocalyptic 2029 to 1984 Los Angeles to kill Sarah Connor (Linda Hamilton). The human resistance fights back as lone soldier Kyle Reese (Michael Biehn) is sent to protect her.

Within the opening minutes, Cameron grabs your attention with a bleak, post-apocalyptic Los Angeles that shows giant machines crushing human skulls. When the story transitions to 1984, a different type of fear is introduced when two completely naked men emerge from a violent, crackling electrical storm. Both search for clothes in different ways: The Terminator's innate brutality arrives as an unstoppable, silent force of nature, killing a group of punks, including ripping through one's torso. Meanwhile, Reese is set up as the desperate underdog, without that same strength.

A truly delightful sci-fi story, WALL-E helped young viewers fall in love with the genre like never before. The story follows WALL-E, a lonely trash-compacting robot on a ruined, abandoned Earth who follows a sleek probe droid named EVE across the galaxy to help humanity rediscover its home. A beautifully filmed, philosophically tinged wonder, WALL-E remains one of Pixar's best.

Within the first 10 minutes, the film uses pure visual and auditory storytelling to build instant empathy for a rusty old robot on a ruined planet, without a single word of dialogue. The wasteland is strikingly juxtaposed with the upbeat, toe-tapping vintage sounds of "Put On Your Sunday Clothes" from Hello, Dolly! As the titular character is introduced, WALL-E becomes instantly endearing as he embarks on his daily routines, hoarding treasures and artifacts like a lighter, a Rubik's Cube, and the film's VHS. His childlike curiosity mirrors our own, letting our wonder join him on his extraordinary journey.

#3427. Apple announces Fitness+ Gym Strength program with personalized workout plans

Apple wants to help you get stronger. Apple Fitness+ is expanding to the gym with a new strength training experience. Gym Strength is now available in beta, bringing personalized workout plans, exercise demonstrations, and Apple Watch logging to your lifting routine.

Gym Strength creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment. After you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weight you logged.

The feature is designed for a range of experience levels, from people trying strength training for the first time to experienced lifters looking to make progress. It also aims to help anyone who wants to build a more consistent routine.

When building a plan, you choose your workout days and the body areas you want to focus on. You can select five exercises per workout, which Apple estimates will take about 20–30 minutes, or seven exercises for about 45–60 minutes, depending on your pace.

Each workout recommends exercises, reps, sets, and how much weight to lift.

You move through the workout at your own pace, with short video demonstrations from Apple Fitness+ trainers available for each exercise. The demonstrations can be expanded to show the movement from three different angles.

Apple says Gym Strength includes over 350 exercises across more than 30 types of strength training equipment, including dumbbells, kettlebells, suspension trainers, cable machines, and barbells. Dumbbells are the minimum equipment requirement.

Plans account for the equipment available to you, so the experience can work in a commercial gym or a home gym.

If a machine is occupied or you’re training somewhere with different equipment, you can swap equipment or choose an alternative exercise with a similar movement and body focus. You can also add sets or skip exercises.

Gym Strength requires an iPhone running iOS 27.3 or an iPad running iPadOS 27.3. An Apple Watch running watchOS 27.3 optionally lets you view exercises and log reps and weight from your wrist, while tracking heart rate and calories burned.

Gym Strength also introduces Training Note, an optional feature powered by Apple Intelligence that previews workouts, explains progression, and highlights milestones. Training Note requires an Apple Intelligence–enabled iPhone or iPad with the device set to English.

Gym Strength is included in the existing Fitness+ subscription. It joins a library of trainer-led workouts spanning 12 workout types, including Strength, HIIT, Yoga, Pilates, Core, Cycling, Rowing, Dance, Kickboxing, treadmill walking and running, and Mindful Cooldown.

Fitness+ also offers guided meditations, personalized recommendations, and Custom Plans for scheduling workouts, with new sessions added every week.

Fitness+ is also included in Apple One Premier, which costs $39.95 per month in the U.S. and bundles Apple Music, Apple TV, Apple Arcade, Apple News+, and 2TB of iCloud+ storage.

#3426. Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars Officially Arrives November 12

Project Hail Mary was one of the best movies of the year, and whether you're a fan of the film or the book by Andy Weir, you'll have something new to look forward to this November. Billed as an untold chapter, Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars sees Ryland Grace and Rocky return for one more adventure. A new trailer debuted at the end of October, ahead of Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars' official release date on November 12, 2026.

Story details on Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars are pretty scarce. We know it's a side story to both the book and film, allowing fans to experience a part of Grace's mission that Andy Weir wrote for this exact purpose. Thankfully, the latest trailer briefly shows off Rocky, so we know the beloved Eridian is back. The upcoming VR game is available to preorder now from Meta, and also offers up three exclusive preorder bonuses. You can view the trailer below.

"Work together in the face of disaster to keep the Hail Mary intact and bring their world-saving cargo to Eridani — Rocky’s home planet, and Grace’s new home," reads the official description for the game. As Ryland Grace, players will get to manage the ship and its cargo, diagnose failing systems, and improvise scientific solutions while abord the Hail Mary. Perhaps most importantly of all, you'll be able to interact with Rocky on the journey to Eridani. And, yes, this is a brand-new story not featured in the movie or book.

Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars will work with Meta Quest 3S, Meta Quest 3, and Meta Quest Pro. Right now, the game has a discount, so you can snag it for $17.99 versus its MSRP of $19.99. Preordering through the Meta storefront will earn you three gold xenonite sculptures as an in-game pre-order bonus.

Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars is developed by Maze Theory, which has made licensed VR games for other familar IPs like Peaky Blinders and Doctor Who, as well as Thief VR: Legacy of Shadow. If you don't have any of the compatible Meta devices, Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars is also planned for release on PICO and Android XR.

While this isn't the sequel some fans may have been hoping for, Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars is at least a way to spend more time with Rocky and Ryland Grace without having to worry about what a full-fledged follow-up might do to two widely-adored characters (in other words, we don't have to worry about it ruining anything). Honestly, just getting to hang out with Rocky sounds like enough of a selling point.

It will be interesting to see what this new chapter adds to the current story seen in the book and film. Even if it offers up nothing groundbreakingly new, it'll at least be nice to return to the Hail Mary again. For all the fans of Project Hail Mary out there, be sure to mark your calendars for November 12.

Based on the novel by Andy Weir (The Martian), Project Hail Mary is an action-adventure sci-fi film that stars Ryan Gosling as an astronaut who must save Earth from an oncoming ice age by heading to a faraway galaxy.

Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited is a PS5 pad for pro players

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I’ve spent thousands of hours with my PS5 since launch. But in all that time, every single one of the best PS5 games I’ve enjoyed has been played on a stock DualSense controller. I’ve never used a so-called “pro” controller.

That was until this week, when I got my hands on Nacon’s new Revolution 5 Unlimited controller, designed for use with Sony’s current generation console (and PC). It’s opened my eyes to a whole new way of experiencing competitive gaming. It's made returning to my regular old DualSense a challenge (sadly, the Revolution 5 Unlimited sometimes needs to charge).

This $230 / £179 pad most definitely qualifies as a pro controller, offering a vast array of features and upgrades: Magnetic TMR joysticks, dual-mode actuation triggers, and seven (yes, seven) fully programmable shortcuts. And that’s just the start; there’s one upgrade that stands out most of all, and it turns this third-party controller into a genuine game-changer.

Designed for the PS5 and with competitive online gaming in mind, the Nacon R5U is a proper pro controller. Its biggest upgrade is the built-in display, which lets you customize any of its seven shortcuts on the fly, and it also sports TMR joysticks, dual-mode actuation triggers, and a docking station for easy charging. It's also compatible with PC.

You can’t fail to notice the biggest thing that sets the Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited apart from a stock PS5 DualSense. It’s not the offset sticks, redesigned d-pad, or all those extra buttons on the back of the controller. No, the eye-catcher is the (roughly) 1.8-inch display on the controller face.

Replacing the DualSense’s largely useless touchpad (on the R5U the touchpad is reassigned to a button between the d-pad and right analog stick), Nacon calls it the “command screen,” and it’s a very fitting name.

The display gives you instant access to the controller’s “mapping” features, letting you select inputs for the four back buttons, two buttons on the top of the controller, and even reassign the “touchpad” button. I recommend keeping the latter set to the default input, as most games require it.

There’s no need to mess around in the PS5’s settings menus or use a companion mobile/desktop app; you can assign each additional button directly on the controller’s display. While I haven't used a controller that requires an app, I can't imagine not having a built-in display now. Assigning shortcuts on the fly is unbelievably convenient and makes experimenting with different input combinations straightforward.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The controller also offers up to eight individual profiles, which you can swap between directly on the R5U at the touch of a button. This allowed me to create input combinations tailored to the various games I’m playing right now, and leap between them instantly. It’s a breeze!

Sadly, it’s not all upgrades. While this new Nacon controller is officially licensed, it doesn’t include some DualSense-exclusive features, namely haptic feedback and adaptive triggers. And it can’t be used to turn on your PS5 console, which is a small inconvenience in the grand scheme. Plus, to connect it wirelessly, you’ll need to use the supplied USB dongle.

There isn’t really a scientific way to judge whether I play better on the DualSense or the Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited, but I’d say I feel more in control when playing with the R5U.

Well, I do now, at least; that was most certainly not the case initially. A pro controller like this is designed for competitive online play, and what better way to test it out than on the recently released Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, the latest installment in the annual shooter series.

Turns out that trying to unlearn more than 30 years of muscle memory playing on a standard controller is kind of hard, and out of the gate, my fingers were confused, caught behind using the back buttons to shoot and the regular triggers. But this adaptation period didn’t hold me back for too long, and eventually I was able to start developing new muscle memory.

I’m a pretty average CoD player in general (my K/D averages out to an unspectacular 1.0), and while using the R5U hasn’t seen my performance suddenly leap up into e-sports pro territory, in a game like CoD where micro-seconds count, I feel like I’m getting the drop on enemy players where previously I might not. But this could be a placebo effect, of course.

Another game I’ve been using to test out the R5U this week is Star Wars: Galactic Racer, and this is one where I can say the R5U has made a difference. Assigning my speeder’s boost and drift to back buttons (X and Square on a DualSense) means I never have to take my fingers off either stick. My racing lines have never been cleaner, and my lap times better.

Nevertheless, if you’re more of a single-player gamer, I don’t think there’s much of a case for a controller like the R5U. But if you enjoy competitive online play, it offers additional control options, and because it’s so customizable, you can find the setup that enhances your skills.

We’ll have a full review of the Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited on Tom’s Guide soon, but as far as initial impressions go, it’s quickly become my preferred PS5 controller. As somebody who’s loved the standard PS5 DualSense since day one, that is a very big compliment.

#3424. iOS 27.3 adds all-new Apple Health app, details here

Apple released iOS 27.3 beta 1 today, and it reintroduces the all-new Health app that was first available for testing during the iOS 27.2 beta. Here’s what’s new.

iOS 27.3 will launch with an upgraded Apple Health app. The new app was initially tested during the iOS 27.2 beta, but it’s back today in iOS 27.3 beta 1 and will ship to all users next month.

Today on Apple Newsroom, the company outlined what to expect from the new Health experience.

Three central new Health features are highlighted for iOS 27.3:

Insights tab: “surfaces timely, holistic summaries spanning heart, sleep, readiness, fitness, vitals, and cycle tracking data throughout the day. A dedicated For You section delivers intelligent recommendations tailored to a user’s daily habits — such as practical guidance to adjust a wind-down routine following consecutive nights of interrupted sleep. The app pairs data with dynamic health content, offering educational videos and articles featuring Health app clinical experts.”

Longevity tab: “analyzes longitudinal metrics across heart health, sleep, mental wellbeing, movement, metabolic health, hearing, and nutrition. Central to this tab is Health Age, a feature that translates data from Apple Watch — including VO2 max, resting heart rate, sleep, and heart rate variability — into a metric that reflects how a user’s body is tracking relative to their chronological age. Users can also incorporate clinical laboratory data, such as A1c and LDL cholesterol, to enrich their long-term health picture.”

At-home movement evaluations: “make physical assessments accessible without requiring specialized equipment. Using an iPhone camera and Apple Watch, users can measure their flexibility, strength, balance, movement mechanics, and VO2 max with real-time audio and visual feedback. Powered by on-device vision-based AI models and developed with clinical experts, the experience runs entirely on device; no video is ever recorded, stored, or shared.“

Additionally, Apple says that the new Health app offers expanded language support. It is available in global English, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), French, Japanese, Korean, Norwegian, Portuguese, Spanish, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

#3423. Why I'd Choose the Oura Ring 5 Over the Cheaper Ultrahuman Pro

Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro is now officially on sale in the U.S., which makes this the perfect time to consider how this new device compares to the reigning champ in the smart ring market, the Oura Ring 5. Here's the short answer: While there’s a lot to like in the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, ultimately I think the Oura Ring 5 is just better at doing its job.

I’ve spent plenty of time with both rings, and admittedly, many of the differences between the two will come down to personal preference—for example, do you like the biohacking concept and the “next best actions” suggestions in the Ultrahuman app, or do you favor the soothing vibes of the Oura app? But when it comes to the devices themselves, there are big differences between them in terms of size, cost, and overall ease of use. Here’s my take on each, and why Oura is still my top choice.

The Oura Ring 5 is impressively small, and when you have to wear something on your finger, size matters a lot—and generally, smaller is better. The Oura Ring 5 is the smallest and most comfortable smart ring I’ve ever worn. I have a ton of photos here comparing it in size to other smart rings (including RingConn, older Oura rings, and an older Ultrahuman); suffice it to say, the Oura Ring 5 wins this category easily.

When it comes to the interior fit, both rings are similar: mostly smooth on the inside, without any intrusive bumps. But considering the overall shape and feel, the Oura Ring 5 is just more comfortable to wear throughout an entire day.

The Oura Ring 5 comes with a plug-in charger, which isn’t very convenient, but will get the job done. You can buy a slim, rounded charging case that easily fits in your pocket for $99. You need to match the size of the case to the size of your ring, and the charging case is not compatible with earlier versions of the device. It’s good for 30 days of charge, according to Oura.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro comes with a charging case that is heavy and bulky with prominent corners, but good for an extra 45 days of battery life. The case fits any size of Ultrahuman Ring Pro, but is not compatible with previous versions. You can have the case play sounds if you’ve misplaced it.

The Ultrahuman ring lasts slightly longer on a charge: eight to 10 days, according to the company, versus six to nine for the Oura Ring 5. The Ultrahuman ring also has several different battery modes, with “chill mode” lasting me about two weeks.

To sum up: the Ultrahuman ring lasts longer on a charge and has more capacity in its charging case. You also get the charging case for free. But the Oura Ring 5’s charging case is smaller and much easier to carry around. Once again, we’re looking at two decent options: The Oura case is more expensive for what you get, but it’s also nicer to use.

Oura is the most expensive smart ring out there, and it requires a subscription. That makes it the priciest option, giving Ultrahuman an opening to beat it simply by virtue of being cheaper. But this one is closer to a wash, depending on the choices you make. If you’re looking for the cheapest possible smart ring, well, you’d probably end up with something else entirely, like a RingConn Air. But between the Oura Ring 5 and the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, the latter is cheaper than the Oura Ring 5...but only if you’re saying no to all the extras. Let me break it down.

The Oura Ring 5 costs $399 for the shiny black and silver models, and $499 for gold, rose, and the matte versions of the black and silver. The subscription costs $5.99/month (or $69.99/year, which is only a $2 savings), and the Oura is basically useless without the subscription.

Here's how the cost works out on an annual basis:

Oura Ring 5 in black or silver: $399 + $5.99/month subscription = $470.88 for one year, $542.76 for two years

Oura Ring 5 in other colors: $499 + $5.99/month subscription = $570.88 for one year, $642.76 for two years.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro is $479 for all colors, and there is no subscription for basic use of the ring. But you can't necessarily stop there, because the Ultrahuman app includes “PowerPlugs” that will give you extra features or analysis screens. Some are totally free, including the caffeine window,  smart alarms, a new parent mode, and a limited version of the cycle and ovulation tracker, but others carry a monthly fee. And if you consider all the optional subscription fees for different PowerPlugs, they can quickly add up:

HealthEx, to connect medical records: $4.99/month

Most people probably wouldn't choose all of them, but even if you just wanted, say, respiratory health and cycle & ovulation pro, you’d quickly outstrip the price of an Oura Ring’s subscription. On the other hand, Ultrahuman also offers an Ultrahuman Max plan for $9.99/month or $99.99/year that includes all the PowerPlugs mentioned above, plus the Les Mills workouts that normally run $11.99/month. That's cheaper than subscribing to all of the options individually, but it will also make the Ultrahuman Ring Pro more expensive than the Oura Ring 5: $578.99 total for one year, or $678.98 for two years. In short, if you want everything that each ring has to offer, the Ultrahuman will cost you more.

Here's the big caveat: I wouldn't recommend bothering with most of the PowerPlugs. For example, "UltraSync for Tesla" recommends settings for your car based on how rested you are, which will be useless if you don't have a Tesla, and probably even if you do. "Cardio adaptability" measures a metric that Ultrahuman says is subtly different from HRV; Oura doesn't measure this adaptability metric, but it's not clear to me whether it's even worth measuring at all (I'd argue probably not).

Ultrahuman's respiratory health PowerPlug ($3.99/month) records sounds while you sleep, which Oura doesn't do; but Oura reports breathing disturbances based on the ring's data, which Ultrahuman doesn't do. Ultrahuman's feature is more expensive.

Ultrahuman offers a premium version of its cycle tracker for $3.99/month, while Oura has a partnership with Natural Cycles that cost $149.99/year. Either will provide more detailed (and, each company says, more accurate) cycle tracking than the basic tracking each app provides without the extras. Oura's option is more expensive.

Ultrahuman's HealthEx Powerplug ($4.99/month) displays information from your medical records throughout the app; Oura lets you import your medical records for free, but uses them mainly in the Advisor (chatbot) and dedicated areas of the app. Ultrahuman's option is more expensive.

Oura's app gives you scores for your readiness, sleep, and recent activity, and it tracks how stressed you seem to be throughout the day. A message at the top of the main screen gives you advice for what to do that day—for example, scaling back your workouts if you seem to be tired or stressed. Ultrahuman does pretty much the same thing, giving you a "next best action" that changes throughout the day, but tends to stick to predictable themes: get more activity if you've been sitting, and that sort of thing.

Both give detailed breakdowns of the factors that contribute to your scores, and both likely overstate how useful their scores are (you don't actually need to change your workout plans just because you had a less-than-perfect night of sleep). But the apps handle the basics pretty similarly: Both have partners and integrations, and you can book blood tests through either app, if you want to do that for some reason.

Ultrahuman gives you a bit more guidance on circadian rhythms, urging you to get in extra steps during certain times of day, and offering to micromanage your caffeine intake. It has a "longevity" tab that puts your long-term habits in terms of how many years they are supposedly subtracting from (or adding to) your lifespan, including measurable metrics like VO2max and a few things that are more inscrutable, like arterial stiffness.

Oura has a whole tab of "vitals" that it calculates from your day-to-day data, which I find more useful than Ultrahuman's data views. The items here include "resilience," which compares your stress to your recovery; a "symptom radar" that can sometimes flag when you're sick; and metrics of sleep regularity and how you're breathing. And, of course, you can check your "cardiovascular age" to see how much younger (or older) you should feel.

Overall, I prefer Oura's approach because the metrics make more sense, are easier to find, and are less likely to feel like they're going way out on a limb relative to the underlying science. Ultrahuman wants you to feel like a cutting-edge biohacker; Oura does a bit more to keep things down to earth. It is a bit funny to remember that both apps, and their wealth of data, are basically just pulling from heart rate readings throughout the day and night. Neither app gives you any truly important information the other doesn't, but Oura's makes more sense to me.

#3422. iOS 27.3 and macOS 27.3 add Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode, and more to Safari

Apple just released the first betas of iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3, with some big changes to Safari. The updates add a new vertical tab layout, Adaptive Dark Mode, and Siri AI Custom Actions.

Safari in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3 is adding a new Vertical Tabs design option. If you choose this design, you’ll see your tabs arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari rather than along the top, as in the traditional Safari design.

By default, Vertical Tabs show as icons in order to maximize vertical and horizontal space. If you’d like, you can also resize the tab bar to see website titles.

To try Vertical Tabs in the new iOS 27.3 beta, head to the Settings app, choose Apps, tap Safari, then look for the new Vertical Tabs option. On Mac and iPad, the feature can also be enabled via the “View” menu in the Safari app directly.

Vertical tab layouts have become an increasingly popular web browser feature. Arc from The Browser Company popularized the option. Arc, however, ceased development last year, and The Browser Company announced last month that it will discontinue it altogether in December.

If you regularly visit a website that doesn’t support Dark Mode, Apple’s next round of software updates adds Adaptive Dark Mode. This will automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t support the feature.

If Dark Mode is enabled on your iPhone, iPad, or Mac and you visit a website that doesn’t support it, you’ll see a new “Try” button. If you tap this, Safari will automatically create a Dark Mode version of the website.

You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

Finally, Siri AI can now take direct action on tabs in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3. This includes things like using Siri to move, sort, organize, and close your tabs.

In a future update, Siri’s on-screen awareness will also expand to include the entire content of a website, not just what’s visible on the screen at a particular moment.

iOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and iPadOS 27.3 are rolling out to developers for beta testing today. The update will likely be released to everyone sometime in December. What do you think of these new Safari features? Will you try out the new Vertical Tabs feature? Let us know down in the comments.

The Shark AquaReach Pro is a decent option for homes with hard floors. Its cordless design offers mobility, smaller attachments reach tight spaces, and it effectively lifts grime. However, the non-retractable extendable hose looks clunky in storage, dock self-cleaning is very loud, and the one-hour battery life limits longer cleaning sessions.

Roller mop is good at scrubbing the floor

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Vacuuming alone won’t keep the hard floors in your home clean. And a quick mop isn’t always enough to lift all the grime from everyday activities. One of the best vacuum mops, like the Shark AquaReach Pro, is a great addition to any home.

There’s a great deal to like about the Shark, including how it effortlessly gets into tight spaces and can be moved anywhere thanks to the cordless design. It effectively lifts grime, and the roller mop is fast.

But it’s not all roses. The extendable hose is clunky in storage, and the self-cleaning process on the dock is extremely loud. The one hour of battery life may also put off some users. To find out more, read on for my full Shark AquaReach Pro review.

The Shark AquaReach Pro is available to purchase from Amazon U.S. for $529. In the U.K., you can buy the cleaner directly from the SharkNinja website for £499.

It’s a little cheaper than the Roborock F25 ACE Pro, which costs $599, but this model effortlessly glides along the floor, and means you’re not always manually pushing the mop. That said, if you want the convenience that comes with smaller attachments to get into small spaces, then the Shark is the better option for you.

I’ve also tested the Dreame H15 Pro Heat, which costs $899. This wet/dry vacuum is a better option if you tend to find more stubborn stains in your home, as the water can be heated. But keep in mind that the heated water means the battery life will diminish a lot faster. So if you just want a basic clean, the Shark is a good option.

The Shark AquaReach Pro is a good-looking home device. Its rose gold and blue accents make it look like a well-thought-out home design piece. When not in use, the Shark sits on a docking station. This is where the device self-cleans, and it has a tray on the side to store smaller attachments for the nozzle.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The docking station plugs into a power outlet and charges the Aqua Reach Pro, and the 5.9-foot power cord means you'll need to keep it near a power outlet. The extendable wand lets you reach surfaces the roller mop can't, and the two extra included attachments get into smaller gaps.

Although this extendable hose helps you get into those hard-to-reach places, It’s probably my least favorite feature of the device from a design perspective. The hose is simply far too long, and when storing the device, it doesn’t retract, as I’m used to with other vacuums and mops. Instead, it clips to the body of the AquaReach Pro and springs back out. I’d love for this to have a more slinky design, so it isn’t fully extended at all times. However, since it has a cordless design, there aren’t any wires to carry around with you, which I appreciate.

There’s a clean water tank on the front of the Shark, and this easily clips on and off. The dirty water tank is on the side, and this has a max fill line so I knew when it needed to be emptied.

For simple floor cleaning, I prefer the design of the Roborock F25 Ace Pro. It looks a lot more basic, but I found it a lot more convenient to use.

The control buttons at the top of the device light up when each mode is in use. After reading the included instructions for the first few uses, I got to grips with each function quickly.

The Shark AquaReach Pro did a great job of making the floors in my kitchen and bathroom incredibly shiny. I filled the clean water tank with water and topped it up with the included cleaning solution as per the guidance on the tank.

The device works by letting out water and then sucking it back up with a vacuum. If a tougher stain requires a bit more help, you can use the trigger on the handle to squirt out more cleaning solution.

This device is designed to be used on hard surfaces, so firstly, I carried out my usual lab testing. I splashed some mayonnaise, soy sauce and ketchup on the floor and allowed them to dry down. The process wasn’t as quick as when I tested the Dreame H15 Pro Heat, but since that’s a heated floor cleaner, I also had to use less elbow grease than with this Shark vacuum mop to lift stains.

The Shark AquaReach Pro brought up all of the mess with relative ease though. Initially, the condiments were moved around the floors but in just six passes, all of the grime had been lifted.

I then took the AquaReach around the house to clean windowsills and in small spaces such as the toilets where the roller mop can’t quite reach. This was very useful, and it left everything feeling fresh. The smaller attachments are very useful; I still wish the hose design was more compact though.

Follow Tom's Guide on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our up-to-date news, analysis, and reviews in your feeds.

The Shark AquaReach Pro needs to be stored on its docking station. This means that it will have a permanent home near a power outlet wherever you set it up. It measures 4.53 x 11.61 x 11.02 inches, which is about the same size as a vacuum cleaner, so it’s not a home appliance that can be hidden.

It’s self-cleaning; however, this operation is very loud. When I measured the process using the Decibel X app, I got readings between 60db and 75db. This is what I expect when I’m testing a blender. The self-cleaning on the Dreame H15 Pro Heat is much quieter.

The battery life of the Shark AquaReach Pro lasts for around an hour, which is around the same as the Dreame H15 Pro Heat, which has 72 minutes of cleaning time. And this would be good if I were only cleaning the hard floors in my home.

But that’s not all the AquaReach Pro is for. Since I can use it on all hard surfaces in my home because of the extendable arm and attachments, I needed more than an hour when using it for cleaning.

It also takes three hours to fully charge, and I felt like I was waiting around forever when I just wanted to get on with cleaning.

The Shark AquaReach Pro is a decent option if you have hard floors throughout your home. It has a cordless design, so you’re not limited by power outlets when cleaning, and it can reach into tight spaces with its smaller attachments. It effectively lifts grime, and the roller mop does a great job of agitating the stains on the floor to completely lift them.

However, there are awesome things I don’t love. The extendable hose looks clunky when in storage as it doesn’t retract, and the self-cleaning on the dock is very loud. The hour of battery life may also put you off when you can use it for so many jobs around your home that will certainly take longer than an hour to complete.

I’d recommend it for basic cleaning of floors and baseboards, but if you want something more heavy-duty for other areas of your home like the bathroom, I’d opt for something with a longer battery life.

#3420. Five Creative Ways to Spend Your FSA Funds Before the End of the Year

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), you know the drill: Use the funds before the end of the year, or lose them. Unfortunately, chances are slim you can pack the rest of the year with doctor's appointments. Does that mean your hard-earned funds go to waste? Definitely not. You can spend your remaining FSA funds on other qualifying healthcare costs. And what counts as "qualifying" might surprise you—for instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch.

As the end of the year approaches, here are all the ways you can spend any leftover money in your FSA balance.

Many over-the-counter medications and health items are FSA-eligible, including pain relievers, cold medicine, bandages, dental care products, menstrual products, and more. Scan your medicine cabinet and make a list of anything you need to stock up on.

FSA/HSA eligibility for smartwatches and other fitness wearables is real, but the main “catch" (as I’ve previously explained) is proving the device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN).

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. Similarly, smartwatches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does, as long as you can link a relevant documented health concern. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches.

If you want to get creative with it, the official FSA store lets you filter by "surprisingly eligible." Similar to the section above, for some of these items, you'll want to brush up on how exactly to get an LMN to justify certain tech as FSA-eligible for you personally. In the meantime, go crazy and snag yourself Epsom salt for $8.99, Supergoop! sunscreen for $38.00, or perhaps a snazzy massage gun for $349.99.

Knee braces, wrist splints, compression socks, and other orthopedic items can help relieve chronic pain issues. Rather than wait for these issues to rear their heads down the line, use FSA money to offset the costs of these fixes now. If you use eyeglasses or contacts, consider using your FSA dollars to update or refresh your prescriptions. Don't forget to stock up on eye drops and lens solution, too.

If you have medical procedures scheduled for early next year, many healthcare providers will allow you to pre-pay the estimated costs this calendar year using FSA funds. This includes dental work, physical therapy, chiropractic visits, Lasik eye surgery, and more.

However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste. After all, it came out of your paycheck. Check in with your employer’s rules for any balance remaining on Dec. 31 this year, so you aren’t left forfeiting your hard-earned funds. You can find a complete list at the FSA store here.

#3419. watchOS 27.3 beta adds new Siri Recap and Live Rewind features for Apple Watch

Apple has released the first beta of watchOS 27.3 for developers, including two new Audio Intelligence features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4: Siri Recap and Live Rewind.

Apple first announced these features at its special event in September, saying they would “arrive in beta later this year.”

As a refresher, Siri Recap creates high-level summaries of conversations that you can review later. When the feature is enabled, Apple Intelligence will automatically generate a title and key points that you can review in the Siri app on iPhone.

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Your summaries auto-delete after 7 days if you choose not to save them.

You can turn on Siri Recap in the Watch app on iPhone. When you enable it, you can set a schedule based on time and/or location, or you can manually turn it on or off. You can also access it via Control Center on Apple Watch.

Live Rewind, meanwhile, helps you recall what was just said in a conversation. You can activate Live Rewind by double-pressing the Digital Crown, and then see a transcript of the previous 15 seconds of a conversation.

Live Rewind recalls what was just said in the last 15 seconds by showing a text snippet on your Apple Watch when you double-press the Digital Crown, so you can catch something you missed or are less familiar with. You can ask Siri about the content of the snippet or simply save it to the Siri app.

Siri Recap’s summary is described as a “brief, high-level summary of conversations,” not a transcript. Apple says it will “exclude sensitive information like financial information or government-assigned identifiers.”

Live Rewind text snippets and Siri Recap summaries are end-to-end encrypted. Apple says the features “do not create or store audio recordings, and raw audio used for processing is completely inaccessible to the operating systems, apps, the user, or Apple.” The company uses the S11 chip’s Secure Exclave to power the features, a “dedicated hardware-isolated compartment that processes audio in complete isolation from the rest of the system, then immediately deletes it.”

Siri Recap and Live Rewind are available in beta with watchOS 27.3, which is available now for developers.

#3418. 10 Most Perfect Thriller Movies of All Time

One simply can't get enough of thriller movies. Fast-paced, heart-pounding, and packed with twists and surprises, the genre feeds off the reactions of audiences as they are pulled to the edge of their seats. A good thriller delivers suspense, but an excellent one reinvents classic thriller elements, all while staying relevant to the anxieties of the era it was released in.

Whether it's the effects of corporate culture, a rookie police officer taking on 30 levels of criminals, or a chef who's sick and tired of serving uppity patrons, these movies show that there's more than one way to deliver the adrenaline. That said, here are 10 intense thriller movies that are perfect from start to finish.

What happens when a revolutionary loses his spark? One Battle After Another introduces us to Bob Ferguson (Leonardo DiCaprio), a former demolition expert for a militant group who, 16 years later, has become a jaded single father to the teenage Willa (Chase Infiniti). But when a secret is revealed about Willa’s true origins, she goes off the grid, prompting the washed-up Bob to reignite the fire he once had.

One Battle After Another has the makings of a classic thriller. However, there is a refreshing comedic edge to him. Considering that he’s not as energetic and physically limber as he used to be, he falls and stumbles as he evades the cops. Bob can barely run without losing his breath, but with his daughter kidnapped, he’s not catching a break anytime soon.

Sinners refuses to be boxed into conventional thriller norms. When twin brothers Smoke and Stack (Michael B. Jordan) open a massive juke joint on the outskirts of town, the last thing they expect is for a group of vampires to crash the party. As the night wears on, these undead intruders begin turning the brothers’ human guests one by one.

Historical, breathtaking, and full of movement, Ryan Coogler has a knack for using horror to bring up broader themes like racial identity and systemic oppression. In Sinners, blues music serves as the voice of the marginalized, giving power to those who play it. Coogler goes one step further by portraying blues as a near-magical force that can literally open portals to the supernatural.

No other thriller has tested an audience’s perception of reality more than Oldboy. For reasons unknown, a drunken Oh Dae-su (Choi Min-sik) is abducted and imprisoned in a sealed room with no communication to the outside world. 15 years have passed, and the now disoriented Dae-su is suddenly returned to society — this time framed for the murder of his wife.

It’s mystery after mystery in Oldboy, but it all boils down to a hyper-specific revenge ploy. Sometimes, death is too swift and merciful a solution — although the movie does boast graphic scenes like the violent hallway fight. Instead, the most effective kind of revenge is one that twists a person’s cognition, leading them to make immoral decisions by their own doing.

Corporate gets cold-blooded in American Psycho. Although modern movies like The Wolf of Wall Street show the high-adrenaline rush from working in investment, Christian Bale’s performance as banker Patrick Bateman is much more polished and restrained — but even more deadly. A swanky apartment and a ridiculous salary aren’t enough to fill his empty void, prompting him to find alternative sources of pleasure.

Thus begins the true thesis of American Psycho — the rich aren’t devoid of feeling because they lack material wealth; it’s because they can’t appreciate what they have. Capitalism emphasizes the idea of having more. Unfortunately, the more Bateman tries to gain — whether status, money, or women — the less satisfaction he finds, until he finds something that cannot be bought: the ability to control whether someone lives or dies.

The only thing that’s separating a 20-man SWAT team and one crime lord in The Raid is a 30-story rundown apartment. But like Dante’s nine circles of hell, each level in the building is infested with all sorts of criminals. From drug dealers to machete-wielding killers, rookie officer Rama must conquer the threats on each floor before getting his hands on the feared underworld kingpin, Tama Riyadi.

There is a non-stop, relentless pace that drives The Raid from start to finish. The not-so-fun part about raiding a high-rise building is that there is practically no way of escaping. The hallways are tight and narrow, meaning that any criminal could just jump on Rama from whichever direction, amplifying the anxiety from being only literally one step away from being stabbed by a knife.

There's no knowing where a Quentin Tarantino thriller might go, and the in-your-face Inglourious Basterds is as unpredictable as they come. Lt. Aldo Raine (Brad Pitt) is responsible for his "Basterds," a crew of Jewish-American soldiers whose job is to infiltrate Nazi spaces and kill them. Somewhere in the French countryside, Shosanna Dreyfus (Mélanie Laurent) has a personal vendetta against the infamous "Jew Hunter," Hans Landa (Christoph Waltz).

Inglourious Basterds doesn’t skimp on the anxiety of being hunted like helpless prey, and much of that tension comes from Walt's performance as Landa. Widely regarded as one of cinema’s greatest villains, Waltz plays him as chillingly polite one moment and completely ruthless the next, especially when he suspects he has found a Jew in his presence.

In Parasite, the resourceful Ki-taek (Song Kang-ho) does everything he can to pull his Kim family out of their scrappy, cramped basement apartment. His luck changes when his son, Ki-woo (Choi Woo-shik), secures a tutoring position with the affluent Park family. With no proper qualifications, he sweet-talks his way into the job, gradually bringing the rest of his family into the Parks’ lives.

Parasite challenges the audience’s pre-existing notions about the rich versus the poor. While it may seem unethical for the Kim family to manipulate the Parks, they are simply doing what they can to achieve upward mobility. The Parks, on the other hand, appear kind because they have the resources to afford generosity. The film suggests that privilege itself enables the ability to be “nice.”

A weekend out of the city goes sideways in Get Out. Black photographer Chris Washington (Daniel Kaluuya) accepts an invitation from his white girlfriend, Rose Armitage (Allison Williams), to a family gathering at her home in the countryside. Unbeknownst to him, her parents have a horrifying pastime of hypnotizing and lobotomizing Black individuals as a vessel for immortality.

Get Out reimagines how modern-day slavery would take place. The scariest part is that, unlike in the past, with recorded accounts of white masters being viciously cruel, Rose’s family initially welcomes Chris with open arms. This sense of niceness — almost too nice — strikes a nerve, considering that Chris is the only Black person in the countryside with no outside communication.

Unlike Marco Pierre White and Gordon Ramsay, Chef Julian Slowik (Ralph Fiennes) is cool as a cucumber — the perfect facade to hide his taste for revenge in The Menu. Obnoxious food snob Tyler (Nicholas Hoult) takes his less-than-enthusiastic date Margot (Anya Taylor-Joy) to a group fine dining experience at Chef Julian's secluded island restaurant, only for the night to get bloody.

Despite the terror they face from the disillusioned Chef Julian, there’s something darkly funny about paying $1,250 per person only to end up getting killed. Then again, The Menu is about a service industry man’s attempt to get revenge on the entitled guests who have caused him to lose his passion for the simple joy of cooking. The wealthy will pay anything for an “experience,” and that is exactly what they’re going to get.

Nobody can trust anyone in The Handmaiden. Set in Japanese-occupied Korea in the 1930s, Sook-hee (Kim Tae-ri) is appointed as the loyal handmaiden to the Japanese heiress, Lady Hideko. Unlike the tales of cruel masters, Lady Hideko (Kim Min-hee) shows nothing but compassion to Sook-hee. Unbeknownst to them, the male powers shadowing over them plan to use them as pawns for material and colonial gains.

The Handmaiden is as much of a period piece and a forbidden romance as it is a thriller. Considering the context of the time, the two leading women, despite their class differences, are no less put into precarious positions. For all its sickening plot twists, the bond between Sook-he and Lady Hideko gives the thriller a strong sense of heart. After all, the two are only trying to escape from their oppression, even if that route requires manipulation.
